evidence.rubric:
# Public f35v motif comparison, fixed before opening the additional plates

Previously seen: Beinecke f35v, the black-ivy detail and Ethel Voynich oak-grape note reproduced on p. 24 of Zandbergen's 2012 slides, and full BnF latin 6823 f60r. Expected familiarity with ordinary silhouettes of the named plants. New comparator categories fixed using headings and documented plant names only. Use two compact Tractatus de herbis witnesses as available, Latin 6823 and Egerton 747, preferentially both witnesses per group. Seek the named black ivy and oak/gall tree, with three depicted alternatives (grape, elder and a lobed-leaf rooted herb, white bryony where catalogued). Where the requested entry has multiple drawings, retain all candidates or use separately illustrated entries if the source distinguishes them before viewing, rather than pick a nearest shape. Keep captions and neighboring plants outside the illustration where possible. When contours touch words, neutral mask the text without removing contours and log the exception. Record plates under shuffled codes before joining the identities. This is caption-masked, with one observer and incomplete blinding.

Use only outlines of the drawing: color may locate a contour, but it earns no points. For each feature use 1 visible, 0 visibly discordant or visibly missing on a complete plate, ? genuinely ambiguous or cropped. Record all 12 codes and matched count per region, with possible upper counts for unknowns. Equal weights; no hypothesis test. Describe where matches arise. Multiple manuscripts can transmit a drawing tradition, so report each witness without treating them as independent statistical draws.

Fruit (F)
F1. At least two discrete clusters of three or more rounded enclosed units, counting each unit once; scattered solitary fruits do not count.
F2. At least one such cluster terminates a distinct stalk, with recognizable grouping and no enclosing common fruit body or backing leaf.
F3. No acorn-like cup, enclosing husk, or lobed capsule around the rounded units; mark unknown if outlines are unreadable, zero if no rounded units.

Leaf (L)
L1. At least two individually outlined side leaves attach at distinct levels below the top foliage.
L2. Those side leaves are simple and visibly lobed, with at least two broad rounded lobes per side.
L3. The strongest lobing repeats along the long axis on both sides of the leaf; do not count a three- to five-point palmate leaf, a smooth small leaf, or individual leaflets along a rachis.

Crown/stems (C)
C1. A compact upper foliage outline distinguishable from lower lateral leaves or fruit.
C2. Multiple upward stalks fan toward that upper outline from a relatively narrow common point or band.
C3. Two lower lateral stems visibly cross in front of or around a distinct upright axis; a single fork without crossing does not count.

Roots (R)
R1. Clearly drawn roots and aerial stems meet at a common basal junction.
R2. Major lateral roots or primary branches bear at least three recognizable hooked or curved tips in aggregate.
R3. Strongly asymmetric lateral spread, roughly 2:1 or greater from the stem center measured against opposite side, with the longest root roughly horizontal for much of its run.

For a caption-free target, all 12 features are the prespecified matches; F2 and C3 will also be reported under a sensitivity analysis dropping either if attachment or topology proves uncertain on the scan. The rubric is target-conditioned, so results test specificity among documented controls, not identification in the abstract.
evidence.scoring_key: Per card and region, 1 is visible correspondence, 0 is absent or discordant, ? is obscured or ambiguous. Range counts definite to possible matches.
evidence.sensitivity: Dropping F2 changes fruit-perfect controls from 7 of 12 with 3/3 to the same 7 with 2/2. Dropping C3 preserves all control ranks because C3 is zero for every control. Dropping either criterion leaves the region split unchanged. Ignoring the side-leaf position requirement would raise the foliage match for Latin 6823 galla and glandes because the rounded lobes are visible elsewhere in their drawings.

detail.statement: An outline checklist applied to 12 caption-masked illustrations from three manuscripts in the Tractatus de herbis tradition gives full fruit scores to both black-ivy plates, both elder plates, one bryony plate and both Sloane grape views. The Egerton galla tree best reproduces the combination of offset rounded-lobed side leaves and compact crown. BnF galla and glandes also carry rounded lobing, with cupped fruits on all three oak plates. No comparator visibly meets the doubled aerial crossing or hooked, strongly asymmetric root criteria, and all match at most seven of the 12 features even if uncertain features count as matches. The black-ivy fruit parallel and oak foliage parallel are regional correspondences, with insufficient specificity for a botanical anchor.

Use only outlines of the drawing: color may locate a contour, but it earns no points. For each feature use 1 visible, 0 visibly discordant or visibly missing on a complete plate, ? genuinely ambiguous or cropped. Record all 12 codes and matched count per region, with possible upper counts for unknowns. Equal weights; no hypothesis test. Describe where matches arise. Multiple manuscripts can transmit a drawing tradition, so report each witness without treating them as independent statistical draws.

Fruit (F)
F1. At least two discrete clusters of three or more rounded enclosed units, counting each unit once; scattered solitary fruits do not count.
F2. At least one such cluster terminates a distinct stalk, with recognizable grouping and no enclosing common fruit body or backing leaf.
F3. No acorn-like cup, enclosing husk, or lobed capsule around the rounded units; mark unknown if outlines are unreadable, zero if no rounded units.

Leaf (L)
L1. At least two individually outlined side leaves attach at distinct levels below the top foliage.
L2. Those side leaves are simple and visibly lobed, with at least two broad rounded lobes per side.
L3. The strongest lobing repeats along the long axis on both sides of the leaf; do not count a three- to five-point palmate leaf, a smooth small leaf, or individual leaflets along a rachis.

Crown/stems (C)
C1. A compact upper foliage outline distinguishable from lower lateral leaves or fruit.
C2. Multiple upward stalks fan toward that upper outline from a relatively narrow common point or band.
C3. Two lower lateral stems visibly cross in front of or around a distinct upright axis; a single fork without crossing does not count.

Roots (R)
R1. Clearly drawn roots and aerial stems meet at a common basal junction.
R2. Major lateral roots or primary branches bear at least three recognizable hooked or curved tips in aggregate.
R3. Strongly asymmetric lateral spread, roughly 2:1 or greater from the stem center measured against opposite side, with the longest root roughly horizontal for much of its run.

For a caption-free target, all 12 features are the prespecified matches; F2 and C3 will also be reported under a sensitivity analysis dropping either if attachment or topology proves uncertain on the scan. The rubric is target-conditioned, so results test specificity among documented controls, not identification in the abstract.
evidence.scoring_key: Per card and region, 1 is visible correspondence, 0 is absent or discordant, ? is obscured or ambiguous. Range counts definite to possible matches.
evidence.sensitivity: Dropping F2 changes fruit-perfect controls from 7 of 12 with 3/3 to the same 7 with 2/2. Dropping C3 preserves all control ranks because C3 is zero for every control. Dropping either criterion leaves the region split unchanged. Ignoring the side-leaf position requirement would raise the foliage match for Latin 6823 galla and glandes because the rounded lobes are visible elsewhere in their drawings.

step.json.statement: An outline checklist applied to 12 caption-masked illustrations from three manuscripts in the Tractatus de herbis tradition gives full fruit scores to both black-ivy plates, both elder plates, one bryony plate and both Sloane grape views. The Egerton galla tree best reproduces the combination of offset rounded-lobed side leaves and compact crown. BnF galla and glandes also carry rounded lobing, with cupped fruits on all three oak plates. No comparator visibly meets the doubled aerial crossing or hooked, strongly asymmetric root criteria, and all match at most seven of the 12 features even if uncertain features count as matches. The black-ivy fruit parallel and oak foliage parallel are regional correspondences, with insufficient specificity for a botanical anchor.

detail.statement: fleet-fable's corrections settle the generator front for now: a chain with one glyph table and no drift, with whole-word reuse from a memory of 300 words, meets all 17 established facts as a whole book (P-G-007), and one table and one memory per dialect reaches the A/B dialect contrast (P-G-009), the last long-range target we had. Two code changes for the attack layout are in review with different trade-offs: fleet-fable's lays a whole book onto every manuscript page (keeps page order, but a writer can tune text to each position), fleet-opus's draws book pages at random (nothing can be tuned to a page, but the book's order is not the manuscript's); a reviewer should pick one, not both. Next, in order: anchors, where a word can be tied to something outside the text (a label beside a drawn object, with exposure-screened annotators, P-L4-006); the invented-language test only if it predicts something a copying procedure does not; and an end to registering text-statistic facts unless the author first shows that a one-table reuse chain misses them.

detail.statement: The catalogue accurately describes the scope and limits of Ardıç’s 2025 Turkish article. The comparison itself is exhibit-based, with selected examples on pp. 87–90, and p. 90 n. 22 points to a companion interpretation for a complete sentence. P. 80 n. 14 points to a separate, explicitly unfinished ATA table. Its methodological notes 5–8 retain alternatives, permit an exception to consistent one-to-one assignment for harmony, acknowledge omitted characters, and say that old and revised values can appear together. Row 10 also relies on an illustrated bridge traversal order. The separate f33v proceedings article, version pp. 15–16, proposes distinct endings for the first line and displays slash-separated alternatives at five of the seven positions of the first-line transliteration. Taking those alternatives literally gives 108 combinations before applying contextual constraints. These examples document the discretion a fixed, independently reproducible projection would need to resolve.

detail.check: Compare a further annotator's features and first guesses for f42v and f56r with these, before reading either annotator's names; the feature lists, not the names, are the part to agree on.
detail.statement: Second, separate annotator for fleet-sol's P-L4-006 panels, as its check asks. Exposure logged before viewing: I knew Tucker and Talbert's taxa for f5v, f6v, f9r, f24r, f25r, f32r (pilot), f13r, f23v, f30v, f45r (my P-L4-005 round), and I saw the candidates for f36v and f23r when reading the step, so I annotated only f42v and f56r, extracting their folio and canvas ids by script without the names, and had no prior knowledge of a proposal for either. I wrote features and a guess for each on the Yale scans (canvases 1006157 and 1006184) before printing the candidates. f42v: a whorl of about eight broad untoothed lanceolate leaves at mid-stem, a single bare stem ending in one pale yellow star-shaped flower with a dark eye-like centre and spiky rays, sparse brown fibrous roots; guess an Ornithogalum-like Asparagaceae or Gentiana lutea. f56r: one pale stem; two lower branches ending in dark blue rounded bodies fringed by green spiny bracts; above, two blue funnel-shaped flowers and a large coiled branch with paired dark-blue lanceolate leaflets; a braided base; guess Convolvulaceae for the funnel flowers, with the spiny heads suggesting Asteraceae (Cynareae). Reveal: f42v, Tucker and Talbert propose Calathea (Goeppertia) loeseneri, Marantaceae; fleet-sol's masked guess was Paris, Melanthiaceae; mine disagrees with both. f56r, they propose Phacelia campanularia, Boraginaceae in the broad sense; fleet-sol's masked guess Heliotropium agrees with that family; mine (Convolvulaceae) does not, though I recorded the coiled branch that carries the Boraginaceae reading. Features agree better than names: both annotators recorded the star-like terminal structure with a dark centre on f42v and the coiled branch with dark bodies and two dark corollas on f56r. Summary across the masked rounds so far (pilot, P-L4-005, P-L4-006): independent genus or family agreement with the proposed taxa is rare outside the two most published folios, and two annotators rarely agree with each other at family level, so these drawings do not carry enough diagnostic detail to support an anchor at genus level, New World or Old. No anchor follows.

detail.check: To repeat the audit, implement the circular recurrence interval exactly and count adjacent identical types and repeated ordered pairs separately. Predeclare the transliteration, line inclusion, seam handling, metrics, and structured controls, then test whole-token, within-page and within-line permutations. Evaluate the metrics jointly against independent realizations and natural texts before making any claim about the source of the local order signal.

evidence.generators: Pinned vs.generators.g_self_citation and g_grille use the public fit pages. Six additional one-table whole-word-reuse backgrounds use the stationary copy condition of P-R-009/P-J-005 fitted on the public fit pages, with no edit reuse or time drift. The stationary iid and piecewise iid controls have 1,536 possible abstract tokens and Zipf weights proportional to rank^-0.9. In the piecewise case six independent probability vectors each blend 70% randomly permuted Zipf weights and 30% original weights and are assigned to six consecutive equal-page-count groups by floor(6i/P) for zero-based page i. The iid token drawings are independent conditional on the probability vector, so they contain no local transition rule. Generator seeds 901–908, stationary-copy seeds 901–906, iid seeds 901–924.
evidence.input: The public practice Zandbergen–Landini and independent Takahashi transcriptions were intersected on 615 paragraph-line IDs with all tokens certain and in the fixed ordinary EVA letters acdefghiklmnopqrsty. The sample occupies 31 public practice pages. The page and line order of the retained primary lines was kept. Natural controls are contiguous windows with the same token count, sampled using Random(901) from the named pinned works and cut to identical line lengths. These are length-matched illustrations, without a genre or writing-system match. The article’s full manuscript and original corpora are distinct from this layout.
evidence.limitations: Topology measures beyond the explicit degree and selectivity implementations, the approach to language ranking, and the paper’s compatibility density estimates were outside scope. Single windows from four books do not reproduce its language reference distribution. Generated texts illustrate multiple mechanisms behind a rejection. A match to a direction or a null rejection can occur with materially different effect sizes.
evidence.method: Primary ratios use observed metric divided by the permutation mean. The longer manuscript run uses 999 permutations at each of the global, page and line levels, independently in both editions, fixed NumPy seed 98900 plus 100 per successive null. Each two-sided P is twice the smaller add-one tail probability clipped at one, counting ties in each tail. Holm adjusted values cover seven metrics within each edition and each null. The adjacency sensitivity excludes between-line edges on every permutation. I and I50 in that check are unchanged because time still runs across the retained token sequence. Simulations and natural controls use 99 permutations, with unadjusted rejection counts provided only as calibration summaries. All input distinctions are fixed across permutations.

metric_details.B_pairs: Alternate literal reading of duplicated bigrams, the number of ordered adjacent pairs occurring at least twice regardless of whether the two tokens are the same type.
metric_details.B_types: Distinct types with at least one self-adjacency, the literal definition in the first-order Statistics section on p. 7. Table 1 labels B Betweenness and the compatibility prose says duplicated bigrams.
metric_details.I: Mean over word types of frequency at least 5 of population SD of the circular recurrence gaps divided by their mean. Eq. 6 closes the boundary gap so each type’s gaps sum to the stream duration.
metric_details.I50: As for I over the top 50 by count, lexically breaking frequency ties.
metric_details.k_out: Mean distinct outgoing neighbors on the directed adjacency graph described in Methods, retaining a self-loop when present. With fixed length and vocabulary, k_out is directly related to total repeated-edge surplus.
metric_details.s: Mean of twice word count divided by the number of distinct neighbors in either direction, as in Methods. For the seam-exclusion check the convention is to use a denominator of one for a type isolated by removing line boundaries.
metric_details.s50: s over the 50 most frequent types.

evidence.publication_scope: Table 3 reports observed/shuffled mean ratios 1.433 (I), 1.890 (I*), 2.637 (B), and 0.949 (k). Its C* interval 0.981–1.017 is the only displayed one that includes 1. The prose on p. 5 says the other intervals include it, whereas Table 3 and the argument require exclude. The authors report B and I* as exceptions to the comparisons with their natural-language distribution in Table 4. They explicitly propose topic shifts as one reason for increased I*. The authors used ten global shuffles and Eq. 8 error bands. This audit uses permutation tails. Hence its P values cannot be compared numerically to their standardized distances. The article makes no deterministic glyph or language assignment that can be entered as a key.

detail.statement: Amancio et al.’s reported excess intermittency against global token shuffles is reproduced qualitatively in two public practice editions. All 24 independent page-conditional token streams per layout also exceed that null for both intermittency summaries. Preserving each page’s vocabulary and frequencies reduces the Voynich ratios to 1.005–1.016 and removes significance in both editions. Repeated distinct ordered pairs and reduced directed degree remain after line shuffles and after excluding cross-line adjacency. Pinned self-citation and a stationary one-table reuse chain also depart from the line-preserving null on these metrics, with different effect sizes. The result limits the evidential scope of global shuffles and identifies a residual local order signal for comparisons between specified generators.

attack.json.method: The codebook enumerates the fixed WORD_MAP plus every possible output of decode_token at commit ba3ffea6d517721b389e22af3a67f78db3674e73. Direct entries take precedence, followed by the published no-qo variant and then the k, p, op and t prefix expansions. Entries were expanded from the published finite stem inventory alone. Unknown tokens emit no Italian, matching the reader’s unknown marker. The claim runner uses Zandbergen–Landini EVA, while the author’s reader uses Takahashi EVA. This audit covers the published token resolver and the proposed Italian target. The compiled table agreed with the published function on all 969 generated parity probes, including unknown tokens and prefix collisions. An additional public practice evaluation on Takahashi returned the same five failing checks as Zandbergen–Landini.

Each two-sided P is twice the smaller add-one tail probability clipped at one, counting ties in each tail. Holm adjusted values cover seven metrics within each edition and each null. The adjacency sensitivity excludes between-line edges on every permutation. I and I50 in that check are unchanged because time still runs across the retained token sequence. Simulations and natural controls use 99 permutations, with unadjusted rejection counts provided only as calibration summaries. All input distinctions are fixed across permutations.

metric_details.B_pairs: Alternate literal reading of duplicated bigrams, the number of ordered adjacent pairs occurring at least twice regardless of whether the two tokens are the same type.
metric_details.B_types: Distinct types with at least one self-adjacency, the literal definition in the first-order Statistics section on p. 7. Table 1 labels B Betweenness and the compatibility prose says duplicated bigrams.
metric_details.I: Mean over word types of frequency at least 5 of population SD of the circular recurrence gaps divided by their mean. Eq. 6 closes the boundary gap so each type’s gaps sum to the stream duration.
metric_details.I50: As for I over the top 50 by count, lexically breaking frequency ties.
metric_details.k_out: Mean distinct outgoing neighbors on the directed adjacency graph described in Methods, retaining a self-loop when present. With fixed length and vocabulary, k_out is directly related to total repeated-edge surplus.
metric_details.s: Mean of twice word count divided by the number of distinct neighbors in either direction, as in Methods. For the seam-exclusion check the convention is to use a denominator of one for a type isolated by removing line boundaries.
metric_details.s50: s over the 50 most frequent types.

evidence.publication_scope: Table 3 reports observed/shuffled mean ratios 1.433 (I), 1.890 (I*), 2.637 (B), and 0.949 (k). Its C* interval 0.981–1.017 is the only displayed one that includes 1. The prose on p. 5 says the other intervals include it, whereas Table 3 and the argument require exclude. The authors report B and I* as exceptions to the comparisons with their natural-language distribution in Table 4. They explicitly propose topic shifts as one reason for increased I*. The authors used ten global shuffles and Eq. 8 error bands. This audit uses permutation tails. Hence its P values cannot be compared numerically to their standardized distances. The article makes no deterministic glyph or language assignment that can be entered as a key.

step.json.statement: Amancio et al.’s reported excess intermittency against global token shuffles is reproduced qualitatively in two public practice editions. All 24 independent page-conditional token streams per layout also exceed that null for both intermittency summaries. Preserving each page’s vocabulary and frequencies reduces the Voynich ratios to 1.005–1.016 and removes significance in both editions. Repeated distinct ordered pairs and reduced directed degree remain after line shuffles and after excluding cross-line adjacency. Pinned self-citation and a stationary one-table reuse chain also depart from the line-preserving null on these metrics, with different effect sizes. The result limits the evidential scope of global shuffles and identifies a residual local order signal for comparisons between specified generators.

established: Stolfi sees a comparatively flat head, small rays, visible bract-like details and diagonal stalks as possible similarities. He reports that only one of the three heads has the flat form and that the large central disk is a weaker match for wild sunflowers.

He describes the manuscript leaves as radially divided, with rounded tips and an apparently central petiole attachment. His sunflower comparators have a heart- or spade-shaped undivided blade and an edge attachment. He reports a further difference in the disk texture and grounds his rejection chiefly on the leaf morphology.

Jerusalem artichoke gives an analogy for the enlarged underground structures, with differences in shape, proportion and leaf attachment. Stolfi leaves wider Asteraceae affinity open and observes that the family is not geographically diagnostic.

evidence.alignment: For each homologous pair, take the highest exact score and the highest fuzzy score over all rotations of the second ring in each direction. The ordinal view compares the first min(n,m) positions. The primary equal-arc view compares the midpoints of min(n,m) equal fractions of a ring by projecting each midpoint to both respective slot counts using floor, then advances the second ring through all of its rotations. The method uses ordinal ranks as geometry proxies and makes no claim of exact angular equality. Sensitivity comparisons apply literal clock sorting of the locally anomalous Libra block, or include all full rings on different panels.
evidence.inputs: The pinned ZL3b-n.txt, IT2a-n.txt and RF1b-e.txt contain the same 12 Zodiac panels. P-L4-007 flattens label words per panel, producing 350 ZL words, 367 Takahashi words and 343 RF words. The same set of physical Lz identifiers is used when moving to a locus-level test. Alternatives are parsed according to vs.ivtff and uncertain spaces split.
evidence.interpretation: The exploratory IT flattened exact result varies across editions and loses significance when the comparison uses physical rings and whole labels. Label meanings remain open. The assay can miss a roster if ring segmentation varies by sign, if corresponding slots are displaced by unequal gaps, or if the same category uses divergent word forms.
evidence.legacy_method: For each pair i<j in the supplied order, score the prefix overlap at equal ordinal positions. To optimize alignment, cyclically rotate j by each offset, then truncate the two sequences to the shorter length and sum exact or at-most-one raw EVA character edit matches. Use the best per pair and sum across the 66 pairs. The sensitivity also permits rotating i individually. The original reports 41 and 115; our explicit convention gives 40 and 110. Allowing either side gives 40 and 117. The sample and the unchanged 0.1787% original exact-match fraction are reproducible; the exact optimum depends on unequal-length conventions and the edit unit.
evidence.null_and_power: Use NumPy RNG seed 61304 and 999 permutations. Shuffle labels independently within the applicable page or ring, with missing ring slots fixed. P is the upper-tail add-one rank with ties. For power, use 24 seeds 2401–2424 and 199 shuffles per simulated instance. For each full-ring group independently choose k positions in its shortest ring and project to each ring by the same fractional construction. Rotate each ring’s planted positions independently, keep the original unknowns, then substitute one distinct shared pseudolabel per position where available. Test exact agreement for the same main comparison. Sign-dependent renamings, variable mappings between ring layers and hypotheses with just one stable position are outside this power result.

evidence.ring_method: Interpret each ZL @Lz group as one block of labels following the scan and ZL ring headers. Keep the innermost and outermost full figure rings as separate comparison groups. Cancer has a middle full ring with no primary homologous partner. Exclude four groups from primary comparisons: the Pisces central star and the Gemini, Scorpius and Sagittarius partial rows. One full-locus label joins all its words with an explicit separator. The first-word view retains just its first token. Both are segmented with EVA-basic and label loci containing uncertain or absent tokens retain their geometric slot as a missing observation. Missing observations never match, including another missing observation. Fuzzy similarity is at most one insertion, deletion or substitution of an EVA-basic unit.

Four figures above the outer ring form a separate partial group; the full rings remain distinct.

detail.statement: The pooled ZL page test reproduces 0.18% exact same-position agreement and gives 40 exact and 110 one-edit agreements after optimizing rotation across 66 pairs. Its 999-permutation P values are 0.246 and 0.312. Takahashi’s flattened exact-word result is nominally unusual at P=0.016 but moves to P=0.081 when the shorter and longer page can each be rotated. The historical layouts contain distinct rings and some partial rows. Using 285 figure-label loci and comparing equal ring positions under independent rotations and both relative directions, the exact whole-label P values are 0.887, 0.846 and 0.899 across the three editions. Planting two repeated positions in both full-ring groups gives detections in 24 of 24 simulations, while one repeated position gives 0 of 24. The result weighs against a broadly shared ordered roster that uses the same visible labels at comparable positions across the rings.

# P-L4-002 geometry and ordered-feature check

Past exposure: f69v and the two Bodleian lunar mansion pages, and chapter II opening of the Greater Bundahišn while cataloguing Herrmann. This pass scores by fixed criteria with source-aware preparation and one observer. Three manuscript editions are frozen before retrieving the comparator name lists. Preserve one radial locus per green-ended bar in clockwise ZL locus order. Compare candidate lists in official source order, with all 28 rotations and both directions. No fit of source-specific glyph values. All 28 supports known from previous exposure. The prior has no public mapping for the 20 reported correspondences.

Order-sensitive measures fixed before source extraction. First-symbol equality pattern is a binary partition of the 378 unordered pairs of index positions. Score the Pearson correlation of the manuscript and comparator partitions, maximizing over the identical 56 alignments. A constant vector is uninformative. Use both Arabic orthographic names with articles and bare names stripping only an explicitly specified Arabic definite article (or Latin spellings that directly render it when the edition makes this possible). Report alternative treatment as sensitivity. Phrase lengths count retained glyphs across the locus. Compare normalized average ranks to the comparator's normalized grapheme counts, taking the positive Pearson correlation maximum over the same alignments. Word boundaries, diacritics and source-specific digraphs are conventions to record. Test both scores independently against 3,999 whole-name shuffles of the comparator, holding names with their grapheme counts and initials intact. Treat the families of views as exploratory. Include fixed random-prefix controls and an exact circular rotation positive check. Match the source-label count, per-letter class sizes and lengths through name permutations, with no weight for the shared count of 28.

Visual checks fixed before retrieving additional plate images. Record one visible legend or text group per sector, regularly alternating radial styles, radial separators making enclosed compartments, isolated star groups with variable dot counts, identifiable grouping marks at a different level and a fixed start cue. List unknown where any region is missing or not shown in a documentary text witness. Caption masks are meaningful for images that can be paired to the same criteria. The already recognized Voynich and Bodleian pages provide no independent blinded evaluation of provenance.

Scope: these are structural comparisons applicable only to hypotheses that preserve some first-symbol grouping or length order. No text interpretation and no anchor unless a separately frozen per-slot prediction gains external corroboration.
evidence.scope: This is one-source-aware-observer work with no independent blind annotator. The historical signals are conditional on simple length or first-class preservation. The six spellings or lists and two scores per edition were exploratory, and the three transcriptions represent the same manuscript. The Henry Bate prose and quarter tests followed the initial finding. A result at the table-selected fixed shift does not substitute for an independent fixation of the shift.
evidence.score_details: Compute the Pearson correlation between the 378-element binary equality vectors for initial-class membership, and separately between the average-rank length vectors. A missing RF locus excludes the relevant point and all its initial-class pairs. Candidate length ranks are computed on the complete witness before applying the RF mask. For each score maximize over 56 alignments. Forward index k maps manuscript position i to source (i+k) modulo 28. Reverse index k maps i to 27-((i+k) modulo 28). Thus reverse index 5 maps f69v.4 to the table’s 23rd entry. NumPy random seed 69128 and 3,999 whole-name permutations hold the letter class and length of each candidate entry together. Ties count in the upper tail and the reported P adds one to its numerator and denominator.

source_tables.normalization: Use the ordered printed names as transcribed into the English translation. Count Roman letters and strip spaces or hyphens. This is a spelling witness, with no claim that the editor reproduces medieval Pahlavi letter counts.

source_tables.locus: Al-Farghānī, Golius 1669 edition, printed Arabic pp. 77–79 (LOC scan pages 49–50)
source_tables.normalization: Use head terms and their immediate lexical modifiers, omitting glosses and alternative names. Keep unpointed Arabic letters, treating hamza-bearing letters as one each. Sensitivity removes a leading written definite article from the first word only.

source_tables.locus: Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī, al-Muʿīniyya II.3[11], Ragep et al. English translation p. 45
source_tables.normalization: The reported Arabic nomenclature appears in a Persian astronomical work. Use the translation’s romanized terms as printed. Strip combining marks, preserve ʿ and ʾ, count sh, gh, dh, th and kh as single graphemes, and count the written connector in phrases.

source_tables.locus: Sela et al. 2020 edition of Pal. lat. 1407, chapter 5.2 prose pp. 247–248 and table pp. 249–250
source_tables.normalization: Use only the first edited name on each of 28 numbered lines, without editorial apparatus or Latin glosses. Count letters and keep letters restored by the editors. The table supplies the primary Latin list. Remove initial al in one mechanical sensitivity. Many of these Latin manuscript names render Arabic terms, so language of the witness and origin of the names are distinct.

detail.statement: The Yale scan has 28 labeled radial loci and 28 green-ended bars in alternating dark and pale styles. Two known historical mansion diagrams use different arrangements of sectors and celestial signs. Under 56 circular alignments, neither the Bundahishn names nor the two Arabic nomenclature witnesses have unexpectedly ordered initials or lengths in the two complete transcriptions. The Henry Bate Latin table gives a nominal length-rank association of 0.637 to 0.685 in three transcriptions, with the same reverse alignment and P values 0.011, 0.005 and 0.01325. Conditioning on four quarters of seven weakens it. The adjacent Latin prose list reaches its own maximum at a shift two slots away. Across the twelve planned scores per edition the smallest Holm-adjusted P is 0.060. The length result is exploratory, with no independent starting cue or name correspondence.

The six spellings or lists and two scores per edition were exploratory, and the three transcriptions represent the same manuscript. The Henry Bate prose and quarter tests followed the initial finding. A result at the table-selected fixed shift does not substitute for an independent fixation of the shift.
evidence.score_details: Compute the Pearson correlation between the 378-element binary equality vectors for initial-class membership, and separately between the average-rank length vectors. A missing RF locus excludes the relevant point and all its initial-class pairs. Candidate length ranks are computed on the complete witness before applying the RF mask. For each score maximize over 56 alignments. Forward index k maps manuscript position i to source (i+k) modulo 28. Reverse index k maps i to 27-((i+k) modulo 28). Thus reverse index 5 maps f69v.4 to the table’s 23rd entry. NumPy random seed 69128 and 3,999 whole-name permutations hold the letter class and length of each candidate entry together. Ties count in the upper tail and the reported P adds one to its numerator and denominator.

source_tables.locus: Greater Bundahišn II.2, Anklesaria names in Peterson’s digital edition
source_tables.normalization: Use the ordered printed names as transcribed into the English translation. Count Roman letters and strip spaces or hyphens. This is a spelling witness, with no claim that the editor reproduces medieval Pahlavi letter counts.

source_tables.locus: Al-Farghānī, Golius 1669 edition, printed Arabic pp. 77–79 (LOC scan pages 49–50)
source_tables.normalization: Use head terms and their immediate lexical modifiers, omitting glosses and alternative names. Keep unpointed Arabic letters, treating hamza-bearing letters as one each. Sensitivity removes a leading written definite article from the first word only.

source_tables.locus: Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī, al-Muʿīniyya II.3[11], Ragep et al. English translation p. 45
source_tables.normalization: The reported Arabic nomenclature appears in a Persian astronomical work. Use the translation’s romanized terms as printed. Strip combining marks, preserve ʿ and ʾ, count sh, gh, dh, th and kh as single graphemes, and count the written connector in phrases.

source_tables.locus: Sela et al. 2020 edition of Pal. lat. 1407, chapter 5.2 prose pp. 247–248 and table pp. 249–250
source_tables.normalization: Use only the first edited name on each of 28 numbered lines, without editorial apparatus or Latin glosses. Count letters and keep letters restored by the editors. The table supplies the primary Latin list. Remove initial al in one mechanical sensitivity. Many of these Latin manuscript names render Arabic terms, so language of the witness and origin of the names are distinct.

step.json.statement: The Yale scan has 28 labeled radial loci and 28 green-ended bars in alternating dark and pale styles. Two known historical mansion diagrams use different arrangements of sectors and celestial signs. Under 56 circular alignments, neither the Bundahishn names nor the two Arabic nomenclature witnesses have unexpectedly ordered initials or lengths in the two complete transcriptions. The Henry Bate Latin table gives a nominal length-rank association of 0.637 to 0.685 in three transcriptions, with the same reverse alignment and P values 0.011, 0.005 and 0.01325. Conditioning on four quarters of seven weakens it. The adjacent Latin prose list reaches its own maximum at a shift two slots away. Across the twelve planned scores per edition the smallest Holm-adjusted P is 0.060. The length result is exploratory, with no independent starting cue or name correspondence.

detail.check: Lay any whole-book text with the practice draw of code-P-G-007-fleet-opus and count lines that land on more than one evaluation page; it should be zero after the fix.
detail.statement: Two code changes in review give attacks a whole-book layout under the same name (cut book): mine (branch code-R-book-cut-fleet-fable: the text is laid onto every page of the manuscript in order and measured on the evaluation pages) and fleet-opus's (branch code-P-G-007-fleet-opus: the attacker sends a book of at least 226 pages, the scorer draws one book page per evaluation page, in book order, and each evaluation page reads on from its drawn page). P-LEAD-013 asks a reviewer to pick one. I ran the same three one-table texts of the P-G-007 correction through both on the practice split, to see whether the choice changes a verdict. It does. In my layout all 17 established facts hold on 3 of 3 seeds; in the random-draw layout (book cut into pages of 19 lines, the largest that keeps 226 pages inside the 512 KiB limit for a text of this size; paragraph-opening lines spread evenly) F-014, the share of word types occurring once, fails on 2 of 3 seeds and the rest hold. Cause, checked by counting: an evaluation page longer than the attacker's book page reads on into the following book pages, and when the next evaluation page drew one of those, both receive the same lines. On the practice draw two of the 34 evaluation pages run into the next drawn page, and about 50 of the 821 lines laid (6%) are laid twice (21 lines, 2.6%, with pages of 23 lines; my count takes every line from the ordinary stream, so it is approximate). Repeated stretches lower the singleton share, which is what F-014 measures, and they must also raise page-to-page similarity and reuse for the pages involved, which favours an attacker on F-009, F-011 and F-016; so the defect cuts both ways and is not a matter of taste between the two designs. An attacker cannot avoid it: book pages long enough for the longest manuscript pages would put a 226-page book far over the size limit. Fix within that design: draw the pages as now, but let each evaluation page read from where the previous one stopped if that is later than its own drawn page (never the same line twice). What I have not checked: the held-out draw (it comes from the season seed), other page sizes, and whether F-014 still fails once lines are not repeated. On the difference that is a matter of judgement, as P-LEAD-013 puts it: in my layout a procedure can fit its text to a position in the book (the drifting window and the per-dialect tables do exactly that); in the random-draw layout it cannot, and position still roughly follows book order. Either is defensible; the one-table text needs neither. Nothing here is scored on hidden pages.

model.json.statement: Components were chosen by greedy forward selection under 4-fold cross-validation over scribe 1's public training pages only (pool: vocab, chain, position, letters order 2-5, copy windows 3/5/10/20/50 with 0 or 1 edits, templates prefix 0-3 x suffix 0-3), stopping when a component gained under 0.002 bits per word. Cross-validated: 11.31 bits per word against 11.75 for the bag of words and 11.40 for glyph trigrams alone. The same search run separately on scribes 2, 3 and 4 and on the whole text picked the same core every time (letters order 3 first; copy with a wide window; position; templates), with cross-validated gains over the bag of 0.39, 0.39, 0.58 and 0.38 bits per word; scribe 5 has too few training words. In every scope most of the gain is glyph trigrams alone, the word-to-word chain is selected late or never (under 0.01 bits per word), and the memorized vocabulary is never selected once letters order 3 is in. Negative side: nothing in the current component language gets much below a glyph trigram model (0.04 to 0.16 bits per word), so a production process is not yet separated from spelling habit.
model.json.title: Scribe 1: glyph trigrams + page-local copy (window 50, exact and one-glyph-changed) + line position + prefix templates + chain

ratings.note: Two fully exposed scale fields and a partly hidden third. Pale central marks suggest axial attachment but painted overlap prevents tracing it. Three separate round disks on sparsely branching roots.
Dotted tapered head with short marginal strokes. Broad smooth arcs in near pairs and many bare thin strands below the join.
Patterned mature head plus a bud. Basal lamina joins, one dominant curved root.
Patterned oval head and short narrow edge. Soil line without an exposed root system.
Separate fruit and flower spikes. Star-shaped broad blades, center attachments and mostly thick branching roots.
Two heads with radially spreading blades and no clearly textured central field. Narrow leaves and thin rootlets off one axis.
Dense rounded disc. Overlapping exterior leaf and head margins complicate blade lengths and leaf joints. Exposed thin roots.
Multiple rounded heads. Repeated long blades, low detail center and thin fibrous roots.
Basal rosette with several long-stemmed heads. Center detail uncertain at this scale.
Several clusters of separate small flowers. Several leaves appear attached inside the margin. A round basal knot with many filaments.
Many oval textured heads with spines rather than blades. Clearly paired leaves and many slender branches below the root join.
Reproductive head not depicted. Deep divisions follow one axis per blade. Dominant long roots with sparse thin branches and no round knot.

detail.record:
# Two sunflower proposals, two different figures

Ardıç proposes a sunflower on f33v. Stolfi's institutional note compares f33v with sunflower, including leaf attachment and the round underground objects, and prefers another possibility. Janick's published sunflower iconography reproduces **f93r**, cites O'Neill's earlier proposal and describes the single stalk and large seed head with suggestions of rays. These are two different folios. The claims are documented in the open [Ardıç companion](https://www.turkicresearch.com/Research/SubPages/Voynich), [Stolfi note](https://www.ic.unicamp.br/en/~stolfi/EXPORT/voynich/98-01-17-sunflower/) and [Janick 2020, pp. 1123–1125, figs. 9 and 11](https://www.notulaebotanicae.ro/index.php/nbha/article/download/12015/8986/48289).

## Scans and method

[Beinecke f33v](https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006139) and [Beinecke f93r](https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006238) are the public target scans. Load the corresponding Yale IIIF image IDs at 1200 px wide. The botanical cards are public-domain historical illustrations, shown by open sites. The Dodoens sunflower and both Voynich targets were known before the rubric. I fixed the eight control categories and twelve binary features before viewing the newly sourced prints. I prepared the crops, saw the full pages while doing so, and scored the shuffled grayscale cards. Masking removed the captions from the comparison views. My visual recognition and memory of the sources could still affect the scores. The work has one observer.

Features apply to the drawings as depicted. The head criteria are a densely patterned central field, distinct peripheral blades at least a quarter of the field's transverse width, a rounded outline of that field as opposed to a tapered silhouette, and a single terminal head on the plant. Buds on separate terminals count as evidence of multiple heads. In a spray of separate flowers without a shared field, the first three criteria are uncertain. Leaves are scored for a broad blade, obvious lobes or divisions, at least three major ridges spreading radially, an illustrated stalk–blade join visibly inside the margin, and a repeated opposite or near-opposite arrangement. Roots are scored for an exposed drawing below the stem join, many thin filaments and bounded round bulbs or knots. Compare agreement on known features and retain all uncertain comparisons. Color, relative figure size and dates carry no score.

The Yale f33v head fields are oval despite their perspective. The pale central marks on its leaves hint at a center attachment. The painted overlap makes the exact join and radial ridges uncertain. The three round objects visibly connect to branching underground strands. The dotted head on f93r has a tapered outline and short marginal strokes under the blade-length criterion. Its near-paired leaves are smooth curved arcs. The root join opens into many thin filaments. The paler form near the manuscript text was excluded as possible show-through.

## Comparison cards

Crop bounds and caption-mask coordinates in `cards.json` are pixels in the original downloads, in left, top, right, bottom order. Convert to grayscale, paint mask rectangles gray (245 of 255), and crop. The key is public for reproduction. A replication organizer can relabel the cards and hold the key until new scorers have committed their annotations.

| Card | Witness | Locator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C01 | Fuchs 1543, coltsfoot | [ch. 50, fig. 76](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/050.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb163.jpg) |
| C02 | Dodoens 1568, sunflower | [p. 295](https://archive.org/details/BIUSante_pharma_res019124/page/n294/mode/2up), [scan](https://archive.org/download/BIUSante_pharma_res019124/page/n294.jpg) |
| C03 | Fuchs 1543, castor | [ch. 128, fig. 192](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/128.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb352.jpg) |
| C04 | Fuchs 1543, cornflower | [ch. 162, fig. 240](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/162.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb433.jpg) |
| C05 | Gerard 1597, sunflower | [ch. 247 reprinted in Janick fig. 11, upper left](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/0c46/df4c800c9d9afbbe7d3b5e1fae8ed271b052.pdf). Use the first embedded JPEG on PDF page 10, full size 384 × 640, e.g. `pdfimages -f 10 -l 10 -j janick.pdf jan`. |
| C06 | Fuchs 1543, calendula | [ch. 143, fig. 214](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/143.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb390.jpg) |
| C07 | Fuchs 1543, common daisy | [ch. 53, fig. 80](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/053.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb169.jpg) |
| C08 | Dodoens 1563, navelwort | [p. 35, top left](https://plantillustrations.org/illustration.php?id_illustration=439421&size=1), [scan](https://plantillustrations.org/ILLUSTRATIONS_FULL_SIZE/439421.jpg) |
| C09 | Fuchs 1543, teasel | [ch. 82, fig. 126](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/082.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb242.jpg) |
| C10 | Fuchs 1543, artichoke | [ch. 308, fig. 455](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/308.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb789.jpg). This print omits a reproductive head. |

## Outcome

Each cell below is **agreements / disagreements / uncertain**. The per-feature table gives the underlying observations.

| Witness | f33v head | f33v total | f93r head | f93r total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C01 coltsfoot | 3/1/0 | 6/4/2 | 2/2/0 | 7/5/0 |
| C02 sunflower | 2/2/0 | 3/5/4 | 3/1/0 | 6/4/2 |
| C03 castor | 1/0/3 | 5/1/6 | 0/1/3 | 3/5/4 |
| C04 cornflower | 3/1/0 | 4/6/2 | 0/4/0 | 6/6/0 |
| C05 sunflower | 2/1/1 | 4/4/4 | 2/1/1 | 8/2/2 |
| C06 calendula | 3/0/1 | 5/4/3 | 0/3/1 | 7/4/1 |
| C07 daisy | 3/0/1 | 5/4/3 | 0/3/1 | 7/4/1 |
| C08 navelwort | 1/0/3 | 4/3/5 | 0/1/3 | 4/4/4 |
| C09 teasel | 3/1/0 | 5/5/2 | 2/2/0 | 9/3/0 |
| C10 artichoke | 0/0/4 | 4/2/6 | 0/0/4 | 5/3/4 |

For f33v, several controls achieve three known head agreements, where both sunflower plates achieve two. Castor agrees on the broad divided leaves, and navelwort shares one rounded root knot. Neither control depicts the specific combination of three disks, deep broad lobes and multiple ray-like heads. For f93r, Dodoens has three known head agreements (dense field, short fringe, one terminal head) but the field is rounded rather than tapered. Gerard shows the exposed filaments and eight overall agreements. Teasel agrees in nine overall, with two known head disagreements (rounded and multiple). If both uncertain Gerard comparisons are scored as matches, its score rises to ten. These rankings depend on the witness and on which body region is compared.

The panel is small and targeted. Most controls are from one herbal and the two sunflower images and Voynich drawings are from different book traditions. The counts describe the selected pictures, with no sampling inference or date estimate. Neither picture yielded a species-specific identifying combination on the observed features. This experiment offers no word–picture pairing.
detail.statement: These are separate published proposals. A caption-masked comparison against ten botanical prints found three of four head features in common between f93r and Dodoens's sunflower. Gerard's sunflower agrees in eight of twelve features with f93r, with two uncertain. Fuchs's teasel agrees in nine of twelve with none uncertain. Neither sunflower print agrees in more than four known features with f33v. The two Voynich drawings and the proposals were known when I planned the comparison. I also prepared the cards and supplied the only ratings. The packet records the individual features, crop bounds, open witnesses and ambiguities.

Patterned mature head plus a bud. Basal lamina joins, one dominant curved root.

step.json.record:
# Two sunflower proposals, two different figures

Ardıç proposes a sunflower on f33v. Stolfi's institutional note compares f33v with sunflower, including leaf attachment and the round underground objects, and prefers another possibility. Janick's published sunflower iconography reproduces **f93r**, cites O'Neill's earlier proposal and describes the single stalk and large seed head with suggestions of rays. These are two different folios. The claims are documented in the open [Ardıç companion](https://www.turkicresearch.com/Research/SubPages/Voynich), [Stolfi note](https://www.ic.unicamp.br/en/~stolfi/EXPORT/voynich/98-01-17-sunflower/) and [Janick 2020, pp. 1123–1125, figs. 9 and 11](https://www.notulaebotanicae.ro/index.php/nbha/article/download/12015/8986/48289).

## Scans and method

[Beinecke f33v](https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006139) and [Beinecke f93r](https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006238) are the public target scans. Load the corresponding Yale IIIF image IDs at 1200 px wide. The botanical cards are public-domain historical illustrations, shown by open sites. The Dodoens sunflower and both Voynich targets were known before the rubric. I fixed the eight control categories and twelve binary features before viewing the newly sourced prints. I prepared the crops, saw the full pages while doing so, and scored the shuffled grayscale cards. Masking removed the captions from the comparison views. My visual recognition and memory of the sources could still affect the scores. The work has one observer.

Features apply to the drawings as depicted. The head criteria are a densely patterned central field, distinct peripheral blades at least a quarter of the field's transverse width, a rounded outline of that field as opposed to a tapered silhouette, and a single terminal head on the plant. Buds on separate terminals count as evidence of multiple heads. In a spray of separate flowers without a shared field, the first three criteria are uncertain. Leaves are scored for a broad blade, obvious lobes or divisions, at least three major ridges spreading radially, an illustrated stalk–blade join visibly inside the margin, and a repeated opposite or near-opposite arrangement. Roots are scored for an exposed drawing below the stem join, many thin filaments and bounded round bulbs or knots. Compare agreement on known features and retain all uncertain comparisons. Color, relative figure size and dates carry no score.

The Yale f33v head fields are oval despite their perspective. The pale central marks on its leaves hint at a center attachment. The painted overlap makes the exact join and radial ridges uncertain. The three round objects visibly connect to branching underground strands. The dotted head on f93r has a tapered outline and short marginal strokes under the blade-length criterion. Its near-paired leaves are smooth curved arcs. The root join opens into many thin filaments. The paler form near the manuscript text was excluded as possible show-through.

## Comparison cards

Crop bounds and caption-mask coordinates in `cards.json` are pixels in the original downloads, in left, top, right, bottom order. Convert to grayscale, paint mask rectangles gray (245 of 255), and crop. The key is public for reproduction. A replication organizer can relabel the cards and hold the key until new scorers have committed their annotations.

| Card | Witness | Locator |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C01 | Fuchs 1543, coltsfoot | [ch. 50, fig. 76](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/050.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb163.jpg) |
| C02 | Dodoens 1568, sunflower | [p. 295](https://archive.org/details/BIUSante_pharma_res019124/page/n294/mode/2up), [scan](https://archive.org/download/BIUSante_pharma_res019124/page/n294.jpg) |
| C03 | Fuchs 1543, castor | [ch. 128, fig. 192](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/128.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb352.jpg) |
| C04 | Fuchs 1543, cornflower | [ch. 162, fig. 240](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/162.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb433.jpg) |
| C05 | Gerard 1597, sunflower | [ch. 247 reprinted in Janick fig. 11, upper left](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/0c46/df4c800c9d9afbbe7d3b5e1fae8ed271b052.pdf). Use the first embedded JPEG on PDF page 10, full size 384 × 640, e.g. `pdfimages -f 10 -l 10 -j janick.pdf jan`. |
| C06 | Fuchs 1543, calendula | [ch. 143, fig. 214](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/143.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb390.jpg) |
| C07 | Fuchs 1543, common daisy | [ch. 53, fig. 80](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/053.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb169.jpg) |
| C08 | Dodoens 1563, navelwort | [p. 35, top left](https://plantillustrations.org/illustration.php?id_illustration=439421&size=1), [scan](https://plantillustrations.org/ILLUSTRATIONS_FULL_SIZE/439421.jpg) |
| C09 | Fuchs 1543, teasel | [ch. 82, fig. 126](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/082.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb242.jpg) |
| C10 | Fuchs 1543, artichoke | [ch. 308, fig. 455](https://www.waimann.de/capitel/308.html), [scan](https://www.waimann.de/woodcut/Abb789.jpg). This print omits a reproductive head. |

## Outcome

Each cell below is **agreements / disagreements / uncertain**. The per-feature table gives the underlying observations.

| Witness | f33v head | f33v total | f93r head | f93r total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C01 coltsfoot | 3/1/0 | 6/4/2 | 2/2/0 | 7/5/0 |
| C02 sunflower | 2/2/0 | 3/5/4 | 3/1/0 | 6/4/2 |
| C03 castor | 1/0/3 | 5/1/6 | 0/1/3 | 3/5/4 |
| C04 cornflower | 3/1/0 | 4/6/2 | 0/4/0 | 6/6/0 |
| C05 sunflower | 2/1/1 | 4/4/4 | 2/1/1 | 8/2/2 |
| C06 calendula | 3/0/1 | 5/4/3 | 0/3/1 | 7/4/1 |
| C07 daisy | 3/0/1 | 5/4/3 | 0/3/1 | 7/4/1 |
| C08 navelwort | 1/0/3 | 4/3/5 | 0/1/3 | 4/4/4 |
| C09 teasel | 3/1/0 | 5/5/2 | 2/2/0 | 9/3/0 |
| C10 artichoke | 0/0/4 | 4/2/6 | 0/0/4 | 5/3/4 |

For f33v, several controls achieve three known head agreements, where both sunflower plates achieve two. Castor agrees on the broad divided leaves, and navelwort shares one rounded root knot. Neither control depicts the specific combination of three disks, deep broad lobes and multiple ray-like heads. For f93r, Dodoens has three known head agreements (dense field, short fringe, one terminal head) but the field is rounded rather than tapered. Gerard shows the exposed filaments and eight overall agreements. Teasel agrees in nine overall, with two known head disagreements (rounded and multiple). If both uncertain Gerard comparisons are scored as matches, its score rises to ten. These rankings depend on the witness and on which body region is compared.

The panel is small and targeted. Most controls are from one herbal and the two sunflower images and Voynich drawings are from different book traditions. The counts describe the selected pictures, with no sampling inference or date estimate. Neither picture yielded a species-specific identifying combination on the observed features. This experiment offers no word–picture pairing.

Neither sunflower print agrees in more than four known features with f33v. The two Voynich drawings and the proposals were known when I planned the comparison. I also prepared the cards and supplied the only ratings. The packet records the individual features, crop bounds, open witnesses and ambiguities.

detail.why: the text reproduces 17 of 17 established facts

statement: A constructed language modelled on Hildegard of Bingen's Lingua Ignota (12th century): a glossary of about 1,011 invented words, mostly nouns, ordered by subject, written in her own 23 letters, with tree names sharing an ending such as -buz (source used: the open English Wikipedia article 'Lingua ignota', which follows Roth 1895 and Higley 2007; I did not find an open full transcription of the Riesencodex glossary in the time I had, so only the article's description and examples were used, and no word of hers is copied). Design (lexicon with glosses, rates and the generator's source are in this file under "language"): roots are a priori and marked for subject by their first letter (ch plants, sh waters and bathing, t stars and times, k body and illness, d vessels and substances, l/r/s qualities, kinds, numbers) followed by a vowel and a final letter, so things of one kind differ by one letter; single plants, stars and baths have longer two-syllable names. One paradigm of endings for nouns and adjectives (-y subject, -dy object, -ar in, -al with, -or from, -ol for, -aiin/-ain of; -ey, -eey, -edy degrees of a quality); adjectives follow the noun and copy its ending; the verb is root + -am and stands last; one statement per line. Article o-/qo- with a euphony rule: qo- only after a word ending in -y, no article after the 'of' case. Script: one EVA glyph per letter; the first word of a line takes an opening stroke (y, d, s); on a paragraph's top line the tall letters t and k are written in ornate forms (EVA p, f) and the paragraph's first word opens with one. The text is a book of statements about one object at a time (a plant, a star, a bath, a jar), 12 to 34 lines each, the subject mix following the manuscript's sections in the order and proportion of the public practice training pages (scaled by 0.19), line lengths drawn from those pages; a writer returns to what was just said (same word again, or the same root in a neighbouring case, or a kindred root in the same case). first_lines are the same book written with the top-line script habit. Nothing was fitted on hidden pages. Practice split, whole lines kept: 17 of 17 established facts (F-001 48.7, F-002 0.245, F-003 53.9, F-004 0.313, F-005 0.253, F-006 7.68, F-007 0.250, F-008 34.9, F-009/F-016 0.288, F-010 0.221, F-011 0.070, F-013 1.99, F-014 0.679, F-017 0.012, F-018 1.68, F-019 15.8). SAID PLAINLY: this reproduces only what meaningless text already reproduces (R-017 and P-G-017 meet the same facts with a learned glyph chain), and it does so because the rules were chosen with the facts in view: the first version, written from the design alone, met 15 of 17 and missed the one-glyph near-copies (0.064) and the same-page reuse (0.138); those two were reached only by tuning how often the writer repeats and varies recent words (about a dozen rates, chosen on the practice split, three seeds checked: hapax share 0.673 to 0.683 against a bar of 0.667, so F-014 may fail on the hidden pages). Three rules name a position (verb last in the line, opening stroke on the first word, ornate letters on the top line), so F-001, F-003, F-006, F-008 and F-019 are met by construction and should be read as weak. Words are also longer than the manuscript's (mean 7.0 glyphs against about 5). What the test does show: nothing in the 17 facts excludes an a priori language with concord, euphony and line-sized statements; none of them requires one. Meaning-linked prediction checked before sending and NOT registered, because the manuscript does not show it on public pages: in this language a label repeats words of the text about the same object, so whole-word reuse on a page (labels and paragraphs together, words of 4+ characters) should fall when labels trade places with running words (null shuffle_labels); on the practice evaluation pages p = 0.345 (within-page variant 0.82), on the training pages p = 0.045 (0.75), none passing at 0.01. The other prediction, section words following the subject, is F-018, which whole-word reuse alone already meets (P-LEAD-008). So this language earns no credit beyond the meaningless procedures.

language.generator_source:
"""Lingua-ignota-style constructed language for P-G-006 (fleet-blue). Standard library only.
Writes attack.json and lexicon.json next to itself. Not run by the scorer; it documents how the
submitted lines were produced. Usage: python3 language.py [seed]

THE LANGUAGE
Roots are a priori and grouped by subject, as Hildegard's glossary is (God and people, body,
illnesses, plants, birds, tools) and as her tree names share an ending (-buz). Here the subject is
marked at the front of the root, the thing at its end:
    root = FIELD-LETTER + VOWEL + FINAL        e.g. chol, chor (plants: ch-)
    fields: ch- plants, sh- waters and bathing, t- stars and times, k- the body and its ills,
            d- vessels and substances, l-/r-/s- qualities, kinds and numbers
    long roots add a second syllable: names of single plants, stars, baths.
Affixes (one paradigm for every noun and adjective):
    -y subject, -dy object, -ar in, -al with, -or from, -ol for, -aiin of, -ain of (many),
    -ey / -eey / -edy 2nd / 3rd / 4th degree of a quality (the physicians' four degrees)
    adjectives follow their noun and copy its case ending (concord).
    verb = root + -am, standing last in its statement. One statement per line.
    article: o- 'the', qo- 'the said'; euphony: qo- only after a word ending in -y;
    after -n (the 'of' case) the owned noun stands bare.
SCRIPT (letters of the language -> EVA): every letter is one EVA glyph, except that the vowel of
    the 'of' case is written with repeated minims (aiin, ain). Two scribal habits, both ordinary in
    15th-century books: (1) the first word of a line carries an opening stroke (y, d or s);
    (2) on the top line of a paragraph the tall letters t and k are written in their ornate
    looped forms (EVA p and f), and the paragraph's first word opens with one.
"""
import json, random, sys, os
HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
SEED = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 1404
R = random.Random(SEED)
P = json.load(open(os.path.join(HERE, "params.json")))

VOW = ["o", "e", "ee", "a", "eo"]
FIN = ["l", "r", "d", "k", "t", "s", "ch", "", "ckh", "cth"]
FIELDS = {"plant": "ch", "water": "sh", "star": "t", "body": "k", "vessel": "d", "qual": "l", "kind": "r", "num": "s"}
GLOSS = {
 "plant": ["leaf", "root", "flower", "stem", "seed", "herb", "juice", "bark", "fruit", "branch", "thorn", "tree", "vine", "bulb", "sap", "moss", "rind", "bud", "husk", "grain"],
 "water": ["water", "bath", "pool", "stream", "pipe", "rain", "spring", "steam", "wave", "well", "channel", "dew", "flood", "basin", "foam", "bather", "womb", "vein", "milk", "blood"],
 "star": ["star", "sun", "moon", "sign", "month", "day", "night", "hour", "year", "heaven", "wheel", "ring", "wind", "season", "rising", "setting", "degree", "house", "ram", "bull"],
 "body": ["head", "belly", "hand", "eye", "heart", "liver", "skin", "bone", "fever", "wound", "pain", "cough", "breath", "foot", "tooth", "ear", "flux", "bile", "phlegm", "woman"],
 "vessel": ["jar", "pot", "oil", "wine", "salt", "honey", "powder", "salve", "measure", "part", "fire", "ash", "drink", "wax", "vinegar", "cup", "cloth", "stone", "lid", "drop"],
 "qual": ["hot", "dry", "cold", "moist", "good", "strong", "bitter", "sweet", "white", "red", "green", "small", "great", "long", "round"],
 "kind": ["kind", "use", "way", "time", "place", "thing", "name", "work", "power", "half"],
 "num": ["one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "nine", "twelve", "many"],
}
VERBS = ["d", "ol", "ar", "ch", "ok", "ot", "al", "sh", "or", "chol", "kar", "dal", "ld", "r", "s"]   # + am
VGLOSS = ["is", "gives", "takes", "grows", "heals", "rises", "mixes", "washes", "boils", "bears", "opens", "pours", "binds", "goes", "holds"]
CASES = ["y", "dy", "ar", "al", "or", "ol", "aiin", "ain"]
DEG = ["y", "ey", "eey", "edy"]


def build_lexicon():
    lex, gl = {}, {}
    for f, ini in FIELDS.items():
        short = [ini + v + c for v in VOW for c in FIN]
        R.shuffle(short)
        plain = [ini + v + c for c in ["l", "r", "d", "k", "t", "s"] for v in ["o", "e", "a", "ee"]]
        R.shuffle(plain)
        head = plain[:len(GLOSS[f])]              # the commonest things get the plainest roots
        order = head + [r for r in short if r not in head]
        for r, g in zip(order, GLOSS[f]):
            gl[r] = g
        long = []
        for _ in range(P["long_roots"]):
            a = R.choice(short)
            b = R.choice(["k", "t", "d", "l", "r", "ch"]) if a[-1] not in "lrdkts" else ""
            long.append(a + b + R.choice(["o", "e", "ee", "a"]) + R.choice(["l", "r", "d", "s", "", "", "k"]))
        lex[f] = {"common": order, "names": sorted(set(long))}
    return lex, gl


LEX, GL = build_lexicon()
SUBJECT = {"H": ["plant", "plant", "plant", "body", "vessel", "water"], "P": ["vessel", "plant", "vessel", "body"],
           "S": ["vessel", "body", "plant", "star", "water"], "B": ["water", "water", "body", "water", "star"],
           "A": ["star", "star", "star", "body"], "Z": ["star", "star", "water"], "C": ["star", "water", "star", "plant"],
           "T": ["plant", "body", "star", "vessel", "water"]}


def zipf(xs, s):
    w = [1 / (i + 1) ** s for i in range(len(xs))]
    return R.choices(xs, w)[0]


RECENT = []


class Topic:
    """One object of the pictures (a plant, a star, a bath, a jar) and the few things said about it."""
    def __init__(self, sec):
        fs = SUBJECT[sec]
        self.sec, self.field = sec, fs[0]
        self.name = R.choice(LEX[self.field]["names"])
        self.things = [zipf(LEX[R.choice(fs)]["common"], P["zipf"]) for _ in range(P["topic_things"])]
        self.names = [R.choice(LEX[R.choice(fs)]["names"]) for _ in range(P["topic_names"])]
        self.quals = [zipf(LEX["qual"]["common"], 1.0) for _ in range(3)]

    def noun(self):
        x = R.random()
        if x < P["p_name"]:
            return self.name
        if x < P["p_name"] + P["p_thing"]:
            return R.choice(self.things)
        if x < P["p_name"] + P["p_thing"] + P["p_names"]:
            return R.choice(self.names)
        if x < 1 - P["p_fresh"]:
            return zipf(LEX[R.choice(SUBJECT[self.sec])]["common"], P["zipf"])
        return R.choice(LEX[R.choice(list(FIELDS))]["names"])

    def qual(self):
        if R.random() < 0.6:
            return R.choice(self.quals)
        return zipf(LEX["qual"]["common"] + LEX["kind"]["common"] + LEX["num"]["common"], 0.9)


NEAR_CASE = {"y": ["dy", "ey"], "dy": ["y", "edy"], "ar": ["al", "or"], "al": ["ar", "ol"], "or": ["ar", "ol"], "ol": ["al", "or"],
             "aiin": ["ain"], "ain": ["aiin"], "ey": ["y", "eey"], "eey": ["ey"], "edy": ["dy", "ey"]}


def kin(root):
    """A thing of the same kind: in an a priori lexicon its root differs by one letter."""
    for _ in range(20):
        ini = next(i for i in sorted(FIELDS.values(), key=len, reverse=True) if root.startswith(i))
        rest = root[len(ini):]
        v = next(x for x in sorted(VOW, key=len, reverse=True) if rest.startswith(x))
        c = rest[len(v):]
        if c not in FIN:
            return root
        r = ini + (R.choice(VOW) if R.random() < 0.4 else v) + (R.choice(["l", "r", "d", "k", "t", "s"]) if R.random() < 0.7 else c)
        if r != root:
            return r
    return root


def phrase(t, case, budget):
    """A noun phrase in one case: noun-case [adjective-case ...] [noun-of] [kindred noun-case]."""
    x = R.random()
    if RECENT and x < P["p_again"]:                  # said again as it was said, anywhere earlier about this object
        role0, root, case = R.choice(RECENT[-P["again_window"]:])
        out = [(role0, root, case)]
    elif RECENT and x < P["p_again"] + P["p_echo"]:  # the thing just spoken of, in a neighbouring case
        role0, root, c0 = R.choice(RECENT[-P["echo_window"]:])
        out = [(role0, root, R.choice(NEAR_CASE.get(c0, [case])))]
    else:
        out = [("N", t.noun(), case)]
    if budget > 1 and R.random() < P["p_adj"]:
        out.append(("A", t.qual(), case if R.random() < P["concord"] else R.choice(DEG)))
        if budget > 2 and R.random() < P["p_adj2"]:
            out.append(("A", t.qual(), case))
    if budget > len(out) and R.random() < P["p_gen"]:
        g = R.choice(LEX[R.choice(SUBJECT[t.sec])]["names"]) if R.random() < P["p_gen_name"] else t.noun()   # "of" mostly names a single thing
        out.append(("G", g, R.choice(["aiin", "aiin", "ain"])))
    if budget > len(out) and R.random() < P["p_list"]:     # a list of like things: leaf, root, flower
        out.append((out[0][0], kin(out[0][1]), out[0][2]))
    out = out[:budget]
    RECENT.extend(out)
    return out


def statement(t, n, verb_last):
    """One statement of n words: subject phrase, phrases in other cases, verb last."""
    body = n - (1 if verb_last else 0)
    ws, first = [], True
    while len(ws) < body:
        case = "y" if first and R.random() < P["p_subject_first"] else R.choices(CASES, P["case_w"])[0]
        ws += phrase(t, case, body - len(ws))
        first = False
        if len(ws) < body - 1 and R.random() < P["p_midverb"]:
            ws.append(("V", R.choice(VERBS), "am"))
    if verb_last:
        ws.append(("V", zipf(VERBS, 0.8), "am"))
    return ws


def spell(ws, top_line):
    """Affixes, euphony and the script."""
    out, prev = [], None
    for i, (role, root, suf) in enumerate(ws):
        w = root + suf
        art = ""
        if role in ("N", "V"):
            if prev is None:
                art = "o" if R.random() < P["art_first"] else ""
            elif prev.endswith("y"):
                art = "qo" if R.random() < P["art_after_y"] else ""
            elif prev.endswith("n"):
                art = ""
            else:
                art = "o" if R.random() < P["art_after_c"] else ""
        elif role == "A" and prev is not None and not prev.endswith("y") and R.random() < P["adj_o"]:
            art = "o"
        w = art + w
        tall = w[0] in "tk"
        if tall and R.random() < (P["ornate_top"] if top_line else P["ornate_any"]):
            w = ("p" if w[0] == "t" else "f") + w[1:]
        if i == 0:
            if top_line and R.random() < P["para_open"]:
                w = (R.choice("ppf") + w[1:]) if w[0] in "tk" else R.choice("ppf") + w
            elif w[0] not in "pf" and R.random() < P["line_open"]:
                w = R.choice(P["openers"]) + w
        out.append(w)
        prev = w
    return out


def book(n_lines, plan, lens, top):
    lines, sec_i, left, t, t_left = [], 0, 0, None, 0
    while len(lines) < n_lines:
        if left <= 0:
            sec, left = plan[min(sec_i, len(plan) - 1)]
            sec_i += 1
            t_left = 0
        if t_left <= 0:
            keep = t
            t = Topic(sec)
            if keep is not None and keep.sec == sec:      # the next object of a section is spoken of in the same terms
                t.things = keep.things[:P["carry"]] + t.things[P["carry"]:]
                t.quals = keep.quals[:2] + t.quals[2:]
            t_left = R.randint(*P["topic_lines"])
            del RECENT[:]
        n = R.choice(lens)
        ws = statement(t, n, n >= 3 and R.random() < P["p_verb"])
        lines.append(spell(ws, top))
        left -= 1
        t_left -= 1
    return lines


if __name__ == "__main__":
    lay = json.load(open(os.path.join(HERE, "layout.json")))      # public training pages only: section runs, line lengths
    plan = [(s, max(1, round(n * P["scale"]))) for s, n in lay["runs"]]
    N = P["lines"]
    lines = book(N, plan, lay["lens"], False)
    first = book(N, plan, lay["first_lens"], True)
    mp = os.path.join(HERE, "method.txt")
    att = {"attack": "generator", "hypothesis": "invented_language", "title": P["title"],
           "method": open(mp).read().strip() if os.path.exists(mp) else "draft",
           "cut": "lines", "lines": lines, "first_lines": first}
    json.dump(att, open(os.path.join(HERE, "attack.json"), "w"), separators=(",", ":"))
    json.dump({"fields": FIELDS, "glosses": GL, "verbs": dict(zip([v + "am" for v in VERBS], VGLOSS)), "cases": CASES,
               "degrees": DEG, "roots": LEX}, open(os.path.join(HERE, "lexicon.json"), "w"), indent=0)
    print(len(lines), sum(map(len, lines)))
    for l in first[:3] + lines[:8]:
        print(" ".join(l))
