detail.statement: The third statistic proposed in P-L4-013 (a label word recurs in its own page's running text more than in other pages') needs no picture annotation, so I measured it now on the public practice pages only (226 pages; nothing from the hidden pages). Selection: the 46 public pages with at least three label words and at least thirty words of other text (15 pharmaceutical, 12 zodiac, 10 biological, 5 astronomical, 3 cosmological, 1 text), 886 label words of three or more glyphs with no uncertain reading. Statistic: the share of label words that occur somewhere in the non-label text of their own page. Null: the same share after the label sets are dealt to other pages of the same section, 999 deals. Result, exact word: 0.096 on the own page against a null mean of 0.085 (95th percentile 0.097), p = 0.079. Allowing one glyph of difference: 0.366 against 0.335 (95th percentile 0.361), p = 0.030 on 199 deals. By section, exact word, no section is significant on its own: astronomical 0.036 against 0.042, biological 0.200 against 0.190, cosmological 0.174 against 0.108, pharmaceutical 0.068 against 0.066, zodiac 0.091 against 0.074 (p from 0.11 to 0.75). So there is at most a weak page effect for labels, a ratio of about 1.13 to 1. The comparison that matters: ordinary words show a page effect at least as strong as labels do. Holding out the last paragraph line of every public page with six or more paragraph lines (925 words), 0.351 of its words occur in the rest of their own page, against 0.267 in the rest of another page of the same section, a ratio of about 1.32 to 1. Matched for frequency (five bins of how often a word occurs in the public running text, ordinary words reweighted to the labels' mix; the other-page rate here is the average over all other pages of the section, so the label figures differ slightly from the deal above), the ratios are 1.21 for labels (0.096 against 0.080) and 1.35 for ordinary words (0.144 against 0.107). Bin by bin the picture is mixed: among fairly common words (11 to 40 occurrences) labels have the higher ratio, 0.198 against 0.110 where ordinary words have 0.199 against 0.134; among the commonest (over 40) labels show almost none, 0.378 against 0.367 where ordinary words have 0.681 against 0.512. Half of the label words (448 of 886) occur at most once anywhere in the public running text and so can hardly recur on their page at all. This is the page-vocabulary effect already on the record (F-009), and meaningless procedures with a local memory reproduce it. Consequence for P-L4-013: statistic (3) as worded measures page vocabulary, not reference. A procedure that writes labels with the same memory it uses for the text would pass it at least as well as the manuscript does, and the manuscript's own labels pass it only marginally. Re-key existing ring annotations by that rule (their authors can do it from their own recorded clock positions without looking at the scan again) and re-measure agreement between seats on label-matched objects. The correction above fails if, for any of the twelve rings, shifting my pairing by the stated number does not bring the mean distance between figure and marked position under half a figure's spacing. For the instructions: say in join.txt that ring labels are to be paired by the clock markers, which are layout notes and not words, so that using them does not break blindness.
detail.statement: In six blind picture annotations of zodiac wheels (f70v2, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v) I paired each ring's label lines with its figures clockwise from twelve o'clock and said in each statement that the starting point was an assumption. After submitting all of them I checked the assumption against the pinned Zandbergen-Landini file. The file settles it without anyone reading a word: every figure-label line on the zodiac pages carries a clock-position marker for its figure (299 marked label lines on 13 folios; the page notes say 'Clock position is that of nymph'). On those markers the direction I assumed is right, clockwise, and the starting point is wrong on eleven of my twelve rings. The first label of a ring sits between about a quarter to nine and half past eleven, never at twelve. Ring by ring (figures in the ring, clock position of the first label, how many of my pairings fall within half a figure's spacing of the marked position, and the shift k, meaning that the figure I numbered j, counting clockwise from twelve o'clock, should carry the label line I gave to figure j minus k, wrapping round the ring): f70v2 outer: 19 figures, first label at 9 o'clock, 0 of 19 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f70v2 inner: 10 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 8; f72v1 outer: 20 figures, first label at 8.75 o'clock, 0 of 20 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f72v1 inner: 10 figures, first label at 8.75 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 7; f72v2 outer: 18 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 18 of my pairings right, shift by 16; f72v2 inner: 12 figures, first label at 10.5 o'clock, 0 of 12 of my pairings right, shift by 10; f72v3 outer: 18 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 18 of my pairings right, shift by 15; f72v3 inner: 12 figures, first label at 10.5 o'clock, 0 of 12 of my pairings right, shift by 10; f73r outer: 16 figures, first label at 11 o'clock, 0 of 16 of my pairings right, shift by 14; f73r inner: 10 figures, first label at 11.5 o'clock, 9 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 0; f73v outer: 16 figures, first label at 10 o'clock, 0 of 16 of my pairings right, shift by 13; f73v inner: 10 figures, first label at 9.5 o'clock, 0 of 10 of my pairings right, shift by 8. After the shift the mean distance between my figure positions and the marked positions is 0.15 to 0.46 of an hour, so the counts and the clockwise order agree and only the start was off. So on eleven rings every one of my figure-to-label pairings is wrong by a constant rotation; only the inner ring of f73r (nine of ten) and the four figures on top of f73r and f73v, which I paired left to right and which the markers place from about eleven to one o'clock in that order, stand as submitted. What is not affected: the drawings as described, the ring counts, and the assignment of label groups to rings. The markers also confirm two things I had inferred: the group sizes per ring (for example 12, 11 and 7 on f72r3 from the outside in), and which wheel is which on the two-wheel verso canvas (the page notes give the animal wheel as f72v3 and the clothed-figure wheel as f72v2, as I had them). Where features were recorded figure by figure and so travel with the pairing (the blue caps and tub patterns of the f70v2 outer ring, the crown on f72v1, the postures of the f72r3 inner ring in my unsubmitted draft), the corrected label is the submitted one shifted by the number above. The same check should be made on every other seat's ring annotations before any picture-text test uses them: two seats can agree with each other on a pairing and both be rotated. One more of my submitted folios is touched, with weaker evidence: f67r2 has no clock markers, but its page notes number the twelve sectors from the one between nine and ten o'clock, clockwise, and say the sector text starts at ten o'clock. I paired the twelve red outer labels and the twelve moon labels from twelve o'clock, so those pairings are probably rotated by about three places as well; the notes do not say where the moon labels start, so I checked that ring on the scan (canvas 1006194, region 3450,850,800,500), reading the words now that the blind annotation is in: the red moon at twelve o'clock has the word of f67r2.54 under it, the yellow moon at one o'clock the word of f67r2.55, and the red moon at two o'clock the word of f67r2.56. So the moon labels run clockwise from the moon at ten o'clock, and my submitted pairing of that ring is off by two places (the moon I gave line n carries line n plus two, wrapping from 63 to 52). With that pairing and the colour order on which three seats agree, the red moons carry lines 52, 54, 56, 59, 60 and 62 and the yellow moons 53, 55, 57, 58, 61 and 63. Their labels do not divide by colour in form: labels of the same colour share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.13 of pairs, labels of different colours in 0.19 (p = 0.89 against random halves), and first glyphs are split evenly. Twelve labels cannot show much either way. The red outer labels of the sectors I did not check on the scan; they stay probably rotated, by the page notes. For f99r the same file settles the two places I had flagged as ambiguous, again without any reading of words: each label line there carries an object number from an older catalogue of the drawings, with a letter where several labels belong to one object. By those numbers the twelve, seven and seven detached objects I counted in rows 1 to 3 are right, the two-line label in row 1 is one object's (f99r.6 and f99r.7), and the spare label in each of rows 2 and 3 belongs with its neighbour as I had it (f99r.25 with f99r.26 on the sixth object of row 2, f99r.33 with f99r.34 on the first object of row 3). So my f99r pairing stands as submitted, and the three seats who paired every object there differ only in which line of such a pair they named. My other submitted folios (f66r, f68r1, f75v, f99r) have no ring pairing; the page notes agree with how I read the label groups on f66r and f75v and say nothing on the order of the star labels on f68r1. For that page I compared the first seven label lines with the words beside the uppermost stars on the scan, as far as I can read them at 1700 pixels: the transcription takes the stars in loose rows, left to right within a row (the two stars beside the sun, then the five of the next row from the left edge to the right), whereas I numbered strictly by height. My pairing is therefore right for the first three stars and wrong inside the second row (my stars 4 to 7), and very likely wrong inside the lower rows too; I then carried the check through at higher resolution (five tiles of canvas 1006196 at about 1700 pixels each), matching each star's word to the transliteration by eye. Result, as label line for each star in my submitted numbering 1 to 29: 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 11, 12, 17, 18, 15, 16 for the first eleven (so the transcription does run in rows, but the right-hand pair of a row comes after the left-hand ones only loosely), and for the bottom of the page line 31 for the dark-dotted star at the left edge, 32 for the star whose label stands on its left, 33 and 35 for the two ring-centred stars, 34 for the one between them and 36 for the lowest star. The middle of the page I could match with less confidence: lines 19 to 22 go to the four stars of the fourth row from the left edge to the large star, 27, 28, 29 and 30 to the row below, and lines 23 to 26 to the four remaining stars (the one at the left edge of the third row, the two at the right of the fourth row, and the one at the left edge of the fifth) in an order I could not settle. With that pairing the eight ring-centred stars carry lines 14, 15, 17, 18, 30, 33, 35 and one of 24 to 26, and the two dark-dotted stars lines 20 and 31. Their labels do not stand apart from the other stars' labels: the nine with a certain reading share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.31 of pairs against 0.27 for nine labels drawn at random from the page (p = 0.33), and mean length, final y and pedestalled gallows are alike in both groups. So the centre mark, which three seats recorded the same way, predicts nothing visible in the label on this page; twenty-eight labels cannot show a small effect. My submitted f68r1 pairing is wrong for most stars and should be replaced by this one, with lines 23 to 26 marked uncertain. A first use of the rule, on the one ring feature all four seats on the record wrote down for f70v2: which outer figures wear a blue cap. Read in each seat's own clockwise order the four sequences are the same pattern (one capped figure, one bare, five capped, the other twelve bare); two seats began at twelve o'clock and two at the top left, two figures earlier, and once each sequence is laid on the marked clock positions all four agree on all nineteen figures. By the alignment with the least total clock distance the capped figures are the ones labelled by lines f70v2.8 and f70v2.10 to f70v2.14; the seats' clock estimates are coarse, so a slip of one figure was possible, and I checked it on the scan (canvas 1006200, region 1900,500,1500,1500), this time reading the words, which is allowed now that the blind annotation is in: the first capped figure has the word of f70v2.8 beside it, the bare figure after it the word of f70v2.9, and the next three capped figures the words of f70v2.10, 11 and 12, each word standing by its own figure's star. So the first reading is the right one, and the shift of fourteen figures given above for this ring is confirmed on the scan for these five figures. So with a closed feature and the clock rule, independent seats agree completely where the record's score for the same four annotations is 0.41 to 0.75. And a first, very small look at the second statistic of P-L4-013 (figures that share a feature have labels that share glyph groups): the six capped figures' labels share their first two or last two glyphs in 0.13 of pairs, against 0.40 for six labels drawn at random from the ring, and this is the lowest of the nineteen values obtained by sliding the same one-gap-five pattern round the ring. On this one ring the feature predicts nothing about the labels, if anything the reverse; six figures on one page cannot carry more than that. Having read the page notes for this check, I have now seen the transcription's descriptions of f70v1, f71r, f71v, f72r1 and f72r2 and should not be given those folios as blind picture steps.

detail.statement: An extension of P-L4-010 with calibrated positions instead of index order. ZL3b records a clock position (<!hh:mm>) on each label line of the circular zodiac pages; I used those as each label's angle, so no rotation is fitted and no figure-to-word association is guessed. Pages: f70v1, f70v2, f71r, f71v, f72r1, f72r2, f72r3, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v. Rings are the label runs between circular text lines, counted from the outside (ring k on one page is compared with ring k on another); label lines before the first circular text (figures outside the circle on f73r/f73v) are excluded; words with uncertainty marks are dropped, and a label is all its remaining words joined. For every pair of pages and every shared ring, each label is compared with the label nearest its angle on the other page, if within 15 degrees: 1,303 comparisons. Observed: 0 exact label matches and 9 exact-or-one-edit matches (eva-basic glyphs). Null: labels shuffled within each ring of each page, positions kept, 999 permutations: mean 1.72 exact and 12.44 near; p = 1.0 (exact) and 0.89 (near), i.e. matches are if anything fewer than chance. With a 30-degree window (1,344 comparisons, 299 permutations): 0 and 9 observed, null means 1.78 and 12.71, p = 1.0 and 0.91. Power check: planting one shared word at 0 degrees and another at 180 degrees in the outer ring of every page gives 96 exact matches against a null mean of 11.2, p = 0.0033 (the minimum with 299 permutations). So a roster repeated at fixed clock positions, even for only two positions, would have been seen; none is. This agrees with the index-based result in P-L4-010 and is free of its rotation search. Rotating rosters: the same comparison, but for every pair of pages and ring the second page is rotated in 15-degree steps (24 offsets) in both directions and the offset with the most near matches is kept; the null applies the same maximisation to labels shuffled within rings (999 permutations). Observed: 17 exact and 78 near matches in 1,302 comparisons; null means 15.04 and 77.84; p = 0.196 (exact) and 0.543 (near). Power check for this version: planting the same two words at 0 and 180 degrees shifted by 30 degrees more on each successive page (a roster that rotates with the sign) gives 146 exact matches against a null mean of 85.5, p = 0.005 (the minimum with 199 permutations). So neither a fixed nor a rotating roster shared across signs is present at even two positions. Not tested: rosters in a different order on each page (no fixed sequence), which no position test can see.

detail.statement: An independent rerun of P-L4-007's check with my own code. Differences from the original, fixed before running: I used only the figure-label loci (unit Lz) of the twelve zodiac pages, 299 labels (15 on f70v1, f71r, f71v, f72r1; 29 on f72r2; 30 on the rest, f70v2 including its one centre label) where the original used 350; glyph strings with word breaks removed; for each of the 66 page pairs the largest number of agreements over every cyclic offset of the longer page against the shorter, summed; 1,000 shuffles. Two nulls: labels shuffled over the whole page, and labels shuffled only inside their own ring (the groups the transcription marks). Same position, no offset, ZL3b: 1 agreement in 1,403 comparisons (0.07%). Best offset, exact, ZL3b: 27 against a null mean of 24.9 (p = 0.034 whole-page, 0.050 within-ring). Allowing one glyph of difference: 82 against 76.2 (p = 0.028 and 0.027). Other transliterations, whole-page and within-ring: IT2a exact 19 against 17.8 (p = 0.17, 0.18), one-glyph 82 against 75.2 (p = 0.025, 0.012); RF1b exact 20 against 20.5 (p = 1.0, 1.0), one-glyph 69 against 65.7 (p = 0.15, 0.15); GC2a exact 18 against 18.4 (p = 1.0, 1.0), one-glyph 75 against 72.9 (p = 0.27, 0.23). These are eight tests without correction, and the statistic hardly moves under shuffling (for exact agreement the best offset of most pairs is 1 whenever the two pages share any label, whatever the order), so a p of 1.0 only means the observed total sits at the floor. Power: writing four labels in the same order onto every 30-label page is detected in 20 of 20 trials. Where the ZL excess comes from: only two pairs have two or more exact agreements at one offset. f72r2 and f72v3 share one label twice. f73r and f73v, recto and verso of one leaf, share three labels at the same shift of one place: the 6th, 19th and 24th figure labels of f73r (loci f73r.7, f73r.20, f73r.26) equal the 5th, 18th and 23rd of f73v (loci f73v.6, f73v.19, f73v.25); ZL reads them okeody, okeos, oky on both pages. The first two lie in the outer ring and the third in the inner ring, each one place earlier on f73v than on f73r, and ZL's own clock positions for the three are later on f73r by one and a half to two hours each, so the shift looks like a rotation of the whole wheel, not a counting slip. For that pair alone, shuffling one page gives three or more agreements with p = 0.0045 (0.0009 within rings); multiplied by the 66 pairs examined that is 0.30. IT2a reads the same three. RF1b and GC2a agree on the middle one only: on f73v they read a variant glyph in the first word and a different gallows in the third (RF1b oty against oky), and that leaves them one label common to the two pages. Conclusion: I confirm P-L4-007. There is no list of labels repeating in order from sign to sign. The small nominal excess in ZL is one local coincidence on one leaf that depends on how three or four labels are transliterated, and it does not survive the number of pairs looked at. It is worth one look on the scan, since two of the three words differ between editions. Follow-up on the scan, done after the numbers: I looked at the six labels on the Yale canvases at full resolution (regions 1000,900,260,170 and 1500,1850,220,180 of canvas 1006206; 980,1150,260,200 and 1800,1330,220,160 of canvas 1006207; the two labels at f73r.20 and f73v.19 in wider crops). The long label at f73r.7 and the one at f73v.6 have the same outline (o, a two-legged gallows, a small curve, o, a looped glyph, y), and the short labels at f73r.26 and f73v.25 are both o, a gallows, y. But each label is only about a hundred pixels wide in the public scan, and at that size I cannot tell which gallows stands in the short label on f73v or whether the looped glyph in the long one is the ordinary form or the variant RF1b marks. So my look neither supports ZL's reading over RF1b's nor the reverse; the disputed glyphs need a higher-resolution image than this server gives.

detail.statement: A third visual count for P-L4-002 on the Beinecke f69v scan (canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006199, the step's own region pct:6,15,27,61 at 1900 pixels). Exposure: I had read the step and so knew the count of 28 and the claimed alternation before looking; after counting I read the three earlier replies on this step. This is an independent recount, not a blind one. I counted the green caps one by one, clockwise from the cap nearest twelve o'clock, noting each bar's colour as I went: 28 caps, the bars dark blue and pale grey-green in turn with no break, 14 of each; the dark bars reach further out than the pale ones, so the caps sit on two radii. One dark bar, at about four o'clock, is a darker blue-green than the rest. That agrees with both earlier counts. What I add from the same view: the bars spring from a disc at whose centre a cream-coloured star is drawn, its rays dividing the disc into sectors washed in blue and filled with small stars, with one sector at the top painted a solid dark blue-green in which I see no stars. I tried to count the rays on a close crop (region 1650,1450,560,560) and could not settle it: I count seven, possibly eight, and my first count at lower magnification was six, so I give no number. Around the bars stands one short radial word per bar, and outside those three rings of text; in the pinned transliteration the page has 3 circular lines and 28 radial lines, which matches one word per bar. The point for the mansion reading is only this: the centre has its own division and one marked sector, and a proposal that reads the 28 as lunar mansions should say what those are and how many, which needs a ray count by someone with a better view than mine. I did not reach the Bodleian or other comparison images from this seat (the network sandbox refuses those hosts), so I add nothing on the comparison; and I ran no test on the words, which two seats have already done. The count of 28 remains compatible with any tradition of mansions and with none. Later addition: on a second, closer crop made for P-L4-011 (region 1500,1250,900,950) I count eight rays, as a best count, and see one or two stars showing through the paint of the solid sector, so 'no stars' above should read 'almost none'.

statement: A third visual count for P-L4-002 on the Beinecke f69v scan (canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006199, the step's own region pct:6,15,27,61 at 1900 pixels). This is an independent recount, not a blind one. I counted the green caps one by one, clockwise from the cap nearest twelve o'clock, noting each bar's colour as I went: 28 caps, the bars dark blue and pale grey-green in turn with no break, 14 of each; the dark bars reach further out than the pale ones, so the caps sit on two radii. One dark bar, at about four o'clock, is a darker blue-green than the rest. That agrees with both earlier counts. What I add from the same view: the bars spring from a disc at whose centre a cream-coloured star is drawn, its rays dividing the disc into sectors washed in blue and filled with small stars, with one sector at the top painted a solid dark blue-green in which I see no stars. I tried to count the rays on a close crop (region 1650,1450,560,560) and could not settle it: I count seven, possibly eight, and my first count at lower magnification was six, so I give no number. Around the bars stands one short radial word per bar, and outside those three rings of text; in the pinned transliteration the page has 3 circular lines and 28 radial lines, which matches one word per bar. f42v.leaves: one cluster or whorl of about six large entire elliptic leaves partway up a bare stem

ambiguous: Droseraceae (Drosera: coiled scape and fringed leaves)

f56r.underground: a plaited or twisted root drawn in outline

detail.statement: A further masked round on the four panels of P-L4-006 (f36v, f23r, f42v, f56r; Yale canvases 1006145, 1006118, 1006157, 1006184, full pages at 1300 pixels). From the record I took only each panel's folio and canvas; the candidate, feature, guess and comparison fields were not displayed until my own observations were written to a file and hashed (sha256 44ee5cf68506f172e8529d36d27def39c42cb36ab8b48d0b066d3a386416c058 of the observation file reproduced below under 'sample'). Exposure, logged before viewing: I had read the step statement, so I knew that one of the four proposals lies in a broad Boraginaceae and that f42v is compared with Goeppertia loeseneri; from general reading I recalled that f56r has long been likened to a sundew; I had not read the other seats' replies, though the desk's list of steps had shown me a title saying a third annotator gave the same four genera as the first, without naming them. I viewed whole pages, not masked crops. First guesses, one family and genus each, all at low confidence: f36v Fabaceae, Lupinus (palmate fans of narrow leaflets up one stem, dense terminal clusters of small round units); f23r Geraniaceae, Geranium (palmately cut leaves, flat blue five- or six-petalled flowers with a ringed centre, thick jointed horizontal rhizome), Ranunculaceae listed as the ambiguous alternative; f42v Melanthiaceae, Paris (one whorl of about six entire elliptic leaves on a bare stem, a single terminal star of pointed segments holding a dark body); f56r Boraginaceae, Heliotropium (a coiled, unrolling flowering axis with blue units along one side, blue funnel-shaped flowers, two basal leaves fringed with narrow teeth), Droseraceae listed as the alternative. After the reveal: against Tucker and Talbert's proposals (Dorstenia contrajerva, Ribes malvaceum, a Calathea now Goeppertia loeseneri, Phacelia campanularia) that is 0 of 4 genera and 1 of 4 families, and the one family match is the family I had been told beforehand, so the uncontaminated count is 0 of 3. Against the first annotator's masked guesses my four are identical in genus. I cannot claim that agreement as independent in the strict sense: these are the plants a European-trained reader reaches for, and two readers drawing on the same training are not two samples of the truth. What it does show is that the drawings' visible features lead repeatedly to the same Old World genera and not to the published New World ones, which is the comparison the step asks for. On f42v specifically, the published comparison rests on a star-like structure raised on its own stalk; Paris has exactly that (a single flower of narrow pointed segments round a dark ovary, above one whorl of entire leaves), so that feature does not separate the New World candidate from a common European plant, and the step's remark that it favours Goeppertia was made against an African comparison only. No word-to-plant pairing follows from any of this.
detail.title: Fourth annotator on P-L4-006: the same four first guesses again (Lupinus, Geranium, Paris, Heliotropium), none of Tucker and Talbert's genera; only the family I was told about beforehand matches

detail.statement: P-G-006 has been handed back six times (fleet-sol, fleet-blue, fleet-fable, fleet-opus twice, fleet-blue out of time), while one seat (fleet-blue, branch P-G-006-fleet-blue) did file a generator: an a priori language with subject-marked roots that reproduces 17 of 17 established facts on the practice split, all of which meaningless reuse chains also reproduce (P-G-007, P-G-009). By the step's own rule that earns nothing beyond what meaningless text earns. What P-G-006 can still add are its meaning-linked predictions: section words follow the subject (already covered by F-018, which a one-table chain with one memory per dialect also meets), and labels share roots with the text about the same object. The second is exactly what the picture-text statistics measure: label_in_page_text (a label recurs in its own page's running text more than in other pages') and feature_label_share (objects that look alike carry labels sharing first or last glyph groups), on branch code-P-L4-013-fleet-opus, with a null that deals labels among objects. So: (1) register those two as facts on the hidden pages as soon as AGREED picture annotations exist (closed vocabulary, branch M-L4-picture-vocab-fleet-fable), with thresholds fixed before looking; (2) check that a one-table reuse chain does NOT meet them (a meaningless procedure has no access to the drawings, so it should not); (3) only if the manuscript passes and the chain fails is it worth designing further invented languages, and then each must predict the measured label-figure fit, not the 17 text facts. Until (1), re-offering the full language-design task spends sessions on a target that cannot discriminate.

detail.statement: P-L4-011 asks first for a marker on the scan that fixes a starting slot and direction for the 28 radial words of f69v, so that a single alignment can be tested instead of the best of 56. I looked for one on the Yale scan (canvas 1006199; regions 1300,650,1300,700 for the top of the wheel and 1500,1250,900,950 for the centre, each at 1700 pixels), without consulting any mansion list or the earlier seats' alignments. Three things are on the page. (1) Each of the three rings of circular text has a clear blank gap at the top of the wheel, wider than its ordinary word spaces, and the three gaps lie one under another at about twelve o'clock. The pinned transliteration's page note says the same in its own terms (text assumed to start after a wide gap near eleven o'clock), so the transcriber saw it independently. (2) The centre is a cream star whose rays cut the disc into sectors washed pale blue and scattered with small stars; on the closer crop I count eight rays and eight sectors, which is my best count and not a certain one (in my earlier note on P-L4-002 I could not settle it between seven and eight). One sector, the one pointing up toward the gap, is painted over in solid dark blue-green, heavily enough that only one or two stars show through. No other sector is treated so. (3) One of the fourteen dark bars, at about four o'clock, is a darker teal than its fellows; I take this for uneven paint and not a marker, since nothing in the text answers to it. So the page offers one start cue, given twice: the break in all three text rings and the marked sector beneath it, both at the top. Direction follows from the script: the ring text reads clockwise, and the radial words are written to be read from the same side, so the natural order is clockwise from the gap. What the cue does not fix is the exact slot. The gap spans about the width of two bar spacings, and the marked sector covers about three and a half bars (28 bars over 8 sectors), so the first radial word is the one over the bar at twelve o'clock or one of its two neighbours. Proposal, to be frozen before anyone looks at a name list again: test exactly three alignments, clockwise, starting at the radial word nearest twelve o'clock and at the one on either side of it, and correct for three, not for 56 and not for both directions. If the transliteration's convention of numbering the radial lines from about half past nine is kept, twelve o'clock falls roughly six places on from the first radial line (two and a half hours of twelve, over 28 slots); I have not measured angles on the scan, so the three line ids must be fixed by someone who does, before any list is consulted. For the nominal length association already reported with a reversed alignment: it is described as a reverse alignment; if that means counter-clockwise, the script's direction does not support it and it would not be among the alignments to test. I did not check its starting slot against the gap. Limits: the heavy paint on one sector could be a painter's accident; the gaps could mark where each ring of text happened to close, not where the series begins; and eight sectors against twenty-eight bars has no obvious meaning in any mansion scheme I know, which a proposal for this page should address. Addendum, fixing the three line ids without measuring: the pinned transliteration gives a clock position on every radial line of this page (I had overlooked that; my earlier search for such markers covered label lines only). By those markers the radial line at twelve o'clock is f69v.9, with f69v.8 at half past eleven and f69v.10 at a quarter past twelve; the first radial line, f69v.4, is at half past nine, so twelve o'clock is five places on, not the 'roughly six' I estimated above. On the scan the short word standing over the bar at twelve o'clock is consistent with the transliteration's reading of f69v.9, as far as I can read it. The three alignments proposed are therefore: clockwise, starting at f69v.8, at f69v.9 and at f69v.10, and no others. One more candidate cue comes from the transliteration itself and should be weighed against the gap: its last radial line, f69v.31 at a quarter to nine, is the only radial line it gives as two words, and the transcriber chose to begin just after it; whether that reflects something on the page (a wider space, a different hand) or only convention I did not check, and if it is taken as a start cue it adds a fourth alignment at f69v.4, to be declared with the other three before any list is tried.

detail.statement: Two independent checks of P-L4-004's finding. (1) Transcription structure (pinned ZL3b, line ids and unit codes only): on each of the twelve zodiac pages I looked for label lines after the last circular text line, i.e. inside the innermost ring. Only f70v2 has one, f70v2.33, and it carries no clock position (as a centre label would not). f70v1 has five label lines after its last circular line (f70v1.13-.17), but their ZL clock positions run 10:30, 00:00, 02:00, 05:00, 08:00 round the circle, so they are the inner ring's figure labels, not a centre label. f71r, f71v, f72r1, f72r2, f72r3, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r and f73v end on a circular text line, with no label inside it. (2) Scan, during blind picture annotation of seven centres (PIC-f70v2, f72r3, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v, fleet-opus): every centre shows the emblem (fish pair, two clawed animals, balance, blue-robed figure, four-legged animal with sprig, crossbowman, small four-legged animal with curled tail), mostly with one star; the only writing in each centre other than f70v2 is a single word beneath or beside the emblem in a hand and ink that differ from the ring text (darker on f72v2), which matches the Latin-script month annotations, and none has a transcription line of its own. On f70v2 the centre has two writings: a word between the fish and a Voynich word beside the upper star; the step identifies the latter as the one freestanding Voynich string, which fits f70v2.33 being the only centre label line. So no Voynich word is paired with a month annotation inside any zodiac centre; the one centre label (f70v2.33) stands beside a star, not beside the month word. I did not check the month words' spelling or hand date.

detail.statement: P-L4-008 asks, besides a masked rating round that needs comparison plates I cannot reach from this seat, for two things to be settled on the Voynich drawing itself: whether two oak-like leaves genuinely sit below the crown, and how the roots end. I looked at f35v on the Yale scan (canvas 1006143, full size 2853 by 3769; regions pct:50,5,48,60 for the upper plant and pct:20,68,78,30 for the root, at 1500 and 1700 pixels). I had not seen the step's rubric or its comparison plates; I had seen the page before, for a second look at anchor N-005, and knew that it has been compared with ivy and with oak. Leaves below the crown: yes, two, unmistakably separate from the crown. One stands at the left about halfway down the stem, one at the right a little higher; each is a single flat blade on its own curved stalk, with five to seven rounded lobes a side divided by open rounded sinuses, painted the same dark green as the crown. Their stalks leave the thin pale side stems, not the main stem. The crown itself is drawn with the same lobed outline repeated many times and overlapping, so the two lower leaves read as the crown's leaf shown once in isolation. Other things in the same view that a rubric should have a line for: a sheaf of fine parallel lines running from the main stem up into the base of the crown; about fifteen clusters of round blue-green bodies, three to eight to a cluster, each cluster hanging from a thin looped stalk off the side stems, with two clusters partly painted red-brown low on the left; and two pale side stems that leave the base, bow outward and cross: I see one crossing low on the plant, where the two side stems pass over each other and the main stem, and a second higher up, where the left side stem arches over the main stem to the right. I count that as two crossings; the upper one is a side stem over the main stem, not the two side stems over each other, which a rubric line about a 'doubled crossing' should make explicit. Roots: the root is complete on the scan; nothing is cut off by the image. It is red-brown, with one long arm running left along the foot of the page and ending in three or four thin upturned hooks, a row of short downward fingers along its underside, and on the right two or three short thick arms that curl back on themselves. The lowest fingers end at or within a hair of the lower edge of the leaf, so whether a few tips were lost when the leaf was trimmed cannot be told from the scan; the outline shows no finger that is plainly severed. So on the two criteria the step says no comparator met: a double crossing of stems is there in the sense just described, and the root is strongly lopsided and hooked as described. I add no score for any comparator and no opinion on ivy or oak; on this page the fruit clusters and the twining stems point one way and the leaf shape another, which is the step's own conclusion.

detail.check: From data/raw/ZL3b-n.txt take every zodiac figure label (unit Lz) with its first clock marker; group by page and by the label block it stands in; keep groups of seven or more; pair labels across pages by nearest clock position and count exact and one-glyph agreements against the second ring turned by a random angle. detail.statement: The earlier tests of whether the zodiac figure labels repeat from sign to sign (P-L4-007, P-L4-010) had to search over rotations, because the order of the labels in a ring was taken from the transcription's line order. The pinned Zandbergen-Landini file gives more than order: every figure label on the twelve zodiac pages carries the clock position of its figure. That allows a test with a single alignment fixed in advance by the page itself: if the figures stood for a fixed series tied to position in the wheel (days or degrees counted from a common point), the label at a given clock position on one sign should recur at the same clock position on another. Method, public pages only, one transliteration: the 21 rings and rows of figure labels on the twelve zodiac pages that hold seven or more labels (ring sizes 19 and 10; 10 on each of four pages; 15 and 9; 12, 11 and 7; 18 and 12 twice; 20 and 10; 16 and 10 twice; the five-label inner rings and the short top rows are left out); for every pair of rings on different pages and every label of the first, the label of the second whose clock position is nearest; first word of the label only, uncertain readings taken at their first alternative. Null: the second ring turned by a random angle, 400 times. Result: 2 exact agreements in 2415 comparisons against a null mean of 4.1 (p = 0.94); within one glyph, 37 against 33.7 (p = 0.27). So with the alignment fixed by the page and no freedom to rotate, labels at the same place in the wheel do not agree across signs any more than labels at random places do, which removes the one loophole the rotation-searching tests left (that their correction for searching hid a true alignment). It agrees with both earlier results. Limits: I pooled every pair of rings, so outer rings are also compared with inner ones, which a roster split by ring would not predict to match and which dilutes any effect confined to same-ring pairs; clock positions in the file are given to the nearest quarter or half hour, coarser than the spacing of figures in the larger rings, so nearest-position pairing is off by a figure fairly often and an exact positional roster could be blurred by that; rings differ in size, so the same clock position is not the same ordinal; one transliteration. A same-ring-only run and a run by ordinal from a common starting clock position are the obvious next variants and should be declared before they are run. Addendum: the same-ring-only variant, run after it was declared above. Rings were classed by size within their page, the largest as outer (twelve rings, one per sign) and the rest as inner (nine rings); only outer with outer and inner with inner were compared (the two inner rings of f72r3 are thereby also compared with each other, a small impurity). Result: 0 exact agreements in 1239 comparisons against 2.0 under random turning; within one glyph 15 against 16.0 (p = 0.65). Planted control on the same data: I gave one clock position, chosen at random, the same word on every outer ring and reran the test thirty times (100 turnings each); it was detected at p of 0.05 or less in 30 of 30 runs, and likewise with two and with three shared positions. So this test would see a single position in the wheel that carried the same label on every sign, and the manuscript has none. What it cannot exclude is a roster whose words change from sign to sign by more than one glyph, or one tied to ordinal position in rings of different sizes; the by-ordinal variant I did not run, because it is in substance the same-position, no-offset comparison already on the record in P-L4-007 (0.18% of positions agreeing, no more than at arbitrary offsets), which takes labels in the transcription's ring order. Second addendum, removing the one-transliteration limit on the same-ring variant: with the clock positions taken from Zandbergen-Landini and the words from each of the three pinned transliterations in turn, by line id (first word of each label), exact agreements at the same clock position across signs are 0 of 1239 for Zandbergen-Landini (2.0 expected under random turning), 1 of 1239 for Takahashi (1.6 expected, p = 0.84) and 1 of 1239 for the RF reading (1.2 expected, p = 0.71). No reading shows a positional roster.
detail.title: A clock-aligned version of the zodiac label test, with no rotation left free: labels at the same clock position on different signs do not match (2 exact agreements in 2415 comparisons against 4.1 expected)

detail.check: registry items C-002, C-042, C-050 and the four K-*-001 grid cells cited; P-J-003 open
detail.statement: Checked on the record (registry/items.jsonl on origin/main): the three proxies K-016-open-2 asks for are already corpora: Catalan C-002 (Maspons i Labros, Lo rondallayre, 1875), Galician C-042 (Lopez Ferreiro, O Castelo de Pambre, 1895), Old Occitan C-050 (Mahn, Die Werke der Troubadours, vol. 1). Their grid cells are K-catalan-substitution-001 FAIL, K-catalan-verbose-001 FAIL, K-galician-substitution-001 FAIL, K-old_occitan-substitution-001 FAIL. So the family Cheshire's proposal leans on is tested at the grid's measured power in all three and fails. Only the Old Occitan corpus is a medieval text; the Catalan and Galician ones are nineteenth-century prose, so a period mismatch remains for those two. The open work is therefore: (1) the medieval Galician-Portuguese corpus already proposed as P-J-003 (the Cantigas, verse-only); (2) a period Catalan text under an open licence (e.g. Llull or a chancery text); then the substitution and verbose cells for both. Until then, K-016-open-2 should not be re-offered as 'add the corpora'.

corpus.json.notes: License: printed 1846; the archive.org item https://archive.org/details/diewerkedertroub01mahnuoft (contributor Robarts - University of Toronto) is marked possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT. Why this file: the grid already has Catalan (two texts), Galician (1895) and Portuguese (modern Bible), so of the three proxies the step names only Occitan was missing, and it is the one closest in period to the manuscript; this edition is almost entirely Old Occitan verse and prose. Size: 771,281 bytes of OCR; vs/refcorpus.normalize(..., 'old_occitan') gives 589,721 characters. Contamination, measured: lines with two or more common German function words make up about 4.6% of the file (Mahn's German preface and occasional headings); French-like lines about 0.1%. Most frequent words after cleaning are e, que, qu, de, en, no, per, ni, es, non, ieu, lo, vos, ab, mas, as expected for Old Occitan. OCR quality: the Occitan verse reads cleanly on inspection (e.g. the vida of Arnaut de Maruelh); apostrophes and elisions (qu', d', s') become separate one-letter words after normalization. detail.statement: The question left open by Gaskell and Bowern has two halves: can a long session of human-produced pseudotext show the manuscript's clustering of vocabulary by page and by section, or, failing new human samples, can a frozen model motivated by what their volunteers did. The second half already has an answer on this record, and I set it out here so that the question is not worked twice; the evidence is my own earlier work, so this is a pointer and a statement of limits, not an independent result. The model: a glyph chain over the line with ONE table fitted on all public training pages, no drift, no window, nothing fitted by position; its only memory is reuse at the start of a word, with probability 0.20 one of the last 15 words with one glyph changed, and with probability 0.45 a word that stands at least twice among the last 300 words, written again whole. That is copying and varying what was just written, which is the strategy self-citation proposals describe and, as I recall but have not re-checked in the paper, among those the volunteers reported. Written as a whole book (4,500 ordinary and 740 paragraph-opening lines) laid onto every page and measured on the public evaluation pages, it met all 17 facts then established on 3 of 3 seeds (P-G-017), and those include the three the question is about, jointly and in one text: words recur within their page more than chance (F-009), pages close together share more words than pages far apart (F-011: 0.060, 0.043, 0.058 against the manuscript's 0.074), and which word is written depends on the section (F-018). So local clustering and drift across sections arise together from a stationary procedure with a memory of a few hundred words; no section-specific table is needed, because a memory that turns over more slowly than a section is long makes sections differ by itself. What it did not reproduce with one table is the contrast between the two Currier languages (F-020); that needed two tables with separate memories (P-G-018), which is a statement about two stocks of habits, not about meaning. Limits, which are large. All of this is on the public practice split and under my proposed whole-book layout; the hidden-page verdicts on record are for the individual fact attacks, not for the whole-book text. The settings were chosen by me after seeing failures at neighbouring settings (whole-word reuse at 0.25 held F-011 on one seed of two, at 0.35 from 300 words it failed), so the model is frozen now but was not frozen before the comparison, and the margin on F-011 is thin. And it is a procedure, not people: nothing here shows that a human writer sustains such a memory over two hundred pages, which is what the first half of the question asks. That half needs new long handwritten samples and cannot be done by an agent; the useful specification for whoever collects them is the one the model suggests, namely that the session be long enough for the writer's stock of familiar words to turn over several times (several thousand words at least), and that page and section breaks be imposed on the writer's text afterwards at the manuscript's sizes, not chosen by the writer. Addendum, a re-scoring and not a fresh run: I scored the three whole-book texts of P-G-017 again, as they stand on my disk, with the whole-book cut that is now in the main code (the earlier figures came from my own branch of it), on the practice split. All three texts meet all three facts. Page vocabulary (F-009): 0.338, 0.331, 0.325 against the manuscript's 0.311. Neighbouring pages (F-011): 0.060, 0.043, 0.058 against 0.074. Section vocabulary (F-018): 0.865, 0.868, 0.935 bits against 1.183. So the joint result survives the change of code path, and it also shows where the procedure falls short of the manuscript while still passing: its section effect is about three quarters of the manuscript's and its neighbour effect two thirds to four fifths, so the manuscript clusters more strongly by section and by neighbourhood than this stationary memory alone produces. These are the same three texts, not new seeds; the check's fresh-seed run is still owed.

check: Recompute from the pinned ZL3b file: labels of unit Lz on the twelve zodiac pages that carry a clock comment, word breaks removed; cross-page pairs within 15 degrees; within-ring shuffle. A separate seat should test the low-side observation as a registered prediction before it is given any weight, with the window fixed in advance, for example on Takahashi's transliteration placed by the same positions.

detail.check: Recompute from the pinned ZL3b file: labels of unit Lz on the twelve zodiac pages that carry a clock comment, word breaks removed; cross-page pairs within 15 degrees; within-ring shuffle. A separate seat should test the low-side observation as a registered prediction before it is given any weight, with the window fixed in advance, for example on Takahashi's transliteration placed by the same positions.
detail.statement: P-L4-010 compares labels at equal positions in the transcription's list. This extension uses where each label stands on the page instead. The ZL transcription records a clock position for 298 figure labels on the twelve zodiac pages. I took every pair of labels on two different pages whose recorded positions lie within 15 degrees of each other, in any ring (4,902 pairs), and counted how many pairs are the same word, and how many are the same or one glyph apart. No rotation is fitted: the hypothesis tested is a roster tied to fixed places round the wheel. Null: the labels of each ring of each page shuffled among that ring's positions, 1,000 shuffles. The design was fixed before the run and run once; the lower-tail figures below were computed afterwards, when the result turned out to lie on the low side. Result, upper tail: ZL3b 0 identical pairs against a null mean of 5.1 (p = 1.0), 44 within one glyph against 47.4 (p = 0.74); IT2a 1 against 4.0 (p = 0.99) and 42 against 43.8 (p = 0.65); RF1b 1 against 4.3 (p = 0.99) and 29 against 37.1 (p = 0.94), IT2a and RF1b labels placed by ZL's positions for the same loci. Power: writing one word at 3 o'clock in the outer ring of every page is detected in 40 of 40 trials in each transliteration. So there is no roster of words tied to places round the wheel, which agrees with P-L4-010 and P-L4-007 by a route that does not depend on list order or starting figure. The low side: identical labels at matching positions are fewer than chance, 0 where about 5 are expected (lower-tail p = 0.005 in ZL3b, 0.08 in IT2a, 0.05 in RF1b, 3,000 shuffles). This was not predicted and I do not claim it; it would mean that when a word is used again on another page it tends to stand elsewhere on the wheel. Limits: positions are ZL's half-hour clock readings, not measurements; the 15 degree window was my choice and I tried no other; pages with 15 labels and pages with 30 are pooled.
detail.title: Extension of P-L4-010 by position on the page: zodiac figure labels standing at the same clock position on different pages agree no more often than shuffled labels, and in ZL they never agree at all

check: recompute H1/H2 for the four encodings on vs.facts.ref_words('latin', 60000) with the stated constructions; per-source normalisation = H2 x (output length / source length)

detail.check: recompute H1/H2 for the four encodings on vs.facts.ref_words('latin', 60000) with the stated constructions; per-source normalisation = H2 x (output length / source length)
detail.statement: Computed on 60,000 words of the pinned Latin reference text (vs.facts.ref_words('latin')), lower-cased, words joined by spaces. H1 = single-symbol entropy, H2 = conditional entropy of a symbol given the previous one (Bennett's second-order), both in bits. Encodings: (a) a random letter substitution; (b) a reversible verbose code mapping each letter to a fixed distinct pair drawn from 12 new symbols (space kept), length x1.84; (c) padding: a fixed null symbol after every letter, same length x1.84. Results, per output character / per source character (H2 x length ratio): source H2 3.358 / 3.358; substitution 3.358 / 3.358; verbose H1 3.495, H2 2.528 / 4.660; padding H1 3.139, H2 2.097 / 3.866. So (1) normalised by the length of the original source the fall does not persist: per source character the second-order entropy rises under both expansions, because a one-symbol context covers half a source letter; (2) against a matched padding control the verbose fall is not unusual: padding, which adds no information and encodes nothing, lowers per-character H2 further (2.10) than the verbose code (2.53). A low per-glyph H2 in the manuscript therefore cannot by itself point to a verbose cipher over a meaningless or a padded text; any claim needs the per-source-unit comparison and a padding control at the same expansion. Replication across four reference languages and three random codebooks each (H2 per output character / per source character): latin    source 3.36 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.53/4.66 2.47/4.56 2.50/4.61 | padding 2.10/3.87; italian  source 3.12 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.44/4.41 2.47/4.47 2.47/4.47 | padding 2.08/3.76; german   source 3.06 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.50/4.53 2.45/4.44 2.42/4.39 | padding 2.07/3.76; english  source 3.29 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.58/4.67 2.59/4.68 2.53/4.57 | padding 2.16/3.91. Every codebook in every language shows the same pattern: per-character H2 falls by about 0.6-0.8 bits, per-source-character H2 rises by about 1.2-1.4 bits, and padding lowers per-character H2 about 0.4 bits more than the verbose code. This is stable enough to register as a fact about the measure, not about the manuscript.
detail.title: Entropy fall under reversible symbol expansion disappears per source character and is matched by padding (4 languages x 3 codebooks)

Results, per output character / per source character (H2 x length ratio): source H2 3.358 / 3.358; substitution 3.358 / 3.358; verbose H1 3.495, H2 2.528 / 4.660; padding H1 3.139, H2 2.097 / 3.866. So (1) normalised by the length of the original source the fall does not persist: per source character the second-order entropy rises under both expansions, because a one-symbol context covers half a source letter; (2) against a matched padding control the verbose fall is not unusual: padding, which adds no information and encodes nothing, lowers per-character H2 further (2.10) than the verbose code (2.53). A low per-glyph H2 in the manuscript therefore cannot by itself point to a verbose cipher over a meaningless or a padded text; any claim needs the per-source-unit comparison and a padding control at the same expansion. Replication across four reference languages and three random codebooks each (H2 per output character / per source character): latin    source 3.36 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.53/4.66 2.47/4.56 2.50/4.61 | padding 2.10/3.87; italian  source 3.12 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.44/4.41 2.47/4.47 2.47/4.47 | padding 2.08/3.76; german   source 3.06 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.50/4.53 2.45/4.44 2.42/4.39 | padding 2.07/3.76; english  source 3.29 | verbose seeds (per char/per source) 2.58/4.67 2.59/4.68 2.53/4.57 | padding 2.16/3.91. Every codebook in every language shows the same pattern: per-character H2 falls by about 0.6-0.8 bits, per-source-character H2 rises by about 1.2-1.4 bits, and padding lowers per-character H2 about 0.4 bits more than the verbose code. This is stable enough to register as a fact about the measure, not about the manuscript.

No star label line id is assigned to a star: the line ids carry no position and the blind rule forbids reading the words. picture.json.statement: Circular diagram on canvas 1006205 (72v, part). Centre: a balance (upright post, horizontal beam, two pans on cords) with blue wash, and a short word in another script below it (not read). Inner ring: 10 nude women; outer ring: 20 nude women; none stands in a tub. All are drawn radially with feet toward the centre (standing at the top, lying at the sides, upside down at the bottom), and each holds or is tied to an eight-pointed star; several inner stars have blue centres. One outer figure near the top wears a tall pointed crown and has a star on each side. A hole in the vellum right of centre takes most of one inner figure. Choosing the panel: the three 72v wheels are spread over canvases 1006204 and 1006205; this wheel's counts (20 outer, 10 inner) match only f72v1's label blocks (f72v1.2-21: 20 lines; 23-32: 10 lines), while f72v2 and f72v3 both have 18 and 12. Each figure carries its ring's block as label_group; which line goes with which figure cannot be fixed from line ids without reading the words, so labels are null. Clock positions are from the wheel's centre, 12 = top of the scan.

Two rings of nude standing figures without tubs, each with a star and a short label, and four more nude figures in a row outside the wheel above it. The label lines fall into groups of 4, 16 and 10, which I give to the top row (left to right, four figures counted on the scan), the outer ring and the inner ring; I did not manage a secure independent count of the ring figures on this faint drawing, so the 16 and 10 rest on the label groups. Labels assigned from line ids and unit codes only, words not read; ring labels run clockwise from the figure at the top by my assumption, so ids may be rotated by a constant within a ring. Ring figures carry generic features only. Green stains at the lower left look like offset or show-through, not drawing.

Below three lines of text: a face with wavy hair in a circle ringed by small flame- or crescent-shaped ochre marks (upper centre), and at the bottom a face in a circle edged by a yellow crescent and a blue ring, with writing round it. A faint large arc partly encloses the field and a faint pale wash lies behind its middle. Choosing the panel: the 29 stars match f68r1's 29 star-label lines (f68r1.8-36); the middle panel's five top text lines match f68r2. Each star carries that block as label_group. detail.statement: Measured on the record at the time of writing: 21 blind picture annotations of 6 folios (f66r, f67r2, f70v2, f72r3, f75v, f99r) by five seats, 27 pairs of seats on the same folio, scored with the record's own picture_agreement. Agreement ranges from 0.20 to 0.75 with a median of 0.45; no pair reaches the 0.80 that makes a folio AGREED. The loss is not in what the seats saw. Matched objects agree on kind in every pair (median 1.00). On the features both seats happened to name, the median agreement is 0.25, and a matched object shares only about three feature names with its partner. Feature by feature, over all pairs: closed-answer features agree (sex 1.00, cheeks 1.00, facing 1.00, ring 0.81, points 0.80, clothing 0.75), free-wording features do not (posture 0.04, position 0.03, shape 0.03, star 0.00, container_pattern 0.05, colour 0.30, container 0.39). Two seats who both write that a figure stands in a tub score zero on posture unless they chose the same sentence. Label pairing is the second leak: the median share of object matches made through a shared label line is 0.20 (range 0 to 1), because several seats left ring figures unpaired while others paired them clockwise from an assumed start; unpaired objects are then matched by kind in list order, which compares unrelated figures. Consequence: as scored, the picture data will stay DRAFT however many seats annotate, and the picture-text tests that wait on agreed data cannot start. This is a statement about the scoring and the instructions, not about any seat's annotation. I am one of the five seats (eleven of my own folios are in or on their way to the record), so this is not an outside audit; the numbers are reproducible from the registry. Addendum, measured later on every seat's pushed annotation of twelve folios (the six above and f68r1, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v; 44 annotations by five seats, read only after my own were submitted), using quantities that do not depend on wording. The seats agree on structure almost everywhere. Figures per ring are identical for every seat on every wheel that was annotated in full: 19 and 10 on f70v2, 20 and 10 on f72v1, 18 and 12 on f72v2, 16 and 10 with 4 on top on f73r and on f73v, and 12, 11 and 7 on f72r3 where one seat of three has 13 in the outer ring; on f72v3 two seats have 18 and 12 and one has 15 and 12. All seats describe the same wheel as f72v2 (a clothed figure in blue) and the same as f72v3 (a four-legged animal with a small plant behind it). On f68r1 all four seats count 29 stars, and their counts of stars with a mark at the centre are 10, 10, 11 and 11, three of the four splitting them the same way (8 or 9 with a small ring, 2 with a dark dot). On f67r2 the three seats give the identical order of red and yellow moons round the ring. On f75v all four pair the ten upper figures with the same ten label lines. On f99r all four give the jars the same four label lines; the three seats who paired every object agree on the kind of object (jar, detached part, whole plant) for every one of the 29 or 30 label lines they share, and differ only in which of two neighbouring labels they left unpaired in rows 2 and 3. Colour on the same f99r objects shows what free wording costs: for label-matched objects the colour strings are identical in 8 to 12 of about 30, but name at least one colour in common in 17 to 27 of them. Caution on independence: some of these counts may lean on the label-group sizes in the transcription's line ids, as some of mine did, so agreement on a count is not always two independent counts from the scan; the moon order, the star centre marks, the blue caps and the object kinds are read from the scan alone. The point for the scoring: the annotations already agree on what is drawn to a degree the present score (0.20 to 0.75) does not show, and a score built on kinds, counts, ring membership, label pairing and a few closed features would let most of these folios pass.

A code pull request changing picture_agreement or the instructions is for a person to review; existing annotations can be re-keyed to the fixed list by their own authors without looking at the scan again. Passing check: on the re-keyed annotations the median pairwise agreement on the six folios is reported, and it is stated how many folios reach 0.80.
step.json.statement: Measured on the record at the time of writing: 21 blind picture annotations of 6 folios (f66r, f67r2, f70v2, f72r3, f75v, f99r) by five seats, 27 pairs of seats on the same folio, scored with the record's own picture_agreement. Agreement ranges from 0.20 to 0.75 with a median of 0.45; no pair reaches the 0.80 that makes a folio AGREED. The loss is not in what the seats saw. Matched objects agree on kind in every pair (median 1.00). On the features both seats happened to name, the median agreement is 0.25, and a matched object shares only about three feature names with its partner. Feature by feature, over all pairs: closed-answer features agree (sex 1.00, cheeks 1.00, facing 1.00, ring 0.81, points 0.80, clothing 0.75), free-wording features do not (posture 0.04, position 0.03, shape 0.03, star 0.00, container_pattern 0.05, colour 0.30, container 0.39). Two seats who both write that a figure stands in a tub score zero on posture unless they chose the same sentence. Label pairing is the second leak: the median share of object matches made through a shared label line is 0.20 (range 0 to 1), because several seats left ring figures unpaired while others paired them clockwise from an assumed start; unpaired objects are then matched by kind in list order, which compares unrelated figures. Consequence: as scored, the picture data will stay DRAFT however many seats annotate, and the picture-text tests that wait on agreed data cannot start. This is a statement about the scoring and the instructions, not about any seat's annotation. I am one of the five seats (eleven of my own folios are in or on their way to the record), so this is not an outside audit; the numbers are reproducible from the registry. Addendum, measured later on every seat's pushed annotation of twelve folios (the six above and f68r1, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v; 44 annotations by five seats, read only after my own were submitted), using quantities that do not depend on wording. The seats agree on structure almost everywhere. Figures per ring are identical for every seat on every wheel that was annotated in full: 19 and 10 on f70v2, 20 and 10 on f72v1, 18 and 12 on f72v2, 16 and 10 with 4 on top on f73r and on f73v, and 12, 11 and 7 on f72r3 where one seat of three has 13 in the outer ring; on f72v3 two seats have 18 and 12 and one has 15 and 12. All seats describe the same wheel as f72v2 (a clothed figure in blue) and the same as f72v3 (a four-legged animal with a small plant behind it). On f68r1 all four seats count 29 stars, and their counts of stars with a mark at the centre are 10, 10, 11 and 11, three of the four splitting them the same way (8 or 9 with a small ring, 2 with a dark dot). On f67r2 the three seats give the identical order of red and yellow moons round the ring. On f75v all four pair the ten upper figures with the same ten label lines. On f99r all four give the jars the same four label lines; the three seats who paired every object agree on the kind of object (jar, detached part, whole plant) for every one of the 29 or 30 label lines they share, and differ only in which of two neighbouring labels they left unpaired in rows 2 and 3. Colour on the same f99r objects shows what free wording costs: for label-matched objects the colour strings are identical in 8 to 12 of about 30, but name at least one colour in common in 17 to 27 of them. Caution on independence: some of these counts may lean on the label-group sizes in the transcription's line ids, as some of mine did, so agreement on a count is not always two independent counts from the scan; the moon order, the star centre marks, the blue caps and the object kinds are read from the scan alone. The point for the scoring: the annotations already agree on what is drawn to a degree the present score (0.20 to 0.75) does not show, and a score built on kinds, counts, ring membership, label pairing and a few closed features would let most of these folios pass.

detail.statement: Annotated from the Beinecke scan alone (the left-hand panel of the three-panel '68r' canvas, with one crop). Under a few lines of text there is a sun at the top, a round face ringed by flame-like rays with three short words inside its circle; a moon at the bottom, a face inside a blue and yellow crescent with a ring of text around it; and between them twenty-nine scattered stars, each with a short label beside it (to its right, except one near the lower left whose label is on its left). The transcription has twenty-nine star-unit label lines (f68r1.8 to f68r1.36), which matches my count of stars. Their order is not known to me: I numbered the stars from top to bottom (left to right where two are level) and paired the label lines in that order, which is an assumption made from the line ids alone, so the star-to-label pairing may be wrong for any star and should not be relied on without a check against the label positions. The sun and moon are not paired with a label line.

detail.statement: Circular diagram, drawn in faint ink. Centre: a standing figure facing left in a blue knee-length tunic and hose, with a broad-brimmed hat, holding a crossbow pointed down and to the left, on a small dark tufted patch of ground. Around it an inner ring of about 10 and an outer ring of about 16 nude women, drawn radially with feet toward the centre, each tied to an eight-pointed ochre star; above the outer ring at the top stand 4 more nude women with stars, outside the circular text. Upper left, just above the outer ring, a dark blot and two open C-shaped strokes; two green patches in the lower left look like stains or offset. The transcription has 4 label lines before the first circular line (f73v.1-4), then blocks of 16 (6-21) and 10 (23-32), matching the 4 top figures, the outer ring and the inner ring. Limits of this annotation: the ring figures are faint and overlap, and in the time I had I did not resolve them one by one, so each ring is recorded as one group with its approximate count and label block; the 4 top figures are recorded individually, left to right. No label is attached to a single figure, because which line goes with which figure cannot be fixed from line ids without reading the words.

detail.statement: Blind annotators may not read label words, and ZL label line ids carry no position, so on circular and star pages they can say which ring a label is in (the counts match the figures exactly: f70v2 19+10, f72r3 12+11+7, f72v1 20+10, f72v2 and f72v3 18+12, f68r1 29 stars) but not which figure it sits beside; most annotations on the record therefore leave 'label' null or guess an order, and the picture-text statistics (P-L4-013, branch code-P-L4-013-fleet-opus) would have almost no labelled objects. The step: for each of f70v2, f72r3, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v and f68r1, a seat that has NOT annotated that folio opens the scan and the ZL transcription and records, for every label line id (unit L), where the label sits: for rings, ring (outer/middle/inner) and clock angle in degrees from the top, clockwise, measured at the label's first glyph; for f68r1, x and y as fractions of the panel. It also records which canvas and which circle it used (f72v2/f72v3 share a canvas and an identical line structure; record which circle carries which ids, which also settles the panel order the annotators had to assume). Output: one JSON file of {locus: {ring, angle_deg} or {x_frac, y_frac}} per folio, submitted as data. The join to picture objects (nearest object in the same ring by angle) is then mechanical and can be added to vs/dsl.py in the same code PR as P-L4-013. Reading the words is allowed for this step because it records positions only, never meanings; the person doing it must not also annotate the drawings of that folio.

anchor.json.statement: UNCERTAIN; HERE IS WHY. What I checked on the scan myself (canvas 1006196, cropped at full resolution): in the upper-left segment of the f68r3 wheel there is one tight cluster of exactly seven small stars, drawn much smaller and closer together than every other star on the page, with a curved line (a tail) running from the cluster down toward the central moon face. Three Voynich words are near it: doaro immediately to the RIGHT of the cluster, on its baseline, nearer to it than to any other star; oalcheol written ALONG the tail line (ZL gives it a different locus type, La); and dchol,day written directly UNDER the single large star to the left, so it belongs to that star. So if any label names the cluster, doaro is the best candidate on the scan, with oalcheol second. The identification of a tight seven-star cluster in an astronomical diagram as the Pleiades (the Seven Sisters, in Taurus) is conventional and has been made repeatedly (ZL page comment 'probably the Pleiades'; darkstar1 2001 per the forum; Bax 2014), but it is an inference from the drawing, not from any writing on the page. The pairing of doaro with a NAME is weaker still: the only published name proposal I know of is Bax's 'Taurus', and I could confirm only indirectly (the image name 'DoarusComment' in a forum transcript) that it concerns this word; I could not read his paper. Names listed: the Latin names of the cluster (Pliades, Pleiades, Vergiliae) and Taurus, because a label beside the Pleiades could name either the cluster or its constellation, and I do not know which. Recommendation to second-lookers: agree only if you can read Bax's paper and confirm the word is doaro, or find a second independent published source pairing this label with the Pleiades or Taurus; otherwise dissent with that reason.

experiment.json.summary: Step: build a label-position map for the zodiac and star pages (each label line id's ring and angle, or x/y, on the scan), made by a seat that has not annotated the folio, so P-L4-013 can join labels to blind picture objects by position.

step.json.check: one positions file per folio; every label line id of the folio present exactly once; ring counts equal the label-line runs between circular text lines; a spot check of three ids per folio by a second seat
step.json.statement: Blind annotators may not read label words, and ZL label line ids carry no position, so on circular and star pages they can say which ring a label is in (the counts match the figures exactly: f70v2 19+10, f72r3 12+11+7, f72v1 20+10, f72v2 and f72v3 18+12, f68r1 29 stars) but not which figure it sits beside; most annotations on the record therefore leave 'label' null or guess an order, and the picture-text statistics (P-L4-013, branch code-P-L4-013-fleet-opus) would have almost no labelled objects. The step: for each of f70v2, f72r3, f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v and f68r1, a seat that has NOT annotated that folio opens the scan and the ZL transcription and records, for every label line id (unit L), where the label sits: for rings, ring (outer/middle/inner) and clock angle in degrees from the top, clockwise, measured at the label's first glyph; for f68r1, x and y as fractions of the panel. It also records which canvas and which circle it used (f72v2/f72v3 share a canvas and an identical line structure; record which circle carries which ids, which also settles the panel order the annotators had to assume). Output: one JSON file of {locus: {ring, angle_deg} or {x_frac, y_frac}} per folio, submitted as data. The join to picture objects (nearest object in the same ring by angle) is then mechanical and can be added to vs/dsl.py in the same code PR as P-L4-013. Reading the words is allowed for this step because it records positions only, never meanings; the person doing it must not also annotate the drawings of that folio.
