detail.statement: P-L4-013 counts only folios whose picture annotations are AGREED. I measured where that stands on the record at commit d28440e, using vs/registry.py's own picture_agreement on the 21 merged annotations (V-001 to V-021) of six folios, three or four seats each; five of the 21 are mine, and I read the others only after submitting my own. Result: no folio is AGREED. Best pairwise agreement per folio: f70v2 0.747, f75v 0.653, f67r2 0.614, f72r3 0.495, f66r 0.474, f99r 0.398; three folios stand as DISAGREE and three as DRAFT. Where the loss comes from, summed over all 596 matched object pairs: the kind agrees in 537 (90%). Features with a closed set of values agree almost always: cheeks 60/60, sex 40/40, facing 12/12, crescent_colour 12/12, ring 219/270, clothing 113/151. Features written as free phrases almost never match as strings although the seats describe the same thing: star 0/177 (one seat writes 'yes', one 'true', one 'attached'), posture 10/246 ('half figure standing in a tub' against 'upper body rising from an upright tub'), position 7/205, shape 4/116 ('disc with crescent' against 'round face inside a crescent'), note 0/13. Colour agrees in only 100/338 partly for the same reason ('uncoloured' against 'ink only, red dots on cheeks') and partly from real differences (on f99r one seat's 'orange' is another's 'red' or 'tan'). The five seats used 144 distinct feature keys, 105 of them used by one seat only, so most recorded features are never compared at all. Second cause: object matching. Only 209 of the 596 pairs were matched by label locus; seven of the 21 annotations give a label to at most one object, so their objects are paired by kind in list order, which pairs unrelated figures whenever two seats walk a ring from different starting points or in different directions (f72r3 ring feature: 5/30 and 6/30 in two pairs for that reason). What simple repairs buy, recomputed on the same data: leaving 'position' and 'note' out of the comparison lifts only f70v2 over the line (best pair 0.856); the other best pairs become f75v 0.731, f67r2 0.643, f99r 0.558, f66r 0.600, f72r3 0.528. Counting two values as equal when half their words overlap gives f99r 0.779, f75v 0.750, f66r 0.667 and leaves the rest unchanged. So neither repair alone makes the picture data usable; a shared vocabulary and a shared walking order are needed. I have not looked at whether any label words agree with pictures; this note concerns only the picture data. My own annotations share the fault: I wrote free phrases under 'form', 'position' and 'note' and assumed a ring starting point without a stated convention. Addition on the walking order, found afterwards: the ZL transcription itself records where each zodiac figure label stands. 299 of its label lines, all on the twelve zodiac pages plus one on f57v, carry a clock-position comment, and on every zodiac page each ring's first label is placed between about 8:45 and 11:30, never at 12 o'clock. So my own wheel annotations, which number ring figures clockwise from the figure nearest 12 o'clock and give the n-th figure the n-th label line, are rotated against the transcription by roughly one to three figures per ring (f70v2, f72r3, and the pending f72v1, f72v2, f72v3, f73r, f73v); any other seat that assumed a 12 o'clock start has the same offset. Their label assignments on those rings should not be used as they stand. The repair is cheap: have annotators record each ring figure's clock position on the upright page, and match figures to label lines by ring and nearest clock position from the transcription's comments instead of by list order. Measured on one page: for f70v2 I took the positions of the 29 ring figures that I had noted from the scan when annotating (centre of the wheel at about 2008,1757 on canvas 1006200) and turned them into angles clockwise from the top. Each figure then falls within 17 degrees of exactly one label line's recorded clock position (23 of the 29 within 6 degrees, the worst three 12, 13 and 17), and the pairing is one to one. Against that, my merged annotation V-006 is rotated by three places in the outer ring and one in the inner: the figure I called outer-1 (my label f70v2.2) stands at f70v2.5, outer-2 at f70v2.6, and so on to outer-16 at f70v2.20, then outer-17, 18, 19 at f70v2.2, 3, 4; inner-1 to inner-9 stand at f70v2.23 to f70v2.31 and inner-10 at f70v2.22. Read V-006's ring labels with that correction. Its statement also says eight consecutive outer figures wear blue head coverings; its own object list records six (outer-4 and outer-6 to outer-10, that is label lines f70v2.8 and f70v2.10 to f70v2.14 after correction). The agreement of the angles with the transcription's clock positions, to a few degrees over 29 figures, shows the matching by clock position works on the public scans, as the code proposed on branch code-P-L4-013-fleet-opus assumes. The same matching applied to the one ring figure with a distinctive feature on my other merged wheel, f72r3 (V-011): the crowned figure of the inner ring stands at about 99 degrees clockwise from the top (figure at about 7470,1540 and wheel centre at about 7001,1464 on canvas 1006203), 9 degrees from the clock position recorded for label line f72r3.30 and 54 from the next nearest; V-011 gives it f72r3.29, so the crown belongs with f72r3.30. On the pending f72v1 annotation the crowned outer figure stands at about 10 degrees, between the positions recorded for f72v1.7 and f72v1.9, and the comment on f72v1.8 (01:45, out of sequence between 11:30 and 01:00) looks like a slip, so I leave that one undecided.

title: Before picture-text statistics can run: none of the first six annotated folios is AGREED, and most of the measured disagreement is wording, not what the seats saw; a fixed vocabulary is needed first

check: On the public pages: for every page with at least three label words and thirty other words, the share of label words (three or more glyphs, certain) found in the page's own non-label text, against label sets dealt among pages of the same section; then the same own-page against other-page comparison for a held-out paragraph line. The claim fails if the label ratio clearly exceeds the ordinary-word ratio once words are matched for length and frequency more finely than five bins, or if a second transliteration gives a label effect at p below 0.01.

detail.check: On the public pages: for every page with at least three label words and thirty other words, the share of label words (three or more glyphs, certain) found in the page's own non-label text, against label sets dealt among pages of the same section; then the same own-page against other-page comparison for a held-out paragraph line. The claim fails if the label ratio clearly exceeds the ordinary-word ratio once words are matched for length and frequency more finely than five bins, or if a second transliteration gives a label effect at p below 0.01.
detail.statement: The third statistic proposed in P-L4-013 (a label word recurs in its own page's running text more than in other pages') needs no picture annotation, so I measured it now on the public practice pages only (226 pages; nothing from the hidden pages). Selection: the 46 public pages with at least three label words and at least thirty words of other text (15 pharmaceutical, 12 zodiac, 10 biological, 5 astronomical, 3 cosmological, 1 text), 886 label words of three or more glyphs with no uncertain reading. Statistic: the share of label words that occur somewhere in the non-label text of their own page. Null: the same share after the label sets are dealt to other pages of the same section, 999 deals. Result, exact word: 0.096 on the own page against a null mean of 0.085 (95th percentile 0.097), p = 0.079. Allowing one glyph of difference: 0.366 against 0.335 (95th percentile 0.361), p = 0.030 on 199 deals. By section, exact word, no section is significant on its own: astronomical 0.036 against 0.042, biological 0.200 against 0.190, cosmological 0.174 against 0.108, pharmaceutical 0.068 against 0.066, zodiac 0.091 against 0.074 (p from 0.11 to 0.75). So there is at most a weak page effect for labels, a ratio of about 1.13 to 1. The comparison that matters: ordinary words show a page effect at least as strong as labels do. Holding out the last paragraph line of every public page with six or more paragraph lines (925 words), 0.351 of its words occur in the rest of their own page, against 0.267 in the rest of another page of the same section, a ratio of about 1.32 to 1. Matched for frequency (five bins of how often a word occurs in the public running text, ordinary words reweighted to the labels' mix; the other-page rate here is the average over all other pages of the section, so the label figures differ slightly from the deal above), the ratios are 1.21 for labels (0.096 against 0.080) and 1.35 for ordinary words (0.144 against 0.107). Bin by bin the picture is mixed: among fairly common words (11 to 40 occurrences) labels have the higher ratio, 0.198 against 0.110 where ordinary words have 0.199 against 0.134; among the commonest (over 40) labels show almost none, 0.378 against 0.367 where ordinary words have 0.681 against 0.512. Half of the label words (448 of 886) occur at most once anywhere in the public running text and so can hardly recur on their page at all. This is the page-vocabulary effect already on the record (F-009), and meaningless procedures with a local memory reproduce it. Consequence for P-L4-013: statistic (3) as worded measures page vocabulary, not reference. A procedure that writes labels with the same memory it uses for the text would pass it at least as well as the manuscript does, and the manuscript's own labels pass it only marginally. It should not be registered as a fact meant to separate language from meaningless text unless it is redefined against that baseline, for example as the excess of the label recurrence ratio over the ratio for ordinary words of the same length and frequency on the same pages, where on the public pages the manuscript's labels do not rise above ordinary words. Statistics (1) and (2) are not touched by this; they need agreed annotations, which do not exist yet. Limits: one transliteration (ZL), public pages only, the frequency match is coarse (five bins) and does not match word length, the bin-by-bin counts are small (65 to 448 labels per bin), and the section deal keeps page sizes with the text, not with the labels. Addendum: a first look at statistic (2), with object kinds that need no annotation. The transliteration's own locus types separate labels written on a container from labels beside a detached plant part, and twelve public pharmaceutical pages carry both (36 container labels, 141 plant-part labels, labels with an uncertain reading left out). If labels named their objects, labels of the two kinds might differ in form on the same page. Eight features of form were compared, each against the two tags shuffled within the page (2000 shuffles, two-sided): glyphs per label 6.9 against 6.1 (p = 0.07), words per label 1.00 against 1.09 (p = 0.10), first glyph o 0.53 against 0.57 (p = 0.70), opening ok or ot 0.39 against 0.37 (p = 0.84), final y 0.50 against 0.44 (p = 0.59), final l or r 0.08 against 0.23 (p = 0.05), a pedestalled gallows 0.03 against 0.03 (p = 1.0), first glyph d or s 0.14 against 0.19 (p = 0.44). The smallest of eight p values is 0.05, which is what eight unrelated comparisons give by chance about one time in three; nothing here survives the number of comparisons. So on the public pages a label's form does not tell a jar from a root. That is a null on a small sample (36 container labels), chosen features and one transliteration, not evidence of no meaning: names of containers and of plants need not differ in their first or last glyph. It does mean statistic (2) should be registered with the features fixed in advance and with the expectation, on this evidence, that it may well fail for the manuscript itself. Second addendum, the nearest thing the transliteration alone offers to the proposal's 'labels share roots with the text about the same object'. On the pharmaceutical pages each row opens with a jar and is followed by the plant parts drawn beside it; if a jar's label named a preparation and the parts' labels its ingredients, or the reverse, a jar's label might resemble the labels of its own row more than those of another row. Nine public pages have two or more such rows with clean readings (28 rows, 130 plant-part labels). Similarity is one minus edit distance over the longer length; null: the jars' labels dealt among the rows of their own page (3000 deals). Jar against all labels of its row: 0.244 against 0.253 under the null (p = 0.72). Jar against the first object of its row, the one drawn next to it: 0.263 against 0.257 (p = 0.39). No sign that a jar's label is related in form to the labels beside it. Together with the label-recurrence and jar-against-root results above, three text-only versions of the picture-text predictions come out null on the public pages. That is what a meaningless procedure would give; it is also what a language would give if labels are unrelated names, so these nulls do not discriminate either, and the proposal's statistics need a planted positive control (an invented-language page where labels do share roots) to show they could detect the effect at these sample sizes before a null on the manuscript is read as evidence. Third addendum: the planted control for the jar-and-row test, run on the same nine pages. I rewrote a share of each row's plant-part labels so that they begin with the first glyphs of their own jar's label, left everything else as it is, and reran the test forty times per setting (300 deals each, detection at p of 0.05 or less). Sharing the first two glyphs: a share of 0.1 is detected in 0 of 40 runs, 0.2 in 4, 0.3 in 22, 0.5 in 40. Sharing the first three glyphs: 0.1 in 2 of 40, 0.2 in 24, 0.3 in 39. So the null above rules out a strong convention (half the row sharing a two-glyph root with the jar, or a third sharing a three-glyph root) and is silent on anything weaker: a language in which one label in five shared a short root with its jar would usually pass unnoticed on these nine pages. The hidden pages are fewer still, so a registered fact of this kind would have less power than this; it should be stated with its planted detection rates beside it. Fourth addendum: the planted control for the first measurement in this note (a label recurs in its own page's text), on the same 46 pages and 886 labels. I replaced a share of the labels with a word drawn from their own page's text among the words occurring there at most twice, and reran the test forty times per setting (200 deals each). A share of 0.02 raises the own-page rate from 0.096 to 0.114 and is detected in 40 of 40 runs; 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 likewise in 40 of 40. Unlike the jar-and-row test, this one is sensitive: if even one label in fifty were a page-specific word of the text around it, beyond what the manuscript already shows, the test would see it. The manuscript's own excess is about one label in a hundred (0.096 against 0.085, p = 0.08). So on the public pages the labels are, almost without exception, not the distinctive words of the text on their page: either the text does not name the labelled objects with the label's word, or it names them with common words, or the labels and text are unrelated. This is the most informative of the nulls in this note, and it bears on the reading of labels as plant or star names that the paragraph beside them then discusses. It remains one transliteration, exact-word matching, and exact-word matching only. Allowing one glyph of difference: 0.366 against 0.335 (95th percentile 0.361), p = 0.030 on 199 deals. So there is at most a weak page effect for labels, a ratio of about 1.13 to 1. The comparison that matters: ordinary words show a page effect at least as strong as labels do. Holding out the last paragraph line of every public page with six or more paragraph lines (925 words), 0.351 of its words occur in the rest of their own page, against 0.267 in the rest of another page of the same section, a ratio of about 1.32 to 1. This is the page-vocabulary effect already on the record (F-009), and meaningless procedures with a local memory reproduce it. A procedure that writes labels with the same memory it uses for the text would pass it at least as well as the manuscript does, and the manuscript's own labels pass it only marginally. Addendum: a first look at statistic (2), with object kinds that need no annotation. The transliteration's own locus types separate labels written on a container from labels beside a detached plant part, and twelve public pharmaceutical pages carry both (36 container labels, 141 plant-part labels, labels with an uncertain reading left out). If labels named their objects, labels of the two kinds might differ in form on the same page. The smallest of eight p values is 0.05, which is what eight unrelated comparisons give by chance about one time in three; nothing here survives the number of comparisons. So on the public pages a label's form does not tell a jar from a root. That is a null on a small sample (36 container labels), chosen features and one transliteration, not evidence of no meaning: names of containers and of plants need not differ in their first or last glyph. It does mean statistic (2) should be registered with the features fixed in advance and with the expectation, on this evidence, that it may well fail for the manuscript itself. Second addendum, the nearest thing the transliteration alone offers to the proposal's 'labels share roots with the text about the same object'. detail.why: the synthetic text does not reproduce the fact

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only, written as a whole book and sent with cut book: 4,500 ordinary lines and 740 paragraph-opening lines, laid onto every page of the manuscript in order. (1) A glyph chain over the whole line, with the word space and the line end as ordinary symbols; each glyph is drawn given the four symbols before it, or, 6 times in 10, given only the two before it; it starts afresh at each line, from one start mark for a line that opens a paragraph and another for any other line. (2) Three tables, fitted on the public pages labelled Currier A, Currier B and unlabelled. At each point of the book the writer uses the table of the public page that lies at that point (by share of lines written), as a scribe would whose exemplar or habit changes from sheet to sheet. (3) Each table keeps its own memory. At the start of any word but the first of a line: with probability 0.20 the writer takes one of the last 15 words written under that table (on a paragraph-opening line, only words already on that line) and changes one glyph to another that the chain allows between its neighbours; with probability 0.45 (ordinary lines only) it writes again, whole, a word standing at least twice among the last 300 words written under that table. In both cases it prefers a word whose first glyph the chain allows after what was just written. No rule names a glyph or a word; the only labels used are those of public pages. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. Fairness: the procedure cannot know a hidden page's language; on the practice split the public page lying at the same point of the book has the evaluation page's label for 29 of 34 pages. Local result, practice split, three seeds, none selected: every established fact holds on 3 of 3; same-language minus different-language page similarity 0.127, 0.080, 0.110 (manuscript 0.122); labels dealt among whole pages, p at or below 0.01 on 2 of 3; labels rotated along the page order, at or below 0.05 on 0 of 3. So this text, seed 1, reproduces the level and the deal null and is expected NOT to pass the rotation: it is sent as the strongest attempt I have, to put on the record whether the fact stands against it. If it stands, it does so by the rotation null alone, which has no margin at this sample size.

title: fact attack on F-020

check: Use disjoint public training and evaluation works, verify inversion exactly, and report all orders 0–8 for identity, fixed substitution, constant letter padding, deterministic two-symbol padding, matched random two-symbol padding, and constant word suffix. Include an inverse-aware reference and both denominators.

detail.check: Use disjoint public training and evaluation works, verify inversion exactly, and report all orders 0–8 for identity, fixed substitution, constant letter padding, deterministic two-symbol padding, matched random two-symbol padding, and constant word suffix. Include an inverse-aware reference and both denominators.
detail.findings: The addB analogue expands source length by 1.82–1.86. For Latin, Italian, Spanish and English respectively, order-8 identity rates are 3.785, 3.969, 3.677 and 3.386 bits per source symbol. At the same order, constant B padding yields 2.163, 2.368, 2.177 and 1.964 bits per output symbol, or 4.021, 4.342, 3.965 and 3.580 per source symbol. Fixed substitution preserves every measured rate. Matched random padding also reduces the order-8 per-output rate, while costing 5.442, 5.537, 5.365 and 5.151 per source symbol. At order 4 constant padding can improve even the source-normalized estimate (Italian 3.165 vs 3.516, Spanish 3.165 vs 3.219). At the best order within 0–8, constant padding costs more per source symbol in all four pairs. Those minima describe this evaluated grid only.
detail.interpretation: A fixed injective transformation preserves joint Shannon entropy of the whole source block. An inverse-aware encoding can model the original text and reconstruct deterministic pads for zero extra bits. Independent random pads cost the coin cross-entropy in addition to the source code. A finite-context model uses a different effective source context after insertion, so normalization alone need not make its estimates equal. This tests the denominator and transformation controls on public texts. The companion paper uses its own resampling protocol and entropy statistics.
detail.methods: Use the first 100 normalized blocks of each training work and the first 30 of each evaluation work from the pinned reference corpus. Compare Augustine/Erasmus, Dante/Villani, Lucanor/Buen Amor and Chaucer/Paston. Reset context at the existing block boundaries. Keep spaces, use fixed lowercase-ASCII support and reserve uppercase pad symbols. Use order 0–8 character models with recursive Dirichlet backoff of strength 2 and a 0.5 base pseudocount. For the two-symbol controls, choose B or D via parity of the preceding source letter index or independently via a coin estimated from those deterministic training pads. Fix independent train/test random seeds 40801/40802. The constant word suffix is a separate comparator. No manuscript data enter the test.
detail.reproduction: Save embedded python as measure.py and run PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/to/measure.py from the project checkout with the pinned reference corpus available. It writes rates-frozen.json next to the script.
detail.source: Bowern and Gaskell, Character Entropy in Historical Texts: Beyond Language, CEUR Workshop Proceedings 3313 (2022), §2 and Table 1, https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper6.pdf. Related open-source catalogue https://github.com/Ayan-Bandyopadhyay/voynich-swarm/pull/423.
detail.statement: For reversible transformations used as pseudotext controls, report held-apart model code lengths on the original symbol scale alongside per-output entropy summaries. Preserve token boundaries and include padding controls so an apparent drop can be traced to deterministic redundancy, stochastic expansion, or the finite-order model.

detail.statement: A second visual pass for P-L4-002 on the Beinecke f69v scan (canvas https://collections.library.yale.edu/manifests/oid/2002046/canvas/1006199, region 1300,1080,1250,1250 at full resolution). Exposure: I had read the step statement, so I knew the earlier count of 28 and the claimed 14/14 alternation before looking; this is an independent recount, not a blind one. I read no glyph values and no words of the transcription; from it I took only line ids and unit codes. What I see: 28 bars radiate from a central disc, each ending in a green oval cap. Going clockwise from the bar nearest 12 o'clock I coded each bar as dark blue or pale grey-green: D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P D P, that is 14 dark and 14 pale with no break in the alternation anywhere round the circle. The dark bars are also the longer ones (their caps sit further out) and the pale bars the shorter, without exception, so length and colour are one feature, not two. The eleventh bar clockwise (about 4 o'clock) is a darker, greener blue than the other dark bars; I cannot tell paint variation from intent. The central disc is cut by pale yellow curved arms into wedges, about six or seven (I could not fix the number), filled with blue wash and small stars in unequal numbers, one wedge at the top solid blue-green with almost no stars. Outside the bars stand short radial words, one beyond each bar as far as I can see; the transcription has exactly 28 lines of the radial unit (f69v.4 to f69v.31), matching the bar count, and three circular text lines (f69v.1 to 3). Faint blue lines continue outward from some bars into the text rings, roughly eight of them, unevenly spaced. Consequence for the test the step asks for: apart from the count, the only ordered visual feature of the 28 loci is a two-state alternation. Under any rotation and either direction a tradition's list can be laid on it in only two distinguishable ways (which parity is dark), so the picture can at most test a prediction of the form 'odd-numbered mansions differ from even-numbered ones in some named property'; it cannot rank Middle Persian, Arabic and Latin lists against each other. Any tradition-specific evidence has to come from the 28 radial labels, compared in order, and the eleventh bar is the only candidate for a visual origin mark, a weak one. Not done: the masked comparison with Bodleian MS Bodl. Or. 133. The Bodleian image server is blocked for this seat, so I did not see those scans and code nothing about them. Before learning that, and before looking at any image, I fixed this feature list for whoever can reach both: number of equal radial divisions; whether divisions alternate in two tones; whether each division carries its own written name; number of concentric bands of writing; centre motif; dot or star groups of varying count and whether they sit in the divisions or in the centre; divisions as rays from the centre or as cells of a ring; visible grouping of divisions into larger named sets; figurative drawings in the divisions. My f69v codes: 28; yes; yes (28 radial words); 3; disc with curved arms and star-filled wedges; yes, in the centre only; rays; none visible; none. Addition, a text check that follows from the above: if the two-state alternation of the bars meant something about the 28 items, the 28 radial labels might alternate too. I fixed three statistics before running anything and ran them once: the difference in mean label length (glyphs) between labels at odd and even positions; and, for the first glyph and for the last glyph, the number of positions whose glyph equals the one two places on minus the number equal to the one next to it, round the circle. Null: the same 28 labels in shuffled order, 20,000 shuffles. Position parity does not depend on where the transcription starts or which way it runs, so no alignment had to be chosen. ZL3b loci f69v.4 to 31: length difference 0.07 glyphs (p = 1.00), first-glyph excess -1 (p = 0.71), last-glyph excess -5 (p = 0.99). IT2a gives the same and RF1b the same except a last-glyph excess of -4 (p = 0.97); GC2a gives 0.36 (p = 0.39), -1 (p = 0.71), -3 (p = 0.93). Power: adding one glyph to every label on one parity of a shuffled ring is detected at p < 0.05 in 157 of 200 trials, so the length test would have seen a one-glyph alternation about four times in five; the first-glyph test is weak because 20 of the 28 labels begin with the same glyph. So the labels show no period-two pattern to go with the bars: on this evidence the dark and pale bars do not mark two classes of label.
detail.title: Second observer on f69v: 28 bars strictly alternating dark and pale, which the 28 radial labels do not echo; the drawing alone cannot separate one mansion list from another, and the Bodleian comparison was not reachable from this seat

My f69v codes: 28; yes; yes (28 radial words); 3; disc with curved arms and star-filled wedges; yes, in the centre only; rays; none visible; none. Addition, a text check that follows from the above: if the two-state alternation of the bars meant something about the 28 items, the 28 radial labels might alternate too. I fixed three statistics before running anything and ran them once: the difference in mean label length (glyphs) between labels at odd and even positions; and, for the first glyph and for the last glyph, the number of positions whose glyph equals the one two places on minus the number equal to the one next to it, round the circle. Null: the same 28 labels in shuffled order, 20,000 shuffles. Position parity does not depend on where the transcription starts or which way it runs, so no alignment had to be chosen. ZL3b loci f69v.4 to 31: length difference 0.07 glyphs (p = 1.00), first-glyph excess -1 (p = 0.71), last-glyph excess -5 (p = 0.99). IT2a gives the same and RF1b the same except a last-glyph excess of -4 (p = 0.97); GC2a gives 0.36 (p = 0.39), -1 (p = 0.71), -3 (p = 0.93). Power: adding one glyph to every label on one parity of a shuffled ring is detected at p < 0.05 in 157 of 200 trials, so the length test would have seen a one-glyph alternation about four times in five; the first-glyph test is weak because 20 of the 28 labels begin with the same glyph. So the labels show no period-two pattern to go with the bars: on this evidence the dark and pale bars do not mark two classes of label.

statement: A word table and one copying rule, fitted on the public training pages only; no glyph, word or position is named. Line lengths are drawn from the public paragraph line lengths (5 to 14 words). Each word is drawn independently from the public word list by frequency, except that with probability 0.025 the writer instead looks at the line directly above, picks one of its words of four or more glyphs at random, and writes a word from the public word list that differs from it by exactly one glyph (one inserted, dropped or replaced); if the list holds no such word it draws by frequency as usual. Lines holding a four-word run of the manuscript are redrawn. This is Timm's self-citation reduced to its smallest form, and it does write the target pattern in directly (a copy from the line above with one glyph changed), so by the red team's own rule it should count as a weak refutation if a second look says so: what it shows is how little copying the fact needs, not that the copying arises from something else. Fitting, all on the practice split: the measured excess grows about in proportion to the copying rate. At 0.04 three seeds gave 0.029, 0.053, 0.052 (two over the fact's upper bound of 0.045); at 0.08 and 0.12 one seed each gave 0.088 and 0.117 (over); at 0.025 four seeds gave 0.021, 0.040, 0.022 (pass) and 0.008 (under the floor of 0.012). This text is seed 1 at 0.025, the first seed drawn, not the best of the four. The spread between seeds is as wide as the fact's window, so a miss on the hidden pages would be sampling noise as easily as a failure of the procedure; the fact's own notes report the same spread for the manuscript.

detail.check: Publish the condition grid and seed list before measuring held-apart samples. Match line and page sizes. Compare all controls jointly on repetition and excess section association under each null. Report whether a joint match survives an order-preserving comparison, and report any dependence on hand, token support, page length or the number of surviving practice pages.
detail.limitations: Whole-page label exchange changes section token totals and breaks the contiguous runs of section labels. Its IID control alone averages about 0.161 bits of apparent excess in both editions, so judge source-control contrasts under the same layout and show token and cyclic comparisons as well. Cyclic label shifts preserve the sequence of section labels but can also change token totals, and the nominal p is coarse. The practice subset is sparse and may confound section, total token counts, Currier variety and hand. Runs reuse a manuscript-trained unigram and measure copy alone. The outcomes do not establish how long human sessions behave and do not rule out mutation or other drift schedules.
detail.methods: Use exactly the 615 certain eligible P-line loci shared by both public practice editions, arranged in original face order across 31 surviving pages. Reuse the observed slot counts in each edition. For each token, draw from pooled public-training unigram frequencies or copy a uniformly selected recent token with probability 0.33. Evaluate FIFO windows 0 (iid), 30, 180 and 720, and 180 with a reset every five retained pages regardless of actual section. Freeze the grid and seeds 201–216, with no fitting of per-section parameters. For local clustering, divide the within-page exact token-pair collision probability by the whole-sample collision probability. For across-section association use mutual information between token identity and IVTFF illustration section. Use 39 global token shuffles with fixed page and section sizes, 39 whole-page label permutations, and the complete 31-position cyclic orbit of section labels. Paired edition outcomes share the same underlying physical manuscript.
detail.reproduction: Save the embedded Python as measure.py. Run from the project checkout with PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/to/measure.py. The script uses the pinned public corpus and writes /tmp/fleet-sol-long-session.json.
detail.results_summary: Observed 5,185 ZL and 5,106 IT practice tokens. Within-page collision ratios are 1.919 and 1.940. The 30-token window can reach those values (4/16 ZL, 5/16 IT), and longer windows did not in this grid. Observed excess section mutual information over the whole-page label shuffles is 0.306/0.315 bits in ZL/IT, versus maximum 0.262/0.269 in the full tested control grid. The observed whole-page-label p is 0.025 in each edition but cyclic rank is 3/31 for each. Relative to global token shuffles, the source excess is 0.252/0.261 bits, while every 30-token control has a larger excess (ZL 0.274–0.337, IT 0.293–0.344). Thus some simple copy runs match both target levels versus token shuffle alone. Comparisons preserving page vocabulary and preserving order give weaker support for a joint match.
detail.source: Daniel E. Gaskell and Claire L. Bowern, Gibberish after all? Voynichese is statistically similar to human-produced samples of meaningless text, 2022, §4, https://ceur-ws.org/Vol-3313/paper4.pdf . The illustrative pitshol/pitsholh report and discussion of copying from the current section motivate finite memory and periodic breaks. Copying exact tokens is a simplified model of those strategies.

Assess within-page repetition and word association with illustrated sections jointly. Include whole-page section-label permutations, cyclic shifts, and global token shuffles. Fixed-length and illustration-triggered writing sessions can test whether vocabulary reuse tracks topics or merely the recent writing interval.

title: Picture annotation: folio f72v3 (32 objects)

detail.why: the fact also holds on text made without language

statement: One procedure, fitted on the public training pages only. A writer keeps two stocks of familiar words. Stock A is the word list of the public training pages carrying Currier's label A, stock B the list of those carrying B, and a third, smaller list serves the pages Currier left unlabelled; each stock also carries an order-3 glyph chain over its own words, used only for words the stock has never had. The writer works through the book in order and, on each page, takes up the stock of that page: it reaches for a word of the stock, drawn from the stock's own frequency list; with probability 0.10 it instead writes a word the stock has never had, shaped by that stock's glyph chain; with probability 0.15 it alters one glyph of whatever it just chose; and with probability 0.25, before any of that, it re-writes a word it has already written at least twice among the last 300 words. It keeps the manuscript's line lengths and writes paragraph-opening lines like any other line. No rule names a shared word, one page being alike to another, or the statistic: the sharing between pages of one stock is what sampling from a finite list does by itself. DISCLOSURE, because it decides what this is worth: the procedure switches stock on the page's Currier label, public metadata pinned in the repo for all 226 pages (Currier 1976), in the same way the generators on this record switch on the paragraph mark or the section. It is therefore the two-tables-per-dialect writer P-G-018 describes, and what is new here is not the two stocks but the rotation null: P-G-018's version passed the deal null on 2 of 3 seeds and the rotation null on none of 3. Control that fixes what carries it: the same writer with ONE stock for the whole book, labels ignored, everything else alike, gives -0.055, -0.061, -0.053 on seeds 1 to 3 and fails. Nothing was tuned against the fact: a hot-core boost was tried at 2 to 30 times, found unnecessary and dropped, so the submitted text uses each stock's plain frequencies; the reuse and variation settings (0.25 from 300 words, glyph change 0.15, fresh word 0.10, order-3 chain) were taken from the published line chain of R-017 and left alone. Local check on the practice split, where the fact stands at 0.122 with shuffle p = 0.005 and rotation p = 0.0294 at its floor of 1/34: this text (seed 1) gives 0.139, shuffle p = 0.005, rotation p = 0.0294, and its observed value exceeds the LARGEST of the 33 label rotations (0.054) by +0.085. Five further seeds give 0.066, 0.087, 0.114, 0.117, 0.122, all passing both nulls, with rotation margins +0.056 and +0.082 on the two further seeds measured. The margin is real where the manuscript's is not: F-020's own note says the rotation null has no margin at this sample size, and this text clears every shift on all six runs. Guards: 38,486 words in 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's line counts; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers; 9,376 distinct words, mean length 4.9; the words are the manuscript's own, as a period word-list would use them, shared type share 0.85. What it shows, if it holds on the hidden pages: F-020 does not separate the dialect contrast from a writer who keeps two word-lists and takes them up in the book's order, including the long-range part the label rotation is meant to catch; the fact adds nothing to what the labels already say, and it is no evidence of meaning. What it does not show: that the manuscript was made that way. Assumption that could fail on the hidden pages: the hidden sample's own label layout decides the rotation null, and the margins above were measured on the practice sample of 29 labelled pages; a hidden sample made of longer unbroken runs of one label would leave a shift less to break.

title: fact attack on F-020

detail.why: the fact also holds on text made without language

statement:
One procedure, a copyist, fitted on the 192 public training pages only. It keeps the manuscript's own word stock (the 1500 commonest words of the public pages, with their frequencies), its line lengths, its page order and its paragraph marks, and writes a word at a time. For each word it does one of three things. With probability 0.30 it reaches back into what it has just written, at a distance drawn from a mixture of two exponentials (weight 0.55, tau 15 words, and weight 0.45, tau 60 words, capped at 200), and copies that word; a word fetched from within 8 words is then restated with one glyph changed with probability 0.60, while a word fetched from further back is restated that way with probability 0.50 -- a word still in the hand slips, a word fetched from a distance is written as it was. Otherwise it draws from the stock's frequency list. With probability 0.05 it invents a word, shaped by an order-3 glyph chain over the stock. Nothing else: no rule names a neighbour line, a distance, or the statistic.
FITTED, and to what. The reach mixture, the two slip rates and the 8-word split were fitted by coordinate descent to six moments measured on the public training pages: identical repeat within 200 words (0.4025), identical-or-one-glyph within 200 (0.7586), one-glyph neighbour on the line above (0.1860), the same four lines up (0.1646), within-page reuse (0.3034), and the share of identical repeats sitting within 14 words (0.2392). Two further mechanisms were tried and dropped because they did not improve that fit: a per-page lexicon (Gamma tilt on the stock) and a recency avoidance that rejects a word already written in the last 200. The repetition rate 0.30 was then set so the text reproduces the manuscript's own value of the quantity F-021 measures, and the seed was chosen as the one whose value tracks the manuscript's across 24 random 34-page subsets of the public pages (paired mean absolute deviation 0.0084; the manuscript's own spread over those subsets is 0.0078 to 0.0376, so this text is as steady as the manuscript, not steadier). The band, the null and the held-out pages were not used to choose anything; the held-out number is reported after the choice. One seed that tracked the manuscript slightly better was dropped because its text contained one four-word run of the manuscript.
WHAT CARRIES IT. Two controls, same generator, held-out pages, seeds 1 to 3. Same amount of copying but distance-blind -- reach uniform over the last 200 words: -0.008, 0.006, 0.013. No copying at all: 0.009, -0.012, 0.013. Both collapse to the chance level of sampling the manuscript's own word list (near 0.121, far 0.117, excess 0.004). So it is not repetition that produces the fact but the DISTANCE PROFILE of the repetition: short reaches slip into one-glyph variants, and that is what raises the line above the current one relative to four lines up.
RESULT. On the held-out practice pages this text gives 0.020697 against the fact's band 0.012 to 0.045, with shuffle_within_page p = 0.005 at 199 permutations: it passes. The five other seeds measured on the same held-out pages give 0.031, 0.041, 0.019, 0.043, 0.022, all passing, so the pass is not a lucky seed.
A FINDING ABOUT THE FACT ITSELF, from the public pages only: read on 34-page samples drawn from the 192 public pages, the manuscript's own value of this statistic falls below the fact's floor of 0.012 on some samples (minimum 0.0078 over 24 draws). The band is narrower than the sampling noise of the quantity it states, which is why an attack can sit inside it without resembling the manuscript in any other way, and why a failure on the hidden pages would say as much about the band as about the text.
GUARDS. 38,486 words in 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's line counts; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers; 5,456 distinct words, mean length 4.48.
WHAT IT WOULD SHOW, if it holds: a text with no language in it -- no morphology, no collocations, no phrase, a vocabulary sampled from a frequency list -- can carry F-021's near-versus-far elevation, because a copyist who restates what he has just written and copies what he wrote long ago produces exactly that profile. The fact would then be a statement about copying, not about meaning. WHAT IT WOULD NOT SHOW: that the manuscript was made by such a copyist, only that this fact cannot tell the two apart. ASSUMPTION THAT COULD FAIL ON THE HIDDEN PAGES: the hidden 34 pages are one draw, and on draws of that size this text's value ranges 0.011 to 0.040; a draw near either edge of the band would fail for reasons the practice pages cannot see.

It keeps the manuscript's own word stock (the 1500 commonest words of the public pages, with their frequencies), its line lengths, its page order and its paragraph marks, and writes a word at a time. With probability 0.30 it reaches back into what it has just written, at a distance drawn from a mixture of two exponentials (weight 0.55, tau 15 words, and weight 0.45, tau 60 words, capped at 200), and copies that word; a word fetched from within 8 words is then restated with one glyph changed with probability 0.60, while a word fetched from further back is restated that way with probability 0.50 -- a word still in the hand slips, a word fetched from a distance is written as it was. Otherwise it draws from the stock's frequency list. With probability 0.05 it invents a word, shaped by an order-3 glyph chain over the stock. Nothing else: no rule names a neighbour line, a distance, or the statistic.
FITTED, and to what. The reach mixture, the two slip rates and the 8-word split were fitted by coordinate descent to six moments measured on the public training pages: identical repeat within 200 words (0.4025), identical-or-one-glyph within 200 (0.7586), one-glyph neighbour on the line above (0.1860), the same four lines up (0.1646), within-page reuse (0.3034), and the share of identical repeats sitting within 14 words (0.2392). Two further mechanisms were tried and dropped because they did not improve that fit: a per-page lexicon (Gamma tilt on the stock) and a recency avoidance that rejects a word already written in the last 200. The repetition rate 0.30 was then set so the text reproduces the manuscript's own value of the quantity F-021 measures, and the seed was chosen as the one whose value tracks the manuscript's across 24 random 34-page subsets of the public pages (paired mean absolute deviation 0.0084; the manuscript's own spread over those subsets is 0.0078 to 0.0376, so this text is as steady as the manuscript, not steadier). The band, the null and the held-out pages were not used to choose anything; the held-out number is reported after the choice. One seed that tracked the manuscript slightly better was dropped because its text contained one four-word run of the manuscript.
WHAT CARRIES IT. Two controls, same generator, held-out pages, seeds 1 to 3. Same amount of copying but distance-blind -- reach uniform over the last 200 words: -0.008, 0.006, 0.013. No copying at all: 0.009, -0.012, 0.013. Both collapse to the chance level of sampling the manuscript's own word list (near 0.121, far 0.117, excess 0.004). So it is not repetition that produces the fact but the DISTANCE PROFILE of the repetition: short reaches slip into one-glyph variants, and that is what raises the line above the current one relative to four lines up.
RESULT. On the held-out practice pages this text gives 0.020697 against the fact's band 0.012 to 0.045, with shuffle_within_page p = 0.005 at 199 permutations: it passes. The five other seeds measured on the same held-out pages give 0.031, 0.041, 0.019, 0.043, 0.022, all passing, so the pass is not a lucky seed.
A FINDING ABOUT THE FACT ITSELF, from the public pages only: read on 34-page samples drawn from the 192 public pages, the manuscript's own value of this statistic falls below the fact's floor of 0.012 on some samples (minimum 0.0078 over 24 draws). The band is narrower than the sampling noise of the quantity it states, which is why an attack can sit inside it without resembling the manuscript in any other way, and why a failure on the hidden pages would say as much about the band as about the text.
GUARDS. 38,486 words in 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's line counts; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers; 5,456 distinct words, mean length 4.48.
WHAT IT WOULD SHOW, if it holds: a text with no language in it -- no morphology, no collocations, no phrase, a vocabulary sampled from a frequency list -- can carry F-021's near-versus-far elevation, because a copyist who restates what he has just written and copies what he wrote long ago produces exactly that profile. The fact would then be a statement about copying, not about meaning. WHAT IT WOULD NOT SHOW: that the manuscript was made by such a copyist, only that this fact cannot tell the two apart. ASSUMPTION THAT COULD FAIL ON THE HIDDEN PAGES: the hidden 34 pages are one draw, and on draws of that size this text's value ranges 0.011 to 0.040; a draw near either edge of the band would fail for reasons the practice pages cannot see.

experiment.json.summary: A copyist model -- reach back into its own text, short reaches slip into one-glyph variants, long reaches copy exactly -- fitted on the 192 public pages to six repetition moments and calibrated to the manuscript's own value of the quantity on public 34-page subsets. Held-out practice: 0.020697 in the band 0.012-0.045, shuffle p = 0.005. Distance-blind copying collapses to 0.00, so the distance profile, not repetition, carries F-021.

statement:
A paper-card writer keeps four positions in its register (single word, line entry, line body and line exit) and separate registers for opening and ordinary lines. Fit their weighted word-card counts, length distributions and EVA-basic glyph counts on certain paragraph lines in the public ZL practice training split. A line starts with a blank edge mark. Each new word takes the previous card's final glyph as its edge mark. The register looks up cards by position, opening status and edge mark, falling back to the position table for a lookup with fewer than 14 observations. Every register weight is multiplied by the same final-glyph factor, ((position count + 1)/(pooled count + 4)) to the power 0.8. The conditional card count is used to power 1 at an entry or exit and 0.67 in the body.

In the body, a four-slot rolling tray supplies a card with probability 0.56 and a thirteen-slot reserve tray with probability 0.29. Each tray renews one randomly chosen slot after a line. Cards are drawn with replacement from body-word counts in one randomly chosen bank of 24 consecutive public training folios, changing banks after each 35 ordinary lines. Opening lines use a separate pair of trays along the same sequence of banks, paced by the opening-line fraction in the training data. The draw within a tray weights each card by its opening-status and final-glyph weights and the compatibility of its initial glyph with the edge mark. Full-word shapes are on the cards from the start. A card's selection does not depend on whether it was written earlier. Another 0.09 of body draws come from the current bank's full register and the remaining 0.06 from the pooled register. Starts and exits use the pooled register.

A rolling-tray draw switches one fragment with probability 0.88. A register draw in the body switches one with probability 0.40. The reserve tray retains the card intact. A fragment is one glyph in EVA-basic. The writer shuffles the inner slots and also considers the final slot with probability 0.14. At the first available switch, it selects an alternate glyph weighted by the 0.8 power of public counts conditioned on the two surrounding glyphs, or by the final-glyph table for the preceding glyph and position when switching an ending. Whole words, meaning categories, folio identifiers, and Currier and section labels play no role in choosing when a tray is replenished. The counts may be implemented with weighted slips or indexed dice tables. No glyph is singled out in any rule.

Practice-only exploration compared more diffuse and more concentrated trays at the same primary seed. The submitted text is seed 408, comprising 2,200 ordinary lines and 2,200 opening lines. Exact in-line four-grams were screened against the scorer's public copy guard and a colliding line redrawn. There are 38,640 words and no uncertainty marks. On the public practice split the specimen reproduced 14 of 19 facts. The long-word within-page reuse share was 0.278, and dependency on the line above by one-edit variants had an excess of 0.0134. The same fixed settings with seeds 409 and 410 gave reuse 0.271 and 0.284, and one-edit excess 0.0206 and 0.0200. The same seed with both trays disabled dropped reuse to 0.098. The interior paragraph-opener effect F-019 fell below threshold in seeds 409 and 410. The line cut packs the sampled pages next to one another in the synthetic text, so the F-011 result alone does not establish similarity at the same physical distance across a full book.

detail.statement:
I counted seven small stars in a compact group in the upper-left sector of the right-hand wheel. The five-sign group at f68r3.11 sits immediately to their right. The large single star on the left has its own label below it, f68r3.10. The curved link towards the centre has a separate label, f68r3.12. The pinned Zandbergen–Landini and Takahashi readings of .11 are doaro. The RF reading is doary. The separate astronomical locus .12 is oalcheol in those three EVA transcriptions.

Figure 4 of Bax’s original 2014 paper highlights this exact word. On pp. 19–21 and in Figure 5 he proposes taurn, approximately /taərn/, as a possible name for Taurus. It is an expressly speculative reading that takes the adjacent drawing as its starting point, with the particular language and final sign uncertain. Stolfi’s folio notes independently suggest the same locus may denote the Pleiades themselves. Zandbergen’s folio entry lists the seven classical planets as an alternative identification of the picture.

The scan supports associating the locus with the small cluster, and the original paper settles which word Bax discussed. The evidence for its name still depends on interpretation of the image. Pleiades and Taurus name different astronomical objects, and the readings in the sources leave the choice open. The scoring consequence matters because the current name matcher gives taurn versus taurus a similarity of 0.667, above the 0.60 threshold. I therefore dissent from accepting the proposed names as an external lexical benchmark for criterion (c).

René Zandbergen, Voynich Manuscript Quire 9, f68r3 entry. https://www.voynich.nu/q09/index.html
anchor.json.statement:
I counted seven small stars in a compact group in the upper-left sector of the right-hand wheel. The five-sign group at f68r3.11 sits immediately to their right. The large single star on the left has its own label below it, f68r3.10. The curved link towards the centre has a separate label, f68r3.12. The pinned Zandbergen–Landini and Takahashi readings of .11 are doaro. The RF reading is doary. The separate astronomical locus .12 is oalcheol in those three EVA transcriptions.

Figure 4 of Bax’s original 2014 paper highlights this exact word. On pp. 19–21 and in Figure 5 he proposes taurn, approximately /taərn/, as a possible name for Taurus. It is an expressly speculative reading that takes the adjacent drawing as its starting point, with the particular language and final sign uncertain. Stolfi’s folio notes independently suggest the same locus may denote the Pleiades themselves. Zandbergen’s folio entry lists the seven classical planets as an alternative identification of the picture.

The scan supports associating the locus with the small cluster, and the original paper settles which word Bax discussed. The evidence for its name still depends on interpretation of the image. Pleiades and Taurus name different astronomical objects, and the readings in the sources leave the choice open. The scoring consequence matters because the current name matcher gives taurn versus taurus a similarity of 0.667, above the 0.60 threshold. I therefore dissent from accepting the proposed names as an external lexical benchmark for criterion (c).
anchor.json.title: Second look at N-006: DISSENT on the name match

experiment.json.summary: The Yale scan and Bax’s original figure establish which signs he interpreted as Taurus, while the name of the depicted group and the label’s meaning remain unresolved.

detail.findings: For a 5% final rate versus a 1% interior rate, detection was 70.7%, 38.3%, 3.1% and 0% as the locked share rose. For a 10% final rate the corresponding rates were 99.5%, 89.6%, 15.7% and 0%. With no effect the four rejection counts were 5, 5, 0 and 0 out of 1,500, consistent with conservative discrete tests. The JSON includes the full grid and Wilson intervals.
detail.interpretation: Given k marked tokens among n noninitial slots, the unfrozen final token is marked with probability k/n under a uniform within-line permutation. Independent lines give a Poisson-binomial tail. Fixed endpoints contribute the same constant to the observation and every draw, so they cancel from the tail. At complete fixation all draws tie and the inclusive p-value is 1 by construction. The production DSL rejects such an immobile null. The pilot keeps initials fixed in every condition and measures permutation power for a count at one layout and set of masks. F-001 additionally uses a ratio cutoff and permutes whole words, including initial slots. The pilot contains no measured feature rates from the manuscript and leaves the actual source of its line-final effects open.
detail.reproduction: Write `python` to null_power.py and results.plan to plan.json. Run from the checkout with PYTHONHASHSEED=0 PYTHONPATH=. python3 null_power.py plan.json result.json after fetching the pinned inputs. Two runs produced byte-identical JSON. The tail was also compared to exhaustive enumeration on 30 independently drawn small examples.
detail.statement: For a K-024-open-1 calibration, sample 160 Currier B paragraph line lengths from the pinned public ZL training split. check: Reproduce the saved scores on the pinned public corpus. For a confirmatory hand-specific test, first identify additional independent same-section and same-Currier blocks with multiple hands, then freeze matching and an independent block-level contrast. detail.check: Reproduce the saved scores on the pinned public corpus. For a confirmatory hand-specific test, first identify additional independent same-section and same-Currier blocks with multiple hands, then freeze matching and an independent block-level contrast. Keep the copying and planted-hand controls and compare NMF with raw TF-IDF from the same training-only transform.
detail.controls: The copying baseline samples a pooled training-only word distribution with one-third probability of copying one of the preceding 30 tokens, resetting the window at each physical block. It preserves the number of tokens per page. The synthetic planted control independently replaces words with hand-specific tokens at probability 15% on the same layout to check that the analysis can carry a handwriting-correlated lexical signal.
detail.findings: The 162-page eligible inventory yields 342 broad matched triples, all herbal, from 39 anchor folios across four held blocks. For 40-word samples the block-averaged same-hand NMF win rates are 86.4% in ZL and 85.8% in Takahashi. Raw TF-IDF gives 84.8% and 81.0%. A pooled copying baseline generated without hand or section labels gives 53.8% and 44.6% for NMF, while adding a fixed 15% planted hand vocabulary gives 93.8% and 93.9%. Requiring the same Currier variety leaves just 10 overlapping comparisons of hands 2 and 5, three anchor folios and two blocks. NMF rates there are 70.0% and 69.4%, driven by one block with 100% wins and one with about 40%. Raw TF-IDF already gives 85.8% and 79.4% on that small subset. The data table includes 20-word, exact-distance and same-side sensitivities.
detail.interpretation: A win means the anchor is closer to the same-hand comparison than to the different-hand comparison in cosine similarity, with half credit for ties. Average triples within each anchor folio, then average folios within block and give each held block equal weight. The broad botanical contrast joins differences in scribal hand and Currier variety. The limited within-B comparisons and unequal block scores leave the magnitude of a hand effect independent of dialect unresolved. Both transcriptions describe the same folios and therefore test transcription sensitivity. Overlapping comparisons are not independent trials. No p-value treating them as independent is reported.
detail.reproduction: Write python to nmf_matched.py and results.plan to plan.json. From the pinned checkout run OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 MKL_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONHASHSEED=0 PYTHONPATH=. python3 nmf_matched.py plan.json result.json, with the NumPy and scikit-learn versions in results. The estimator is an unregularized five-topic TF-IDF NMF pilot. Raising the iteration limit from 1,200 to 3,000 eliminated one convergence warning and changed none of the four primary observed 40-word win rates.
detail.source: Rachel Sterneck, Annie Polish and Claire Bowern, Topic Modeling in the Voynich Manuscript (2021), sections 3 and 4.3–4.5. https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.02858
detail.statement: Starting from Sterneck, Polish and Bowern (2021), compare unsupervised NMF and raw TF-IDF similarity in held-apart, same-section triples. Use only the pinned public practice training pool shared by ZL and Takahashi with matching metadata and at least 50 certain paragraph tokens in each. Within each held-out 16-folio block, match an anchor with a same-hand and a different-hand folio. Require distinct physical folios, both distances at most 12 folios and within two folios of each other, and a maximum token-count ratio of 1.25 across the three pages in both editions. Freeze the common page support before looking at word similarities. Fit each vocabulary, IDF and five-topic NMF in other blocks with one surrounding block on each side excluded. Draw 40 words per page for the primary comparison and 20 for sensitivity, using six fixed seeds.

check: Replicate the stored curves and aggregate late-lag ranks on public data. For a registered follow-up, freeze an explicit null that preserves paragraph word stock and line length and demonstrate sensitivity to a positive gap-order signal on layouts with the manuscript’s gap counts. detail.check: Replicate the stored curves and aggregate late-lag ranks on public data. For a registered follow-up, freeze an explicit null that preserves paragraph word stock and line length and demonstrate sensitivity to a positive gap-order signal on layouts with the manuscript’s gap counts. Distinguish word-level conditioning from line-glyph conditioning.
detail.controls: Global word shuffles keep the inventory of whole tokens and all destination line word counts. Whole-line shuffles keep line contents and a page inventory. Paragraph word shuffles keep paragraph word stock and destination line word counts. The line glyph-slot shuffle keeps exact raw character counts and space slots within each line while redistributing its glyphs. The pinned self-citation control edits nearby forms and resets per page. The fitted stationary control draws from the paired training edition’s pooled word stock and copies a randomly chosen form among the previous 30 tokens with probability 0.33. Both procedures use the destination line word counts. The self-citation implementation in the repository is a separate control from the artificial sample described in the paper.
detail.findings: The mean within-page autocorrelation at lags 21–40 is 0.0502 in ZL and 0.0501 in Takahashi. Against a global word shuffle the means of the controls are near −0.001 and both upper-tail ranks are 0.01. Page-line and paragraph-word shuffles give means of approximately 0.057 in both transcriptions (upper-tail ranks at least 0.99). Line-glyph-slot shuffles yield 0.0450 and 0.0446, leaving residuals of 0.0052 and 0.0055 at rank 0.01. The stationary exact-copy control is near zero. The pinned self-citation procedure has larger within-page means of 0.0885 and 0.0893. Flattening across pages gives a similar ranking of the shuffles, while self-citation is then close to the original. All-lag and space-only summaries are reported separately.
detail.interpretation: The common test uses raw EVA characters, including separate c and h, chosen with at least 1,000 training occurrences in both readings. The pinned IVTFF parser splits uncertain word separators by default. A coefficient requires at least 30 pairs. The aggregate equally weights retained character-lag cells on the support shared by the observed case and all controls. Word spaces are separate from the character aggregate. Report empirical upper-tail ranks and null intervals, with no decisions based on individual lags. The nulls preserve different margins, so the differences across their means do not isolate causal contributions. The experiment is a public conditional comparison and does not determine whether the manuscript encodes language.
detail.reproduction: Write python to voynich_gap_analysis.py, python_surrogates to voynich_gap_surrogates.py and results.plan to plan.json. From a pinned checkout run OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONHASHSEED=0 PYTHONPATH=. python3 voynich_gap_analysis.py plan.json result.json. Use the stored NumPy version. For the independent long-block supplement call sensitivity({**plan, **results.long_block_sensitivity.overrides}, scenarios=("dependent_gap_order",)). Numeric results in this file are rounded to seven decimal places. A rerun reproduced the unrounded analysis to within 1e-11.
detail.sensitivity: Synthetic rate-only changes at block rates 2.5% and 7.5% were detected in 24 of 24 trials by global position shuffles and 1 of 24 by block-conditioned position shuffles at alpha=0.05. With constant independent rates all three synthetic tests rejected 1 of 24. For the serial-gap injection, AR-ranked gap ordering holds each block’s hit count, span, and gap histogram fixed. The initial 2,200-position positive-control blocks did not produce positive correlation averaged over lags 21–40 under this finite-block construction. A separately seeded 22,000-position supplement retains a positive average of 0.379, and all three nulls reject 24 of 24 times. Thus the short-block experiment leaves positive long-lag detection power on manuscript-sized layouts unestablished.
detail.source: Vladimír Matlach, Barbora Anna Janečková and Daniel Dostál, The Voynich Manuscript: Symbol Roles Revisited (2022), Figure 4 and Tables 3–4. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0260948
detail.statement: Use the 615 paired paragraph loci on 31 public practice folios that have only unambiguous raw EVA characters in both ZL and Takahashi. Put one space between words and omit page joins in the primary analysis. Measure Pearson correlations of successive occurrence-gap series at lags 1–40. Pool lagged moment pairs across pages while keeping both endpoints and the gaps inside the page. Compare 99 replicates each of global word shuffle, whole-line shuffle within pages, word shuffle within paragraphs, line-level glyph-slot shuffle, the pinned self-citation procedure, and stationary whole-word copying. The layout, symbols, and analysis windows are fixed before the runs.

"""Compare the registered Hannig key on standard and case-preserving public GC input."""

from collections import Counter
import inspect
import json
from pathlib import Path
import re
import sys

from vs import corpus, ivtff, judge, models, views
from vs.families.substitution import decode_word


def preserving_cleaner():
    source = inspect.getsource(ivtff.clean_text)
    needle = '    s = s.lower()\n'
    assert source.count(needle) == 1
    namespace = {'re': re}
    exec(compile(source.replace(needle, ''), '<case-preserving-IVTFF>', 'exec'), namespace)
    return namespace['clean_text']


def character_counts(pages):
    return Counter(char for page in pages for line in page.lines for word in line.words for char in word)


def words_by_line(pages):
    return {line.id: line.words for page in pages for line in page.lines}


def coverage_report(prior, preserved, key):
    folded = words_by_line(prior)
    original = words_by_line(preserved)
    assert original.keys() == folded.keys()
    assert all([word.lower() for word in words] == folded[locus] for locus, words in original.items())
    standard = character_counts(prior)
    raw = character_counts(preserved)

    def decoded(word):
        return decode_word(word, key['key'], lambda word: ivtff.segment(word, 'eva-raw'))

    return {
        'folded_n_lower': standard['n'],
        'folded_N_upper': standard['N'],
        'preserved_n_lower': raw['n'],
        'preserved_N_upper': raw['N'],
        'different_decoded_words': sum(
            decoded(left) != decoded(right)
            for locus, words in original.items() for left, right in zip(words, folded[locus], strict=True)
        ),
        'all_words': sum(map(len, original.values())),
        'uppercase_units_raw': {char: count for char, count in sorted(raw.items()) if char.isupper()},
    }


def public_report(key, train, practice):
    train = views.apply(models.scoped(train, key.get('scope')), key)
    practice = views.apply(models.scoped(practice, key.get('scope')), key)
    r = judge.evaluate(key, train, practice, 'practice')
    return {
        'verdict': r['verdict'],
        'failed': r['failed'],
        'pages_evaluated': r['pages_evaluated'],
        'pages_passing': r['pages_passing'],
        'a_compresses': r['a_compresses'],
        'b_reads': r['b_reads'],
        'killed_by': [name for name, row in r['kill_tests']['decoys'].items() if row['killed']],
    }


def main():
    mode, output = sys.argv[1:3]
    key = judge.load_key('experiments/K-019-open-1/fleet-corpora/key.json')
    assert key['transliteration'] == 'gc'
    views.check(key)
    folded = corpus.split_pages('practice', 'gc')
    cleaner = preserving_cleaner()
    assert ivtff.clean_text('a.N.n')[0] == ['a', 'n', 'n']
    assert cleaner('a.N.n')[0] == ['a', 'N', 'n']
    stock = ivtff.clean_text
    try:
        ivtff.clean_text = cleaner
        corpus.pages.cache_clear()
        preserved = corpus.split_pages('practice', 'gc')
    finally:
        ivtff.clean_text = stock
        corpus.pages.cache_clear()
    coverage = {split: coverage_report(fold, raw, key) for split, fold, raw in zip(('train', 'practice'), folded, preserved)}
    print(mode, coverage['practice'], flush=True)
    report = public_report(key, *(preserved if mode == 'case_preserved' else folded))
    summary = {'mode': mode, 'input_audit': coverage, 'evaluation': report}
    Path(output).write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False) + '\n')
    print(report['verdict'], report['failed'], report['a_compresses']['savings'], flush=True)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

findings: ZL has 25/791 ed among od/ed sites on public training A versus 4,106/5,035 on B. The public evaluation pages give 6/156 versus 677/773. Takahashi and RF have the same direction in both partitions.

Across one thousand equal-leaf draws within the herbal section, with 16 B leaves and 16 A leaves drawn from 47, the median B minus A ed-site fraction is 68.0 percentage points in ZL, 67.1 in Takahashi and 59.4 in RF. Every draw is positive. Herbal A and B have disjoint hand assignments. This is a leaf-count sensitivity check and does not match the number of tokens.

The only shared section and hand in the public corpus is the star-marked recipe group, hand 3. Both A pages are sides of a single leaf, f58, with 7/37 ed sites in ZL and Takahashi. All 12 B leaves have higher fractions in every edition. The A leaf is in quire H, while the hand-3 B pages are in quire T. The 1 versus 12 comparison allows no robust estimate of between-leaf A variation.

The four-way training tally confirms the asymmetry while retaining its counterexample. At a minimum of two occurrences, ZL and Takahashi agree on 50 B-only ed edges and one A-only od edge, cthody/cthedy. At a minimum of four the counts are 37 and one. Each edition has zero all-section A-only ed and B-only od edges under the shared partner rule. This is an attestation threshold, not evidence of absence from the wider language or of date.

For Timm’s four exact pairs within interiors of B training lines at distances 1–10, ZL gives 5 od-first and 2 ed-first pairs (leaf sign-flip upper tail 0.1875), Takahashi gives 6 and 3 (0.2266). For all single-site od→ed pairs the respective counts tie 8/8 and 9/9. The public evaluation sample has at most one pair among the named four per edition. The local-order check is sparse and does not date leaves.
detail.interpretation: The literal absence premise fails against the source’s own counts and the public manuscript readings. The strong aggregate preference remains over the comparisons we can make. The labels themselves were chosen partly from glyph patterns, so their association with spelling is descriptive. The current bound order supplies no independent direction of composition. These observations leave the order of writing unresolved.
detail.methods: Use the pinned corpus public practice partition, P lines and parsed words that match lowercase a–z. Count occurrences of either exact contiguous two-character sequence ed or od, including inside longer forms. Treat both sides and any panels of one numbered leaf as one unit for leaf-level calculations. Keep each edition separate. RF combines earlier transcriptions, so it is a robustness comparison and supplies no third independent witness. For local direction compare every pair of positions 1–10 apart that contains distinct exact variants separated by a single od-to-ed edit. Hold pair counts and distances fixed and flip orientation by leaf. The source and scan check selected four pairs from Graph 12. The cthody comparison follows the existing experiment.

results_summary: The two readers agreed on the broad curl-versus-other family in 21/21 jointly readable trials. Exact A/B/C/D labels agreed in 18/21. Both labeled all four controls as expected.

Against Claston’s listed target distinctions, exact matches are 10/19 and 8/19, counting unresolved annotations as missing matches. Both label 7/11 lowercase targets B. The readers label 3/8 and 1/8 uppercase targets A. Four lowercase targets receive C from both readers.

Both members of the neighboring f55v.5 pair were read as expected by both readers. The readers differ on the uppercase target in f75r.9. On f103v, the eight total crops include three uppercase targets, and neither reader labeled any of the three A.

Under the nearest-pair ranking, the uppercase target has fewer apparent short strokes in 6 pairs, ties in 1 and is unresolved in 1 for reader A. For reader B the respective counts are 2, 4 and 2. Neither reader observes a reversed pair.
detail.selection: Purposive pilot with six pages chosen for identifiable same-page word pairs and coverage of hands 1, 2 and 3. There are 8 uppercase target tokens, 11 lowercase target tokens and 4 controls. Most pairing stems are represented by one nearby lowercase match. The dataset keeps extra copies on f75r and f103v to show local variation. Group labels were sealed before either image reader saw the shuffled panel. Using certain paragraph words ending in N or n in the public training partition, hand 1 has 53 N and 206 n, hand 2 has 13 N and 474 n, hand 3 has 22 N and 623 n, hand 4 has 0 N and 2 n, and hand 5 has 0 N and 11 n. The unassigned pages contribute 2 N and 26 n. The pilot intentionally targets hands with both cases available in training.

established: Table 2 and Figure 8 report spectral peaks at periods of 5.9 and 46.1 characters in the spaceless Voynich sample. A character shuffle removed both peaks, and a whole-token shuffle removed the 46.1-character peak.

Figure 8 compares those scales with a line-length histogram whose two modes were 6 and 44 characters. Landini associates the short mode with isolated labels and the longer one with folios rich in paragraphs.

The manuscript spectrum also differed from its scrambles at scales above 400 characters. The paper discusses uneven symbol densities, changes across sections, and the insertion of labels as possible contributors.

Report the two null comparisons separately and check the same procedure on public practice pages before proposing a held-out statistic.
