check: Repeat the recorded contrasts and score both printed and stated-rule readings at the published weights and 5% rank threshold. Verify that matching immediate left contexts leaves both candidate scores equal despite distinct right contexts. Test a separately fitted direct-emission line chain and compare manuscript rank sensitivity to the single-context Pearson convention.

detail.check: Repeat the recorded contrasts and score both printed and stated-rule readings at the published weights and 5% rank threshold. Verify that matching immediate left contexts leaves both candidate scores equal despite distinct right contexts. Test a separately fitted direct-emission line chain and compare manuscript rank sensitivity to the single-context Pearson convention.
findings: For word-position matching only at full matched coverage, eight comparisons met the frequency threshold. The wrong constituents have a better loss in six, while the true ones have a better loss in two. This is 3 of 4 wrong wins in training and 3 of 4 in the separate control blocks. Both alternatives fall within the published 5% cutoff in four cases. At half coverage the wrong option wins 5 of 7 eligible trials, and neither option passes the cutoff in any eligible case.

All 13 eligible comparisons in the exact-left condition tie across the three replacement fractions. All 36 exact-left trials, including below-support cases, have differing right-context incidence counts. The loss depends on the candidate’s left contexts, frequency and self-adjacency. These are shared by X and Z, while the candidate components and their directed pair frequency are fixed. The score therefore ties even when the right contexts differ.

The three shuffled Euler trails change 91.4–92.3% of positions while preserving every loss, over 9,702, 9,702 and 11,132 eligible triplets respectively. This invariance follows from the use of unigram and adjacent-pair counts as the only numerical inputs.

In twelve direct-emission stationary line simulations, m with i,d falls in the best 5% in all twelve, and q with i,e in eight. Under both Rule 3/6 conventions, those results hold without combining any symbols.

For q with i,e, the rarer glyph contributes just one realized incoming context after trimming in each public evaluation edition. The prose-based rank moves from 4.41% to 9.63% in ZL and from 4.39% to 9.86% in Takahashi when assigning loss one instead of zero to that undefined singleton correlation. This crosses the paper’s cutoff with the text and all other rules fixed.
detail.interpretation: A low triplet percentile can arise for an incorrect constituent pair or for directly generated glyphs. This calibration addresses statistical specificity. Independent visual evidence can still support a ligature hypothesis. Most partial fusions lack frequency support, and these contrasts share a first component by design, so the results do not estimate error rates over every possible ligature.

methods.exact_surrogates: For the first natural contrast of each language’s control block at full matched coverage, shuffle the directed adjacency list of every glyph and reconstruct an Euler trail beginning with the original first glyph. The output draws individual glyphs from the fixed edge multiset and never does a pair replacement during generation. It is conditioned on the positive sample’s observed incidence matrix and preserves the entire unigram and adjacent-pair counts by construction. This control tests identifiability from those inputs, not the plausibility of its whole-text generator.
methods.loss: Use the joint adjacency matrix with spaces and zero edges below 0.2% of either their row or column. Rank all ordered triplets whose non-space glyphs exceed the published support ratio 500/229431, excluding a candidate used as its own component, and include ties in the percentile. Hold weights 1,100,1,1,100,1,1,10. Literal mode follows printed Rule 3 (shared contexts) and Rule 6 ((1−min)/max). Prose-based mode uses unshared contexts for Rule 3 and 1−min/max for Rule 6, following the prior experiment’s alternative. The paper describes a zero loss for empty contexts. Our primary analysis also uses zero for a singleton left context, where Pearson is undefined. For the public manuscript we rerun with a loss of one for that singleton. Zero correlation is assigned if either realized vector has zero variance with at least two contexts.
methods.natural_text: Use separate vs.refcorpus train_text and control_text block sets for English, Latin and Italian. Take up to 40,000 characters before the final partial word with single spaces. Fix first and second pairs as th/to and ea/er, en/es and pa/pe, ch/co and de/di respectively. For each word-position class shuffle the two occurrence lists with seed 9141 or 9142, attempt pairs in that order, and discard any pair whose edits overlap or touch previously accepted edits or one another. Shuffle accepted pairs with the same generator. Take 25%, 50% or 100% of the accepted pool, rounding down. Full-pool coverage of all original target occurrences has median 83.9% for positions only and 64.1% when the immediate previous glyph also matches. X and Z have exactly the same counts and no self-adjacent occurrences.
methods.stationary_lines: Fit an initial-glyph distribution and one shared internal character transition table on public practice training paragraph lines for each edition. Use only raw certain ASCII EVA words with single spacing. Independently emit the public evaluation line lengths with the fixed table and seeds 7810–7815, disallowing a trailing space so the scoring stream contains one separator between lines. No pair-to-symbol rule is used. Score the two real public partitions separately in ZL and Takahashi under the same preprocessing.

reproduction.instructions: Extract the script to a scratch location and run PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/voynich_triplet_specificity.py from the repository root with pinned inputs fetched. The two manuscript partitions used are the public practice training and evaluation pages.

statement: A 15th-century copyist carries one rolling word-slip tray, a deeper reserve and a reusable letter jig. At each new quire packet the same physical stock is replenished from neighboring pages of a public practice transcript, using a fixed 18-page packet and a 3.5% card refresh chance per written word. On a turn the writer draws a whole-word slip from the recently written line or page, then from the active packet, or sets a fresh spelling with the letter jig learned from public training pages; ordinary one- and two-glyph copying slips are resolved through local context-conditioned letter cards. The preceding word can guide the next card through the shared edges of slips in the public letter table; a separate card position is used at the beginning and end of a written line. The drawers are reloaded in manuscript order and retained for a packet before the next packet is reached. A page or paragraph boundary clears the short rolling tray, as when a copyist changes leaf or starts a new passage. Card choice uses no semantic categories, section labels, Currier labels, or rule about any target glyph, length, repetition count or page statistic. This single setting and seed were fixed before the practice score was read.

attack.json.method: A 15th-century copyist carries one rolling word-slip tray, a deeper reserve and a reusable letter jig. At each new quire packet the same physical stock is replenished from neighboring pages of a public practice transcript, using a fixed 18-page packet and a 3.5% card refresh chance per written word. On a turn the writer draws a whole-word slip from the recently written line or page, then from the active packet, or sets a fresh spelling with the letter jig learned from public training pages; ordinary one- and two-glyph copying slips are resolved through local context-conditioned letter cards. The preceding word can guide the next card through the shared edges of slips in the public letter table; a separate card position is used at the beginning and end of a written line. The drawers are reloaded in manuscript order and retained for a packet before the next packet is reached. A page or paragraph boundary clears the short rolling tray, as when a copyist changes leaf or starts a new passage. Card choice uses no semantic categories, section labels, Currier labels, or rule about any target glyph, length, repetition count or page statistic. This single setting and seed were fixed before the practice score was read.

check: Extract both scripts and repeat the reported public training and evaluation analyses. Check the shuffled folio and line invariants and confirm that the injected periodic glyph is detected. Re-evaluate on diverse fixed public blocks before defining any closed-page criterion. Report separately the effect of transcription, narrow-bin choice, and how lines are concatenated.

detail.check: Extract both scripts and repeat the reported public training and evaluation analyses. Check the shuffled folio and line invariants and confirm that the injected periodic glyph is detected. Re-evaluate on diverse fixed public blocks before defining any closed-page criterion. Report separately the effect of transcription, narrow-bin choice, and how lines are concatenated.

design.center_and_spectrum: Pool training line lengths across editions. Select the most frequent length after a symmetric triangular histogram smoother with weights 1,2,3,2,1, using the smaller length if tied. This selects 44. Use nonoverlapping windows of 1,024 positions with a periodic Hann taper. For each frequency sum one-hot glyph squared Fourier magnitudes, normalize by the taper energy, and average over full windows. Compare the mean power over periods 0.90–1.10 times 44 and the ratio of that band power to the mean of two shoulder means, with period factors 0.65–0.80 and 1.25–1.50. Each edition uses 25 full windows in evaluation.
design.input: Match public ZL and IT paragraph line ids in ZL physical order. Retain the line when both editions have at least one word and only unambiguous lowercase ASCII glyph codes in every word. Remove all spaces. Keep raw EVA characters as units. The training counts are 3,277 shared lines, with 138,478 ZL and 138,402 IT glyphs. The evaluation counts are 626 shared lines, with 25,910 ZL and 25,918 IT glyphs.
design.nulls: The global permutation keeps the observed overall glyph stock. For each numbered folio, permutation of all interior glyphs together holds the full folio inventory, exact length of each retained line, and positions of both endpoint glyphs. The stronger within-line permutation also keeps each line’s inventory. Verify these invariants for fixed diagnostic seed 512. Use 19 draws per initial training comparison and 99 per primary evaluation comparison. Upper-tail ranks include ties and add one to numerator and denominator. Use each complete simulated text as a replicate rather than counting windows or Fourier bins as independent tests.
design.sensitivities: Repeat in nonoverlapping 512-position blocks entirely within a numbered folio and with 49 draws. Separately retain the shared paragraph loci with any clean words in both editions, omit uncertain words only, and run the fixed 1,024-position test. A pulse control introduces a new glyph at repeated phases of the closest selected Fourier bin, keeping known line edges untouched. A separate geometry-only control simulates independent letters from training first-two, last-two and interior position distributions and the evaluation line-length array.

findings: The ZL and Takahashi training band-to-shoulder ratios are 1.019 and 1.022. Against the folio-interior controls their upper-tail ranks are 0.40 and 0.10. Against the global controls the ranks are 0.35 and 0.15.

The primary evaluation ratios are 0.895 and 0.883. Against the global glyph controls both upper-tail ranks are 1.00. Against the endpoint-preserving folio interiors they are 0.99 and 1.00. Across these four comparisons, total band power is approximately 68–70% of the shuffle median. Leaving every line’s glyph stock intact also gives upper-tail ranks 1.00 for both ratios.

Using only the 16,896 glyphs in complete windows that stay within a numbered folio gives ratios of 1.022 and 1.014. Against folio interiors the ranks are 0.30 and 0.36. Relaxing the word certainty filter keeps 651 matched loci and gives ratios 0.981 and 0.960, with folio-interior ranks 0.70 and 0.86.

The injected pulse at 44.52 characters gives a band-to-shoulder ratio of 1.176 and exceeds all 19 global and all 19 folio-interior shuffles. The six boundary-only realizations have ratios 0.980–1.068, with every global-shuffle upper-tail rank at least 0.10. This small geometry calibration is specific to the chosen edge model.

reproduction.instructions: Write the embedded scripts with the given names to one temporary directory. From the repo root use PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/voynich_spectral_lines.py and then PYTHONPATH=. python3 /path/voynich_spectral_geometry.py. The second script imports the first. Only the public practice split is used.

detail.scope: This is a public robustness check with paired paragraph sampling, explicit treatment of uncertain loci, and Welch band averaging. Landini used a long continuous stream and logarithmic frequency smoothing. An isolated narrow peak or a feature of his original sample requires a separate estimate at that scale. The present public result supports withholding a positive line-band criterion.

detail.additional_text_checks: The exact word fochor occurs once in each of the public pinned ZL, Takahashi and RF texts, at the opening paragraph position on f9v. The literal sequence folor occurs at f43r.1, token 8 in ZL and Takahashi, which makes specifying Vatne’s physical locus important. Textual rarity does not supply an independent plant-name correspondence.
scan_observations: Five separate flowers are visible, with three above and two below. The upper right one shows a wide dark blue lobe above the center, two lateral lobes, and two relatively pale lobes below. The lower flowers have conspicuous pointed strokes near their bases.

The four broad low green blades have pointed tips and shallowly toothed edges. Different narrow, deeply divided appendages arise higher up near nodes. Their relation to the stem is compatible with pansy stipules, though the drawing leaves their attachments ambiguous.
Two paragraphs wrap around the upper three flowers and extends to the left of the stem. I see no independent tag or pointer. f9v.1 and f9v.5 are the two paragraph starts in both ZL and Takahashi.
detail.source_notes: Han attributes the genus comparison to earlier work and reproduces both species from Lindman plate 227. Vatne’s morphology study shows a crop of that plate and her names study shows the full plate alongside a modern photograph. The A and B drawings depict V. tricolor and V. arvensis. Han’s photographs of a garden pansy demonstrate a range of presentations. Han’s flattened-specimen explanation and Vatne’s illustration-error explanation address the same apparent reversal. Han’s observations concern the drawing. Vatne’s proposed translations require her separate reading assumptions.
sources: P. Han (2011), Discussion of the plant illustrated in folio f9v, Fig. 2 and Figs. 3–11. https://www.as.up.krakow.pl/jvs/library/2-7-2011-05-25/pansyvm.pdf

Siv Bugge Vatne (2022), The morphology of the Voynich plants, p. 7. https://crackingthevoynichcipher.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/5_the_morphology_of_the_voynich_plants_siv_bugge_vatne_2022.pdf#page=7
Siv Bugge Vatne (2022), The Voynich Plants and their Names, Part 1, p. 25. https://crackingthevoynichcipher.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/2_1_the_voynich_plants_and_their_names_part_1.pdf#page=25
C. A. M. Lindman, Bilder ur Nordens Flora, plate 227 A and B, and accompanying description of the two species. https://runeberg.org/nordflor/227.html
Harvey Ballard, Ohio University, morphological diagnosis of Viola arvensis and noted intermediates. https://people.ohio.edu/ballardh/vgpena/taxa/violaarvensis.htm
Flora of North America, Viola tricolor var. tricolor, corolla and spur characters. https://efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=250100968
detail.statement: The f9v scan supports a pansy-like Viola candidate through the five broad petal outlines, blue and pale coloration, deeply divided green appendages at the nodes, and branching stalk and root. The front-facing drawing does not give a reliable spur measurement or a consistent view of the sepals. These are useful characters in separating Viola tricolor from Viola arvensis and their intermediates. I agree with the draft’s botanical uncertainty and dissent on confirming a word-to-name anchor. The three pinned editions give twelve paragraph loci and no separate label locus. Vatne proposes multiple readings for words within the two paragraphs. The scan verifies those physical positions. It supplies no line or label pointing from any of them to the plant.

scan_observations: Five separate flowers are visible, with three above and two below. The upper right one shows a wide dark blue lobe above the center, two lateral lobes, and two relatively pale lobes below. The lower flowers have conspicuous pointed strokes near their bases.

The four broad low green blades have pointed tips and shallowly toothed edges. Different narrow, deeply divided appendages arise higher up near nodes. Their relation to the stem is compatible with pansy stipules, though the drawing leaves their attachments ambiguous.
Two paragraphs wrap around the upper three flowers and extends to the left of the stem. I see no independent tag or pointer. f9v.1 and f9v.5 are the two paragraph starts in both ZL and Takahashi.
anchor.json.source_notes: Han attributes the genus comparison to earlier work and reproduces both species from Lindman plate 227. Vatne’s morphology study shows a crop of that plate and her names study shows the full plate alongside a modern photograph. The A and B drawings depict V. tricolor and V. arvensis. Han’s photographs of a garden pansy demonstrate a range of presentations. Han’s flattened-specimen explanation and Vatne’s illustration-error explanation address the same apparent reversal. Han’s observations concern the drawing. Vatne’s proposed translations require her separate reading assumptions.

anchor.json.statement: The f9v scan supports a pansy-like Viola candidate through the five broad petal outlines, blue and pale coloration, deeply divided green appendages at the nodes, and branching stalk and root. The front-facing drawing does not give a reliable spur measurement or a consistent view of the sepals. These are useful characters in separating Viola tricolor from Viola arvensis and their intermediates. I agree with the draft’s botanical uncertainty and dissent on confirming a word-to-name anchor. The three pinned editions give twelve paragraph loci and no separate label locus. Vatne proposes multiple readings for words within the two paragraphs. The scan verifies those physical positions. It supplies no line or label pointing from any of them to the plant.

detail.check: Re-run the included public-corpus scripts and verify both transcribed examples against their Yale scans. Any A-before-B conclusion must be tested against a separate physical or scribal direction indicator.
findings: Re-running the three scripts saved in the prior public P-L1-005 record reproduced its complete stored result objects exactly. A separate recount also matched the main ZL substring totals: training A has 25 ed and 766 od sites (25/791); training B has 4,106 ed and 929 od (4,106/5,035). On the public evaluation pages the counts are 6/156 for A and 677/773 for B. Takahashi and RF have the same direction in both partitions.

Certain exact pair counts on training pages (A/B): ZL chedy 1/405, chedar 0/30, chedal 0/21 and qokeedy 0/279; Takahashi 2/402, 0/26, 0/20 and 0/277; RF 2/300, 0/18, 0/17 and 0/199. The paired od forms remain attested on both sides for each case where the ed form is B-only.

The two A-side exception loci were checked in the public ZL, Takahashi and RF editions and against the linked Yale image crops. At f89r1.7.5, chedy and its neighboring words agree in all three. At f58v.12.5, ZL and Takahashi read chedal followed by dy, while RF leaves the boundary/readings uncertain. The f58v item is in the practice evaluation partition, not the training partition.

For one-site od-to-ed word-form edges whose partner occurs in both varieties, the shared ZL/Takahashi tally is 50 B-only ed edges and one A-only od edge at threshold 2; at threshold 4 it is 37 and one. The reverse exception is cthody/cthedy. Each edition has zero all-section A-only ed and B-only od edges under the same shared-partner rule.

In 1,000 equal-leaf herbal draws, the median B-minus-A ed-site fraction is 68.0 percentage points in ZL, 67.1 in Takahashi and 59.4 in RF; all 1,000 draws are positive. This controls leaf counts, not token counts. The only public section-by-hand overlap is recipe pages assigned to hand 3: both A pages are sides of leaf f58 (7 ed among 37 od/ed sites in ZL and Takahashi), and each of the 12 B leaves has a higher fraction. This leaves one A leaf and twelve B leaves for descriptive comparison.

The selected B-line ordering check is sparse and does not supply a chronological direction: within-line interior pairs from the four named pairs are 5 od-before-ed versus 2 ed-before-od in ZL (leaf-flip upper-tail 0.1875) and 6 versus 3 in Takahashi (0.2266). For all eligible one-site pairs the counts tie at 8/8 and 9/9. The practice evaluation pages contain at most one named-pair comparison per edition.
detail.interpretation: The main A/B spelling association is reproduced across the two independent EVA transcriptions and persists in the equal-leaf sensitivity. The strict absence premise has exceptions, including a ZL/Takahashi-agreed chedy on an A page and a chedal on another A page. Currier variety is also entangled with scribal hand and section: herbal A and B have disjoint hands, while the one shared hand-by-section stratum compares a single A leaf with twelve B leaves. The observed association alone does not date the pages or establish A-before-B; the tested local order is sparse and non-directional.
limits: RF is a merge of earlier transcriptions, not a third independent witness.
Equal-leaf resampling does not equalize the number of tokens per variety.
The scan crops support a reading check but provide no date or direction of composition.
detail.methods: Use the pinned corpus public practice partition, P lines and parsed words that match lowercase a–z. Count occurrences of either exact contiguous two-character sequence ed or od, including inside longer forms. Treat both sides and any panels of one numbered leaf as one unit for leaf-level calculations. Keep each edition separate. RF combines earlier transcriptions, so it is a robustness comparison and supplies no third independent witness. For local direction compare every pair of positions 1–10 apart that contains distinct exact variants separated by a single od-to-ed edit. Hold pair counts and distances fixed and flip orientation by leaf. The source and scan check selected four pairs from Graph 12. The cthody comparison follows the existing experiment.

check: Repeat the comparison at native scan resolution before rating the candidate orders. Have two readers mark openings, ruling, edge crossings and possible offsets on unlabeled images. Compare each proposed junction with current neighbors and matched unrelated margins. Register each mirrored offset against several independent features on the leaf and assess whether the pigment or ruling can be dated to initial production. Report each surviving order and the evidence needed to choose among them.

detail.check: Repeat the comparison at native scan resolution before rating the candidate orders. Have two readers mark openings, ruling, edge crossings and possible offsets on unlabeled images. Compare each proposed junction with current neighbors and matched unrelated margins. Register each mirrored offset against several independent features on the leaf and assess whether the pigment or ruling can be dated to initial production. detail.interpretation: No ruled line or pinhole match was resolved at a candidate between-sheet junction in these normal-light scans. This does not establish an absence of ruling. The counts are exact permutations under optional, stated geometric and opening assumptions, not tests of historical probability. The direct scan comparison provides a strong same-sheet clue in Q13, suggestive opening features in both quires, and a possible Q20 contact at a stage whose date remains uncertain. The evidence distinguishes some features of the candidates but does not identify a unique sequence of the surviving sheets in either quire.

method.arrangements: For a sheet a|b in the tested orientation, a stacked arrangement reads ar, av, br, bv consecutively. Its within-sheet opening is av facing br. The between-sheet openings are bv facing the next ar. For a nested arrangement take the first leaves in order and the second leaves in reverse. Skip missing f109 and f110 when listing visible leaves, and limit layout counts to surviving bifolia with their published orientations.
method.comparison: Use the first text band of the five lower-numbered rectos of Q13 and the six of Q20 as controls for the opening features. Inspect inner margins of the two Q13 same-sheet pairs and the currently facing controls. Compare the two distinct Q13 proposals at their pool-sheet junctions. Examine current and proposed star-sheet contacts separately. Pixel coordinates are approximate on the specified 880 px wide full images, origin at the top left.
method.scope: Test the explicit sheet orders in the paper for Q13 and Q20. All visual observations come from public scans. No transcription, text-similarity fitting, or hidden split is used. Sheet identity, production pairing, an opening or ending surface, and actual contact between sheets have different implications for order.

observations: The pool on f78v has linework entering its right inner margin. On f81r a branch enters the left inner margin between the upper and lower pools. The linework is consistent with the continuation identified by the authors and Zandbergen when the two halves of one parchment are opened together. The currently facing controls f79r and f80v do not show comparable continuations at those margins.

The proposed f76v–f83r connection is a weaker, more local drawing cue. The illustration at the upper left of f83r approaches the fold at the site of the reported continuation with f76v. Even if the mark on f76v is accepted as part of that drawing, this is another same-sheet connection.

An enlarged, extended initial at the upper left of f76r stands out in the opening comparison with f75r, f77r, f78r and f79r. f76r is the only page of this quire without a substantial illustration. This is compatible with a section opening. It would favor the second stacked candidate over the first only if this marks the start of the entire gathering.

Both proposals put the pool-bearing sheets 75|84 and 78|81 next to each other. The second gives f84v facing f78r, with comparable flared and patterned forms near the tops of the two pages. The first gives f81v facing f75r, with similar green figure-filled pools. These are motif similarities rather than measured line joins. Pelling also attained f84v facing f78r in a nested hypothesis by reversing 75|84. The facing pair alone cannot identify the binding structure.

Compared with f103r, f104r, f106r, f107r and f108r, f105r has an especially extended initial and more space above the main first line. This is evidence for special opening treatment. f116v carries a few lines near the top and is mostly uninscribed. Both the published stack and the current binding already end there. The quire mark on f103r pertains to a recorded arrangement, and the first twelve lines of f115r are assigned to another hand, showing that an opening feature can also represent a local division.

In the f115v scan the main leaf has two small reddish marks near the inner edge, roughly (818,123) and (817,246). They are left of the narrow sliver showing f116r itself, so that sliver and its visible stars should be excluded. The first two conspicuously red centers on the f116r scan are near (54,139) and (56,266). The vertical separations are approximately 123 and 127 pixels. The marks are consistent with Pelling's contact report. The approximate spacing and a shared color family are insufficient to identify pigment or date the transfer. No single-star or unrelated-margin false-match rate has been measured.

The f115v–f116r pair faces today. In the published stack f115v would instead face f106r, and f116r would face f103v on its own bifolium. The possible f113v–f115r offset across a flaw of f114 and the weaker reported stray spots are useful targets for sharper registration. They are not scored here as verified connections. If the f115v–f116r contact was made while the order in question was in use, it favors a different layout from the published stack at that stage.

detail.statement: I reviewed the Yale f80r scan and the cited comparison images and records. The figure holds a small bulbous object behind the waist; a short projection angles downward and inward, separated from the body. Keagan Brewer’s 2022 reading of it as a phallic insertion device is a serious published alternative, and the figure’s pose is consistent with that interpretation. detail.statement: Test the layouts of Davis's bridge-gallows by comparing closed-loop and stem features in shuffled Yale scan crops with several transcriptions. Paired gallows are plausible for some paragraph openings. Several superficially similar bridges have a shared lower bar or an ambiguous foot, and the complex labels admit conflicting component readings.

findings: Eight of eleven rows have cth at both aligned endpoints in IT. Four are within an IT word and three use adjacent IT words. The remaining pair is separated by two words at f35r.1. The two cth signs at f42r.1 occur farther right and cannot be counted as the two aligned endpoints.

Every one of the eight IT pairs has GC K at the first endpoint and GC 1 at the second. The independently encoded first endpoint agrees with cth, while the right endpoint has a plain bench reading. An older LSI witness supplies both cth forms for six of the seven within-word or adjacent pairs. The exception is f100v.14, where the First Study Group row reads the first cth but leaves the second unresolved.

All seven same-word or adjacent-word IT pairs stand at paragraph openings across three scribal hands and several sections. The count of seven under this chosen spacing rule does not recover Davis's undocumented list. Reading the locators from the manuscript shows that some open paragraphs midway down a page.

At f68r2.7 ZL encodes a rare sign both near the start and inside the later shape. IT otolchcthy keeps a benched t rather than the predicted k or f. LSI records Mike Roe otolch!tey, John Grove otolchc!hy, and Jorge Stolfi opolchs!hy. Stolfi and Grove even locate the landing of the raised stroke on different signs.

At fRos.33 the ZL and RF forms agree in their rare-code representation, while IT and GC lack a row. The raw interlinear includes John Grove's ofalcfhy for the bridged word, which pairs f with f and falls outside both proposed readings. This transcription is a witness to the ambiguity, without establishing the historical reading.
text_audit.rows_from_raw_zl: Read raw IVTFF text because the practical cleaner collapses extended signs. In a single locus search for a literal ZL brace form with c, code 132, 155 or 216, and optional h, followed by a brace form with c, code 133 or 196, and h. Preserve the text between them and match IT and case-preserved GC by locus. This deliberate shortlist includes mixed shapes and leaves the paper's unnamed examples unresolved.

detail.title: Long gallows bridges recur, with several distinct ink junctions and conflicting endpoint readings

findings: Within the seven IT pairs with close endpoints, two have traceable separate low contacts, including the f8r.14 example and the new f30v.1 example. Contacts are plausible with overlapping ink at f8v.1. At f80r.34 and f86v6.13 the right stem ends in a shared lower bar. The remaining two at f100v.14 and f102r2.16 have unresolved contacts. The long visual spans thus recur, with a range of attachments. The three comparison crops have ordinary short spans.

The spaced f35r.1 pair has two probable lower contacts and supplies an example of the visual pattern spanning additional words. The similarly extended f56r.1 and the more complex f42r.1 and f95v1.1 show why a long span alone is insufficient for assigning paired benched t.

For f68r2.7 the lobes and partial descents are compatible with a multi-part mark. The blinding results leave open whether three fully connected legs and three closed loops are present, and do not distinguish the two allocations proposed by Davis.

For fRos.33 the match to Figure 5 comes from the original Yale canvas rotated ninety degrees clockwise. Both readers independently found two traceable tall legs and an ambiguous pale surface feature above. The photographed ink does not independently reproduce the full three-leg, two-loop inventory. The exact cause of the bright trace and any hidden joined stroke remain unresolved.
visual_audit.method: From the raw shortlist, inspect ten loci with identifiable early line regions, leaving f99v.37 in the text audit only. Add two mixed forms and the rosette, plus three nearby ordinary controls. The two auxiliary image-model readers independently received only shuffled crops with anonymous IDs and the same written observations to record. They did not see the locus mappings, transliterations or tested readings. fRos.33 was supplied later as a supplementary anonymous crop. Counts refer to ink visible on these photographs and include a range for faint or open returns. This is an enriched sample and yields no population frequency.

rows.S01: Two full descents and a middle return, with two or three upper lobes. The left descent ends by the writing and the far right ends at a low curve.
rows.S02: A visible upper span joins the left descent to a short right return. A farther-right curl and lowering stroke are possible. The readers could not fix both loop closure and attachment at the resolution examined.
rows.S03: Long upper span, two discernible descents, one closed or nearly closed head and a more open left return. Both readers see distinct low attachments.
rows.S04: A long pale span and two descents. Separate low horizontals align with the descents and the left join is faint.
rows.S05: Ordinary comparison with a short raised connector. The right descent ends high or is obscured.
rows.S06: Long span from left to center and a shorter rightward connection. Both readers report two outer descents and a higher central return, with two to three loop-like forms and faint outer contacts.
rows.S07: Two descents and long upper span. The left stem ends near an oval and the right meets a short curved stroke.
rows.S08: Two long bars at different levels. The right upper descent feeds into the lower bar and a second independent foot is unresolved.
rows.S09: Long upper trace next to smaller marks. Both readers see a possible gap above the left low stroke and a contact at the right.
rows.S10: Two raised loops and two spans. The left descent goes through the lower span to a low curve and the right ends in the lower span.
rows.S11: Long pale span with two descents. Both readers trace separate low horizontal attachments, with weak contrast at the right.
rows.S12: Long trace toward the right end with a pale gap. The left foot is crowded with rounded ink and the right enters a low horizontal.
rows.S13: Ordinary comparison with a short upper connector. The two descents contact the same low stroke.
rows.S14: Ordinary comparison with a short upper connector and no resolved low bench attachments.
rows.S15: Two descents and a long span. Both readers see separate low contacts as plausible. Brown-red marking and overlapping ink limit the right join.
rows.S16: Two tall descents with a short dark upright near the top, zero secure closed loops and one possible open return at the right. Both readers observe a pale surface line crossing the apparent bridge and no continuous dark ink span that can be traced. The short upright does not show a third descent.

visual_audit.rule_for_comparison: Code both benches as apparent only when both readers can trace a low contact under each separate terminal or judge a contact probable despite a stated overlap. Code a shared-bar ending when both see the right stem ending in the spanning lower bar. Keep faded, aligned but disconnected or crowded foot shapes unresolved. This synthesis was coded after collecting both independent reads.

detail.statement: I reviewed the twelve inner centres on Yale canvases 1006200–1006207, distinguishing writing in the centre from the circumferential Voynich text. f70v2 (1006200; two fish): one Latin-script word between the fish and one freestanding Voynich word beside the upper star; the upper fish lies between that Voynich label and the Latin-script word, and no drawn line joins them. A lower star in the same centre has no label. f70v1 (1006201; horned animal at a plant): a Latin-script word on the animal; no freestanding Voynich word in the centre, and no circumferential text line immediately bounding this centre. f71r (1006202; horned animal at a plant): a Latin-script word on the animal and Voynich writing around the centre; no freestanding Voynich word. I checked this centre in a full-resolution crop. f71v and f72r1 (1006203; bull-like animals): each has a Latin-script word below the animal and circumferential Voynich writing; neither has a freestanding Voynich word. f72r2 (1006203; two figures holding hands): a Latin-script word between the figures and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f72r3 (1006203; two clawed animals): a Latin-script word below the lower animal and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f72v3 (1006204; four-legged animal) and f72v2 (1006204; clothed figure holding a star): each has a Latin-script word beside or beneath the emblem and circumferential Voynich writing; neither has a freestanding Voynich word. The star held by the figure is unlabelled. f72v1 (1006205; balance): a Latin-script word beneath the emblem and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f73r (1006206; animal with looped tail): a Latin-script word beneath the animal, circumferential Voynich writing, and an unlabelled star; no freestanding Voynich word. f73v (1006207; figure with crossbow): a Latin-script word at the feet near the circumferential text; no freestanding Voynich word. In all centres with ring writing, I treated that circular line separately from a standalone label. I find no image-supported pairing of a Voynich word and a Latin-script month annotation: the sole freestanding Voynich label is next to the upper star on f70v2, with the upper fish between it and the month word. I did not transcribe or date the Latin-script words. This is a visual review, so the distinction between a ring word and a nearby centre word where they approach one another remains a judgement by eye.

A lower star in the same centre has no label. f70v1 (1006201; horned animal at a plant): a Latin-script word on the animal; no freestanding Voynich word in the centre, and no circumferential text line immediately bounding this centre. f71r (1006202; horned animal at a plant): a Latin-script word on the animal and Voynich writing around the centre; no freestanding Voynich word. I checked this centre in a full-resolution crop. f71v and f72r1 (1006203; bull-like animals): each has a Latin-script word below the animal and circumferential Voynich writing; neither has a freestanding Voynich word. f72r2 (1006203; two figures holding hands): a Latin-script word between the figures and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f72r3 (1006203; two clawed animals): a Latin-script word below the lower animal and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f72v3 (1006204; four-legged animal) and f72v2 (1006204; clothed figure holding a star): each has a Latin-script word beside or beneath the emblem and circumferential Voynich writing; neither has a freestanding Voynich word. The star held by the figure is unlabelled. f72v1 (1006205; balance): a Latin-script word beneath the emblem and circumferential Voynich writing; no freestanding Voynich word. f73r (1006206; animal with looped tail): a Latin-script word beneath the animal, circumferential Voynich writing, and an unlabelled star; no freestanding Voynich word. f73v (1006207; figure with crossbow): a Latin-script word at the feet near the circumferential text; no freestanding Voynich word. In all centres with ring writing, I treated that circular line separately from a standalone label. I find no image-supported pairing of a Voynich word and a Latin-script month annotation: the sole freestanding Voynich label is next to the upper star on f70v2, with the upper fish between it and the month word. I did not transcribe or date the Latin-script words. This is a visual review, so the distinction between a ring word and a nearby centre word where they approach one another remains a judgement by eye.

detail.check: Repeat the frozen matched-line sampler, recover the same whole-line crops from the Yale IIIF manifest, and give randomized unlabeled crop panels to additional readers. Extend whole-line segmentation to the unsupported layouts. Compare the signed within-line width difference across quires with the least reliable lines retained as unresolved, and measure how often alternative alignments reverse the effect.
interpretation: Both masked readers matched all four edges within 20 native pixels for 14 of the 18 initial crops, spanning ten quires. The certain gap is larger in each measured pair. The equal-quire contrast is +3.75 pixels rescaled to a 700-pixel page. Excluding pages from the original direct ink study leaves 12 of 12 positive cases with an equal-quire contrast of +3.42 pixels. Both left-to-right label orientations give the same direction.

The exception log is part of the result. Two initially mapped photographs do not provide reliable matches to the complete reference row. One crop cuts off the right glyph and one repeated sequence received discrepant placements. Expanded-crop recovery and a tie-breaking reader are reported separately. The alternate locators broaden coverage across compound leaves while keeping the sample small and conditional on visually identifiable glyphs.

All 25 resolved comparisons were wider at the period across 15 marked quire groups. This combines the primary sample, nine supplemental whole-line matches and two recoveries. Only the explicitly specified 14 are used for the primary width estimate.

In the larger archived-pixel analysis, 99 of 121 exact-pair lines on 54 pages or panels favor the certain gap. The equal-quire mean difference is +0.269 threshold units with bootstrap interval [−0.757, +0.892]. An anomalous 242 px comma width at f35r.8 dominates one quire estimate, and our blind strip cannot safely verify the corresponding row. Equal-token-count cases alone have an equal-quire mean of −0.090, showing the dependence of the archive result on how its alignment branches contribute.

This documents the predicted physical spacing contrast in the identifiable same-glyph sample. The proportions cannot estimate the distribution of all spaces or establish the lexical status of either separator. Broad independent confirmation would require a larger set of reliably aligned image lines, especially at dense, interrupted, or heavily illustrated layouts.

primary_method.blinding: Four auxiliary image-model readers independently inspect overlapping groups of anonymous strips, so two readers cover each initial line. Each panel has a native pixel ruler and a detached reference in EVA-basic with every separator removed. Two randomized A and B markers in that reference indicate which stroke transitions to locate, without identifying their separator classes. The reference x positions are unrelated to the photograph. Give readers no physical word locations or separator categories. The panel ordering and marker labels use seed 104081551.
primary_method.companion_checks: The archive's initial folios are f7v, f14v, f23r, f39v, f42v and f56v. Repeat the primary result after excluding them. Independently try one wider crop for the clipped right edge and one additional reader for an exact repeated-glyph alignment disagreement. Keep these recovery measurements outside the primary tally. A further alternative-layout check uses whole-line locators cross-registered with old archive boxes and normal-light Yale crops, without giving the optical readers either target coordinates or separator classes. The whole-canvas width conversion compresses units differently on wide foldouts, so use native edges and the within-line sign for the supplemental comparison.
primary_method.measurement: Each reader matches the full unspaced sequence by inspection, then records the left glyph's rightmost horizontal ink extent and the right glyph's leftmost extent. Use max(0,right-left-1) native pixels so touching or overlapping glyph envelopes contribute zero. Compare the same-line difference after averaging the two estimates and multiplying by 700 divided by native canvas width. Require all four estimated endpoints to agree between readers within 20 pixels; show a 10-pixel sensitivity. Quire means receive equal weight. Repeat the quire-cluster bootstrap 4,000 times with fixed seed 20261126. This is a small convenience sample among eligible lines with measurable geometry, and the intervals are descriptive.
primary_method.sampling: Use the public practice training set. Retain paragraph lines composed entirely of lowercase EVA and literal comma or period after deleting edge paragraph markers. In EVA-basic select a period and a comma on the same line with exactly the same ordered glyph pair. The frozen 27 cases use distinct numbered leaves. Twelve quires contribute two cases of at most two separator ordinals apart and three additional eligible quires contribute one case with a cap of two or four ordinals. Optimize opposite left-to-right label orientations, then ordinal distance and exact pair diversity, with SHA256-seeded tie breaks. The original selection had 16 period-left and 11 period-right cases.
primary_method.whole_line_localization: Use only the S45 image-native baselines and polygons from unique 1:1 row matches, giving 18 lines from ten quires. The existing whole-line correspondence uses continuous glyph counts, without specifying where either sampled separator lies. Exclude seven compound or foldout loci that lack the corresponding S45 crop, and two loci with non-1:1 matches. Native photographs are displayed as padded whole-line strips, retaining useful context for ambiguous tall strokes. There are no imported boundaries or word boxes on the displayed ink.

detail.prior_evidence: Rozanova and Temerev found a strong distinction using Voynichese token boxes. Their direct pixel pilot measures the physical ink but uses those same boxes to locate gaps on six folios. It retains 265 certain and 21 uncertain gaps, giving a mean contrast of +1.84 pixels at 700 pixels page width. Its eighteen exact-pair comparisons were post hoc. The present spot audit matches both glyphs on the same line prospectively and gives the readers no inherited word boxes.

s47_reanalysis_method.comparison: Subtract uncertain width from certain width and divide by the published geometric threshold for that line. Report both pooled results and equally weighted quire means. Recompute descriptive percentile intervals with 4,000 quire resamples and seed 1947. Check orientation, proximity, quire exclusion and the alignment branches with equal or unequal detected versus transcribed token counts. The published table has 2,441 loci with emitted positions, including width-gate failures.
s47_reanalysis_method.independence_limit: S47 ink segmentation precedes transcription alignment, but its width at a separator depends on alignment to transcribed tokens. Some within-token distances are placed at proportional glyph offsets. Guarding on exact ordinal sequence and exact glyph pair leaves this dependency in place. The larger reanalysis tests robustness of the archived measurements and the small blind audit tests independence of the pixel edges.
s47_reanalysis_method.mapping: Read the published S47 positions on public scans. Read the pinned raw ZL paragraph lines using the strict clean-line rule. Reconstruct the entire ordinal sequence of periods, commas and internal positions with the S47 glyph segmentation (EVA-basic plus iiin, iin, in, iir, ir and ee). Require exact agreement to the observed row labels and lengths before transferring any glyph-pair identities. Drop lines with any missing width; use the nearest same-pair cross-class match per line, breaking ties by period ordinal, then comma ordinal. This additional filter avoids choosing gaps by magnitude.

sampling_record.glyph_convention: EVA-basic token-internal segmentation. Glyphs are indexed from zero in the concatenated segmented words. Raw EVA character offsets also start at zero and mark a point between characters.
sampling_record.selection: Two different numbered leaves per A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,M,N,S,T; distance ≤2. Optimize opposite dot/comma orientations, then summed distance, then distinct edge pairs, then seeded SHA-256 order. Add one in each I,O,Q in that order at caps 4,2,4; minimize orientation imbalance then distance then seeded SHA-256 order. IDs sorted by the same seeded hash.

check: Extract the two embedded scripts to one scratch directory and add the repository root to PYTHONPATH. Run original_triplet.py with stdout redirected to replication.json, then run audit_triplet.py to create audit.json. Compare the canonical replication digest and recorded tables. A failure of loss-vector agreement, different cutoff decisions, loss inequality for exact-left-matched candidates, or absence of low ranks in the fixed no-fusion line controls would challenge this audit. The next methodological task is to add a separately specified right-context discriminator and calibrate it on fresh contrasts before using it on manuscript candidates.

detail.check: Extract the two embedded scripts to one scratch directory and add the repository root to PYTHONPATH. Run original_triplet.py with stdout redirected to replication.json, then run audit_triplet.py to create audit.json. Compare the canonical replication digest and recorded tables. A failure of loss-vector agreement, different cutoff decisions, loss inequality for exact-left-matched candidates, or absence of low ranks in the fixed no-fusion line controls would challenge this audit. The next methodological task is to add a separately specified right-context discriminator and calibrate it on fresh contrasts before using it on manuscript candidates.
findings: The complete result object from the recorded P-L1-007 script reproduced exactly, including all 72 planting conditions, three adjacency-preserving surrogates, public ZL/Takahashi partitions and twelve inherited line-chain controls. This replicates that implementation, not the authors' unpublished executable or their full-manuscript numerical results.

With word-boundary positions and candidate counts matched, full-pool replacement supports eight of twelve language/partition/contrast comparisons. The wrong-origin candidate has a lower loss in six and the genuine candidate in two, in both literal and prose modes. In four comparisons both candidates rank within 5%. These selected, shared-first-component contrasts do not estimate a population false-positive rate.

With exact previous glyph also matched, all 36 inherited planting conditions have identical X/Z scores despite different outgoing counts; thirteen meet support when counting all three replacement fractions. The tie follows from equal candidate frequency, equal incoming counts, and zero self-adjacency while proposed components A,B are held fixed. No term uses the right-context distribution of the candidate itself.

Separately written counting and loss code agrees with the inherited eight-rule vectors over 556316 triplet-by-convention evaluations in 32 text/convention conditions; the largest rule discrepancy is 3.3306690738754696e-16. All 176 tracked candidate rank decisions at the 5% threshold agree when the independent ranker includes floating-point ties.

At full matched-pool coverage, four additional fixed pairing seeds each reproduce six decoy wins and two genuine wins among eight supported word-position comparisons. Exact-left matching gives seven supported ties per seed. Across all five seed settings, all sixty exact-left trials have different outgoing counts and equal loss for X and Z. Seed settings were fixed in the audit script before running them; none was selected for its outcome.

A separately implemented first-order glyph line chain fitted only on public practice training lines, with six new seeds per edition, places m|i|d in the best 5% in all twelve emitted texts under both conventions. q|i|e passes in two of six ZL-trained and four of six Takahashi-trained texts. This generator emits one glyph at a time from a single transition table and never performs pair fusion. This is a public specificity control, not a new hidden-page generator submission.

For public evaluation q|i|e, the rarer member has one retained incoming context in each edition. Changing only the undefined-single-context Pearson loss from zero to one changes prose-mode rank from 0.04411764705882353 to 0.09627757352941177 in ZL and from 0.04388786764705882 to 0.09857536764705882 in Takahashi. The cutoff decision reverses. The zero-variance case with at least two contexts retains the inherited convention.
limitations: Public practice and reference partitions only; no hidden-page evaluation or scan adjudication was performed.
The full-support comparisons are a selected subset of twelve conditions. Planting seeds are not independent language samples and do not justify a significance estimate.
The 5% rank threshold is a ranking convention over candidate triplets, not a calibrated statistical p-value.
The fixed candidate triplets are investigated examples, not a search over all possible writing systems. Their low rank without fusion does not establish that manuscript glyphs are indivisible.
Printed/stated-rule differences and undefined Pearson cases prevent calling this an exact numerical reproduction of the original paper.

methods.independent_chain: Fit one character-transition count table per edition on public practice training paragraph lines. Sample initial glyphs from training starts; follow the table using sorted cumulative integer draws. At the last position disallow a space. """Independent numerical audit of P-L1-007 on public practice/reference text.

The inherited script supplies the deterministic planting and line-chain generation.
This module recomputes the loss and rank from separately counted text windows.
"""
import hashlib
import json
import math
import random
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from itertools import product
from pathlib import Path

import original_triplet as original
from vs import corpus, refcorpus

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
WEIGHTS = (1, 100, 1, 1, 100, 1, 1, 10)


class AuditScore:
    def __init__(self, text, single_loss=0):
        self.n = len(text)
        self.count = Counter()
        self.edges = Counter()
        self.row, self.col = Counter(), Counter()
        for i, ch in enumerate(text):
            self.count[ch] += 1
            if i:
                previous = text[i - 1]
                self.edges[previous, ch] += 1
                self.row[previous] += 1
                self.col[ch] += 1
        self.symbols = sorted(self.count)
        self.kept = {edge: n for edge, n in self.edges.items()
                     if n * 500 >= max(self.row[edge[0]], self.col[edge[1]])}
        self.p = {ch: n / self.n for ch, n in self.count.items()}
        self.max_p = max(self.count.values()) / self.n
        self.max_edge = max(self.kept.values()) / (self.n - 1)
        diagonal = [n / (self.n - 1) for (a, b), n in self.kept.items() if a == b]
        self.max_diagonal = max(diagonal) if diagonal else 1
        self.eligible = [ch for ch in self.symbols
                         if ch != ' ' and self.count[ch] * 229431 > 500 * self.n]
        self.single_loss = single_loss
        self.left = {}
        for c, a in product(self.symbols, repeat=2):
            rare, frequent = (c, a) if self.count[c] <= self.count[a] else (a, c)
            contexts = [s for s in self.symbols if (s, rare) in self.kept]
            u = [self.kept[s, rare] for s in contexts]
            v = [self.kept.get((s, frequent), 0) for s in contexts]
            if len(contexts) < 2:
                correlation_loss = single_loss if contexts else 0
            else:
                # Pearson via raw sums rather than the inherited centred vectors.
                n = len(u)
                covariance = n * sum(x * y for x, y in zip(u, v)) - sum(u) * sum(v)
                variance_u = n * sum(x * x for x in u) - sum(u) ** 2
                variance_v = n * sum(y * y for y in v) - sum(v) ** 2
                denominator = math.sqrt(variance_u * variance_v)
                correlation_loss = 1 - min(1, abs(covariance / denominator)) if denominator else 1
            common = sum(x for x, y in zip(u, v) if y) / (self.n - 1)
            uncommon = sum(x for x, y in zip(u, v) if not y) / (self.n - 1)
            self.left[c, a] = common, uncommon, correlation_loss

    def losses(self, c, a, b, version):
        pc, pa, pb = self.p[c], self.p[a], self.p[b]
        common, uncommon, pearson = self.left[c, a]
        probability = lambda edge: self.kept.get(edge, 0) / (self.n - 1)
        return (
            max(pc - max(pa, pb), 0) / self.max_p,
            probability((a, b)) / self.max_edge,
            common if version == 'literal' else uncommon,
            pearson,
            probability((c, c)) / self.max_diagonal,
            (1 - min(pa, pb)) / self.max_p if version == 'literal' else 1 - min(pa, pb) / self.max_p,
            pc / ((pa + pc) * (pb + pc)),
            int(a == b),
        )

    def total(self, triplet, version):
        return sum(w * loss for w, loss in zip(WEIGHTS, self.losses(*triplet, version)))


def verify_text(text, label, single_loss=0, tracked=()):
    audit = AuditScore(text, single_loss)
    inherited = original.Score(text, single_context_loss=single_loss)
    assert audit.eligible == inherited.alphabet
    errors = []
    for version in ('literal', 'prose'):
        checked = 0
        max_error = 0
        universe_losses = []
        for t in product(audit.eligible, repeat=3):
            if t[0] in t[1:]:
                continue
            checked += 1
            av, bv = audit.losses(*t, version), inherited.losses(*t, version)
            error = max(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(av, bv))
            max_error = max(max_error, error)
            assert all(math.isclose(x, y, rel_tol=1e-11, abs_tol=1e-11) for x, y in zip(av, bv)), (label, t, av, bv)
            universe_losses.append(sum(w * x for w, x in zip(WEIGHTS, av)))
        ranks = {}
        inherited_rank = inherited.ranker(version)
        for t in tracked:
            if not all(ch in audit.count for ch in t):
                continue
            score = audit.total(t, version)
            # Include numerical ties, rather than breaking them by floating point round-off.
            rank = sum(x <= score or math.isclose(x, score, rel_tol=1e-12, abs_tol=1e-12)
                       for x in universe_losses) / len(universe_losses)
            previous = inherited_rank(t)
            ranks['|'.join(t)] = {'audit_rank_with_ties': rank, 'recorded_rank': previous['rank'],
                                  'same_5pct_decision': (rank <= .05) == (previous['rank'] <= .05)}
            assert ranks['|'.join(t)]['same_5pct_decision'], (label, t, ranks['|'.join(t)])
        errors.append({'version': version, 'triplets': checked, 'max_rule_absolute_error': max_error, 'tracked_ranks': ranks})
    return {'label': label, 'characters': len(text), 'sha256': hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest(), 'audit': errors}


def main():
    output = {'audited_texts': [], 'matching_checks': [], 'seed_sensitivity': []}
    # Original contrast seeds, plus four fixed new seeds, chosen before this run.
    seeds = [9141, 137, 271, 409, 593]
    for language, contrasts in original.CONTRASTS.items():
        for partition, loader in [('train', refcorpus.train_text), ('control', refcorpus.control_text)]:
            text = ' ' + ' '.join(loader(language))[:40000].rsplit(' ', 1)[0] + ' '
            for index, (target, decoy) in enumerate(contrasts):
                for by_left in (False, True):
                    for seed in seeds:
                        actual_seed = seed + index if seed == 9141 else seed
                        pool = original.paired_positions(text, target, decoy, by_left, actual_seed)
                        encoded = original.encode(text, pool)
                        # Verify planting directly from source offsets, independently of the grouping code.
                        signature_x, signature_z = Counter(), Counter()
                        for i, j in pool:
                            assert text[i:i+2] == target and text[j:j+2] == decoy
                            signature = lambda k: (text[k-1] == ' ', text[k+2] == ' ', text[k-1] if by_left else '')
                            signature_x[signature(i)] += 1
                            signature_z[signature(j)] += 1
                        assert signature_x == signature_z
                        audit = AuditScore(encoded)
                        assert audit.count['X'] == audit.count['Z'] == len(pool)
                        incoming = sum(abs(audit.edges[s, 'X'] - audit.edges[s, 'Z']) for s in audit.symbols)
                        outgoing = sum(abs(audit.edges['X', s] - audit.edges['Z', s]) for s in audit.symbols)
                        eligible = 'X' in audit.eligible and 'Z' in audit.eligible
                        row = {'language': language, 'partition': partition, 'target': target, 'decoy': decoy,
                               'left_matched': by_left, 'seed': actual_seed, 'pairs': len(pool),
                               'eligible': eligible, 'incoming_L1': incoming, 'outgoing_L1': outgoing, 'scores': {}}
                        for version in ('literal', 'prose'):
                            x, z = audit.total(('X', *target), version), audit.total(('Z', *target), version)
                            row['scores'][version] = {'X': x, 'Z': z, 'difference_X_minus_Z': x-z}
                            if by_left:
                                assert incoming == 0 and math.isclose(x, z, abs_tol=1e-12)
                        output['seed_sensitivity'].append(row)
                        if seed == 9141:
                            label = f'{language}/{partition}/{target}-{decoy}/left={by_left}'
                            output['audited_texts'].append(verify_text(encoded, label, tracked=[('X', *target), ('Z', *target)]))
    for edition in ('zl', 'it'):
        for partition, pages in zip(('train', 'evaluation'), corpus.split_pages('practice', edition)):
            text = ' '.join(w for p in pages for ln in p.lines if ln.unit == 'P'
                            for w in ln.words if w.isascii() and w.isalpha())
            for single_loss in (0, 1):
                output['audited_texts'].append(verify_text(text, f'{edition}/{partition}/singleton={single_loss}', single_loss, original.DRAFT_TRIPLETS))
    output['independent_line_chain'] = independent_line_chain()
    (ROOT / 'audit.json').write_text(json.dumps(output, indent=2), encoding='utf-8')
    print(json.dumps({'audited_texts': len(output['audited_texts']), 'seed_conditions': len(output['seed_sensitivity'])}))


def independent_line_chain():
    """Fit a first-order table separately and emit glyphs without any pair fusion."""
    results = []
    for edition in ('zl', 'it'):
        training, evaluation = corpus.split_pages('practice', edition)
        clean = lambda pages: [' '.join(w for w in ln.words if w.isascii() and w.isalpha())
                               for p in pages for ln in p.lines if ln.unit == 'P']
        train = [ln for ln in clean(training) if ln]
        lengths = [len(ln) for ln in clean(evaluation) if ln]
        starts, transitions = Counter(ln[0] for ln in train), defaultdict(Counter)
        for line in train:
            for i in range(1, len(line)):
                transitions[line[i-1]][line[i]] += 1
        for seed in range(18710, 18716):
            rng = random.Random(seed)
            def draw(counts):
                # Sorted, cumulative integer sampling differs from the inherited expanded-list sampler.
                threshold = rng.randrange(sum(counts.values()))
                for symbol, count in sorted(counts.items()):
                    if threshold < count:
                        return symbol
                    threshold -= count
                raise AssertionError('invalid transition draw')
            lines = []
            for length in lengths:
                sequence = [draw(starts)]
                while len(sequence) < length:
                    options = transitions[sequence[-1]]
                    if len(sequence) == length - 1:
                        options = Counter({s: n for s, n in options.items() if s != ' '})
                    sequence.append(draw(options or starts))
                lines.append(''.join(sequence))
            text = ' '.join(lines)
            assert [len(s) for s in lines] == lengths and '  ' not in text
            calculator = AuditScore(text)
            row = {'edition': edition, 'seed': seed, 'characters': len(text),
                   'sha256': hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest(), 'ranks': {}}
            for version in ('literal', 'prose'):
                losses = [calculator.total(t, version) for t in product(calculator.eligible, repeat=3) if t[0] not in t[1:]]
                row['ranks'][version] = {}
                for t in original.DRAFT_TRIPLETS:
                    if not all(ch in calculator.p for ch in t):
                        continue
                    score = calculator.total(t, version)
                    rank = sum(x <= score or math.isclose(x, score, rel_tol=1e-12, abs_tol=1e-12) for x in losses) / len(losses)
                    row['ranks'][version]['|'.join(t)] = {'rank': rank, 'competing': all(ch in calculator.eligible for ch in t)}
            results.append(row)
    return results


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

This replicates that implementation, not the authors' unpublished executable or their full-manuscript numerical results.

With word-boundary positions and candidate counts matched, full-pool replacement supports eight of twelve language/partition/contrast comparisons. The wrong-origin candidate has a lower loss in six and the genuine candidate in two, in both literal and prose modes. In four comparisons both candidates rank within 5%. These selected, shared-first-component contrasts do not estimate a population false-positive rate.

                    for seed in seeds:
                        actual_seed = seed + index if seed == 9141 else seed
                        pool = original.paired_positions(text, target, decoy, by_left, actual_seed)
                        encoded = original.encode(text, pool)
                        # Verify planting directly from source offsets, independently of the grouping code.
                        signature_x, signature_z = Counter(), Counter()
                        for i, j in pool:
                            assert text[i:i+2] == target and text[j:j+2] == decoy
                            signature = lambda k: (text[k-1] == ' ', text[k+2] == ' ', text[k-1] if by_left else '')
                            signature_x[signature(i)] += 1
                            signature_z[signature(j)] += 1
                        assert signature_x == signature_z
                        audit = AuditScore(encoded)
                        assert audit.count['X'] == audit.count['Z'] == len(pool)
                        incoming = sum(abs(audit.edges[s, 'X'] - audit.edges[s, 'Z']) for s in audit.symbols)
                        outgoing = sum(abs(audit.edges['X', s] - audit.edges['Z', s]) for s in audit.symbols)
                        eligible = 'X' in audit.eligible and 'Z' in audit.eligible
                        row = {'language': language, 'partition': partition, 'target': target, 'decoy': decoy,
                               'left_matched': by_left, 'seed': actual_seed, 'pairs': len(pool),
                               'eligible': eligible, 'incoming_L1': incoming, 'outgoing_L1': outgoing, 'scores': {}}
                        for version in ('literal', 'prose'):
                            x, z = audit.total(('X', *target), version), audit.total(('Z', *target), version)
                            row['scores'][version] = {'X': x, 'Z': z, 'difference_X_minus_Z': x-z}
                            if by_left:
                                assert incoming == 0 and math.isclose(x, z, abs_tol=1e-12)
                        output['seed_sensitivity'].append(row)
                        if seed == 9141:
                            label = f'{language}/{partition}/{target}-{decoy}/left={by_left}'
                            output['audited_texts'].append(verify_text(encoded, label, tracked=[('X', *target), ('Z', *target)]))
    for edition in ('zl', 'it'):
        for partition, pages in zip(('train', 'evaluation'), corpus.split_pages('practice', edition)):
            text = ' '.join(w for p in pages for ln in p.lines if ln.unit == 'P'
                            for w in ln.words if w.isascii() and w.isalpha())
            for single_loss in (0, 1):
                output['audited_texts'].append(verify_text(text, f'{edition}/{partition}/singleton={single_loss}', single_loss, original.DRAFT_TRIPLETS))
    output['independent_line_chain'] = independent_line_chain()
    (ROOT / 'audit.json').write_text(json.dumps(output, indent=2), encoding='utf-8')
    print(json.dumps({'audited_texts': len(output['audited_texts']), 'seed_conditions': len(output['seed_sensitivity'])}))


def independent_line_chain():
    """Fit a first-order table separately and emit glyphs without any pair fusion."""
    results = []
    for edition in ('zl', 'it'):
        training, evaluation = corpus.split_pages('practice', edition)
        clean = lambda pages: [' '.join(w for w in ln.words if w.isascii() and w.isalpha())
                               for p in pages for ln in p.lines if ln.unit == 'P']
        train = [ln for ln in clean(training) if ln]
        lengths = [len(ln) for ln in clean(evaluation) if ln]
        starts, transitions = Counter(ln[0] for ln in train), defaultdict(Counter)
        for line in train:
            for i in range(1, len(line)):
                transitions[line[i-1]][line[i]] += 1
        for seed in range(18710, 18716):
            rng = random.Random(seed)
            def draw(counts):
                # Sorted, cumulative integer sampling differs from the inherited expanded-list sampler.
                threshold = rng.randrange(sum(counts.values()))
                for symbol, count in sorted(counts.items()):
                    if threshold < count:
                        return symbol
                    threshold -= count
                raise AssertionError('invalid transition draw')
            lines = []
            for length in lengths:
                sequence = [draw(starts)]
                while len(sequence) < length:
                    options = transitions[sequence[-1]]
                    if len(sequence) == length - 1:
                        options = Counter({s: n for s, n in options.items() if s != ' '})
                    sequence.append(draw(options or starts))
                lines.append(''.join(sequence))
            text = ' '.join(lines)
            assert [len(s) for s in lines] == lengths and '  ' not in text
            calculator = AuditScore(text)
            row = {'edition': edition, 'seed': seed, 'characters': len(text),
                   'sha256': hashlib.sha256(text.encode()).hexdigest(), 'ranks': {}}
            for version in ('literal', 'prose'):
                losses = [calculator.total(t, version) for t in product(calculator.eligible, repeat=3) if t[0] not in t[1:]]
                row['ranks'][version] = {}
                for t in original.DRAFT_TRIPLETS:
                    if not all(ch in calculator.p for ch in t):
                        continue
                    score = calculator.total(t, version)
                    rank = sum(x <= score or math.isclose(x, score, rel_tol=1e-12, abs_tol=1e-12) for x in losses) / len(losses)
                    row['ranks'][version]['|'.join(t)] = {'rank': rank, 'competing': all(ch in calculator.eligible for ch in t)}
            results.append(row)
    return results


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

step.json.statement: I independently reran and audited P-L1-007 on the pinned public practice/reference inputs. All recorded results reproduce exactly. Separate counting, Pearson and loss code confirms the numerical scores and the candidate cutoff decisions. Matched wrong-origin symbols can outscore genuine fusions; equal incoming contexts force ties even when outgoing contexts differ. New direct-emission line controls again yield low ligature ranks without performing symbol fusion. The q|i|e cutoff decision depends on an undefined-single-context Pearson convention. These are limitations of the statistical discriminator; they do not adjudicate physical glyph composition or decipherment.

claims_and_comparisons.attested_persian_diagram: The surviving Greater Bundahišn horoscope diagram is for chapter V A and is a different genre from a chapter II mansion list. It uses a central square and twelve peripheral houses, made by cutting four square corners diagonally. Raffaelli records the textual Cancer ascendant at nineteen degrees and associated zodiac assignments for Jupiter, Saturn, Mars, Venus and Mercury, the Sun, the Moon and the nodes. The manuscript diagrams have copying and placement discrepancies. The Iranian manuscript witnesses postdate the Voynich parchment dating interval. Their appropriate role here is an attested structural comparator and a source of conditional forecasts.
claims_and_comparisons.explicit_text_structure: The Indian and Greater texts describe twelve zodiacal constellations and twenty-eight subdividing asterisms, with four directional chieftains and a chief over them. West and Anklesaria differ in how they place Sataves and Vanand on the south and west axes. MacKenzie cautions that only twenty-seven mansion names are recoverable in the corrupt tradition. The Greater text also puts ordinary and then unmixed stars below the Moon and Sun, a potentially discriminating comparison only when objects and inside-out order are actually identifiable.
claims_and_comparisons.f67v2: Herrmann section 3.4 interprets four words around a small swirling square as sacrifice, lot, power and foundation, and proposes a possible fire context. The attribution depends on his script readings and provides no cited depiction or diagram of a particular rite. The optical check treats the proposed script values as unused.
claims_and_comparisons.f69v: Herrmann section 3.3 reports possible identifications of twenty of twenty-eight lunar mansions. His citation here is Justi's 1868 Bundehesh. He omits the identified positions and readings, so the claimed lexical correspondence cannot be reconstructed from the paper.
claims_and_comparisons.other_shared_structures: The Arabic Book of Curiosities diagram independently uses a zodiac tier and a mansion tier. The scholars' reading distinguishes twelve zodiac constellations, thirty-six other classical constellations and twenty-eight mansions. Or.133 has distinct bands including zodiac and lunar stations with differing red dot patterns. Castilian f21r uses an Arabic-derived text and a radial figurative wheel. Latin Clm 10268 f114r puts asterisms into a grid. These comparators separate writing language from the transmission history of an astronomy system.
claims_and_comparisons.zodiac: Appendix A proposes sign and month readings. Its notes acknowledge visually repeated ram and bull designs, where it tentatively assigns Capricorn and Aquarius. Unpublished lunar positions and tentative zodiac reinterpretations do not supply an objective order to impose on f69v.

extra_periodic_calendar_control.interpretation: Nadal identifies twenty-eight years of the Julian solar reckoning cycle, with pairs of dominical letters every fourth cell, plus a separate inner numerical register. This differs from a ring of twenty-eight lunar stations even though the radial count matches. The right wheel on the manuscript page uses nineteen places for the lunar golden number. These readings identify the control independently of the Voynich hypothesis.
