results.bundahis_sample: The TD2 figure draws a square-house horoscope with diagonal corners and twelve peripheral units. This is physically much more constrained than a round object with an arbitrary count and directly illustrates the value of a testable arrangement. It is from chapter V A, not a picture accompanying the chapter II mansion list. Its later copy and differing diagram labels warrant comparison of patterns, while an identification as the source exemplar would require independent evidence.
results.central_motif: The f67v2 crop and the wide supplement agree on a four-sided pinwheel and distinct axial and diagonal drawings. They supply no clear pedestal, bilaterally flanking figures or isolated upward flame. The known Sasanian example has a distinct raised altar and two flankers, detected despite uncertain details of the crest. This calibrates recognition of those features in one iconographic family. The difference in medium and centuries of transmission limits deductions about a highly stylized fire image.
results.layer_order: The Arabic charts visually present several separate rings, with known roles supplied independently by the manuscripts and scholarship. f69v has an inner hub and surrounding text bands, with no identified Moon or Sun ring or register for fixed asterisms. The Bundahišn layer-order prediction is therefore unscored on this figure, rather than contradicted.
repeated_units: f69v has twenty-eight repeated bars with two alternating paint and length treatments. The matched Castilian mansion wheel has twenty-eight pictorial sectors, Arabic examples have nested name, dot and zodiac tiers, and the Latin grid has twenty-eight used cells. The graphic realization of the count differs in every case. A known scheme's count is useful evidence of compatibility with a mansion reading, but lacks geographic specificity.

No independently marked twelve-supersector hierarchy or four identifiable directional leaders was resolved on f69v. The manuscript's cyclic alternation is preserved by fourteen rotations and fourteen reflections, giving twenty-eight equivalent assignments of the same pattern. Thus alternation alone cannot anchor any one named first unit or a sense of rotation.

Or.133 supplies a distinct example of visual alternation in a twelve-position band, alongside an independently divided outer mansion band. The Latin wind diagram combines a fourfold center with twelve surrounding units. Fourfold structure, concentric organization and repeated treatments recur outside the Persian text.
results.scope: Two source-masked image-model readings per crop, no literal word reading, and selected historical controls. The supported observations concern the listed views and rulings. Neither the unpublished twenty readings nor a unique route of transmission can be tested here.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Concentric bands with four separate cardinal ornaments. Central raised tiered object and two flanking humanlike figures. Possible short upward tongues at the top.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Concentric bands and four outer ornaments. A central upright stacked pedestal and inward-facing human figures flank it. Rising taper probable and exact tongue count uncertain.

visual_pairs.reader_1: About twenty-eight narrow radial sections with heterogeneous pictorial objects. No separate four or twelve grouping. The center has a rider on a long-eared animal.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Twenty-eight traced wedges with varied human and animal figures. No separate four or twelve grouping. A single mounted figure raises an arm in the center.

visual_pairs.reader_1: A five-column by six-row grid with two empty cells. Various dot or star patterns in the remaining cells.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A red five-by-six grid with twenty-eight populated cells. Star counts and arrangements vary. No central image or separate four- or twelve-part tier.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Fourteen long dark and fourteen shorter pale capped bars alternate. No clear independently marked four or twelve. A pale radial center lacks a raised base or flankers.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Exactly twenty-eight capped bars, fourteen elongated dark alternating with fourteen shorter pale. No independently marked four or twelve. Irregular light radial hub.

visual_pairs.reader_1: A curved pinwheel inside a four-sided frame with four green corners and axial marks. No raised base, flanking people or separate upward flames.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A pinwheel in a four-sided frame, green corners and four axes. No upright flames, separate base or flankers.

visual_pairs.reader_1: A central face surrounded by wavy rays and variable stars. No visible ruled radial cells or dominant four or twelve grouping.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A face with wavy rays throughout all directions. About thirty-nine visible stars, three green. No ruled sectors or separately marked four and twelve.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Twelve radial bands plus four diagonal spike groups. The central disk has a probable fourfold subdivision. The fours do not partition the twelve.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Twelve radial motifs with twelve intervening blue scalloped fields. A fourfold cross seems visible in the green center, without rule connections assigning three outer sectors per quarter.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Twelve bounded inner sections, a finer outer tier of about twenty-eight interrupted by seams, red and black distinction in the inner band and diverse outer dot groups.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A separate twelve-cell band with dark and striped alternating sections. The outer ring has about twenty-eight heterogeneous red dot cells, with precise count obscured at the seam.

visual_pairs.reader_1: A broad outer layer consistent with twelve fields, a dense mid-thirties set of finer cells and other finer rings. The middle is a ruled circular text panel.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Twelve broad outer sectors and an uneven finer dot tier with a mid-thirties count. Sparse and dense groups, no alternating bars. A circular ruled central text panel.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Nine main squares in three rows and columns. Four corner diagonals produce twelve peripheral compartments plus one central square.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A nine-cell square grid whose four corner diagonals yield twelve surrounding regions. The central square contains writing. No radiating bars or central figure.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Four axial marks and four separately drawn diagonal stems or heads. Neither delimits surrounding cells. A curved pinwheel sits in a green-cornered frame, without an upright scene.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A pinwheel framed by green corners and four slender axial lines with terminals. Four separate diagonal decorated stems are independent of the central square. No surrounding sectors.

visual_protocol.blinding: Randomize nine crops with seed 28067, then present two anonymous supplementary crops. Two auxiliary image-model readers receive anonymous images, a fixed structural rubric and no identifications or proposed readings. Published captions and article prose are outside the cropped diagrams. Script, media and recognizable stylistic details remain visible. Their absence of a name assignment means blinding is to supplied provenance and predictions.
visual_protocol.inference: A naked count or radial format shared with a well-identified comparator has low specificity. Identify a directional alignment only from differential markers with an independent anchor to the meaning of a direction. Identify an outside-to-inside sphere order only with evidence identifying two named layers. Zero explicit match on these structures leaves the proposed attribution unresolved. No composite similarity score or probability of origin is inferred.
visual_protocol.rubric: Record the dominant topology and visible repeating unit count, independently marked fours or twelves and their relation to the principal unit, alternation, differentiated star groups, central form and whether an upright support, rising flames, flanking people or a four-sided enclosure can be traced. Keep any uncertain count or ambiguous contour explicitly qualified. Code the supplementary f67v2 view for slender axes and separate diagonal decorated motifs.
visual_protocol.selection: Use the two named Voynich targets, an adjacent internal control, the earlier Or.133 comparator, two additional medieval mansion diagrams, one Latin non-mansion wind diagram and one definite historical altar. Use a supplementary attested Persian horoscope and a wider view of f67v2. Keep the differing purposes and media of these controls explicit.

results.bundahis_sample: The TD2 figure draws a square-house horoscope with diagonal corners and twelve peripheral units. This is physically much more constrained than a round object with an arbitrary count and directly illustrates the value of a testable arrangement. It is from chapter V A, not a picture accompanying the chapter II mansion list. Its later copy and differing diagram labels warrant comparison of patterns, while an identification as the source exemplar would require independent evidence.
results.central_motif: The f67v2 crop and the wide supplement agree on a four-sided pinwheel and distinct axial and diagonal drawings. They supply no clear pedestal, bilaterally flanking figures or isolated upward flame. The known Sasanian example has a distinct raised altar and two flankers, detected despite uncertain details of the crest. This calibrates recognition of those features in one iconographic family. The difference in medium and centuries of transmission limits deductions about a highly stylized fire image.
results.layer_order: The Arabic charts visually present several separate rings, with known roles supplied independently by the manuscripts and scholarship. f69v has an inner hub and surrounding text bands, with no identified Moon or Sun ring or register for fixed asterisms. The Bundahišn layer-order prediction is therefore unscored on this figure, rather than contradicted.
repeated_units: f69v has twenty-eight repeated bars with two alternating paint and length treatments. The matched Castilian mansion wheel has twenty-eight pictorial sectors, Arabic examples have nested name, dot and zodiac tiers, and the Latin grid has twenty-eight used cells. The graphic realization of the count differs in every case. A known scheme's count is useful evidence of compatibility with a mansion reading, but lacks geographic specificity.

No independently marked twelve-supersector hierarchy or four identifiable directional leaders was resolved on f69v. The manuscript's cyclic alternation is preserved by fourteen rotations and fourteen reflections, giving twenty-eight equivalent assignments of the same pattern. Thus alternation alone cannot anchor any one named first unit or a sense of rotation.

Or.133 supplies a distinct example of visual alternation in a twelve-position band, alongside an independently divided outer mansion band. The Latin wind diagram combines a fourfold center with twelve surrounding units. Fourfold structure, concentric organization and repeated treatments recur outside the Persian text.
results.scope: Two source-masked image-model readings per crop, no literal word reading, and selected historical controls. The supported observations concern the listed views and rulings. Neither the unpublished twenty readings nor a unique route of transmission can be tested here.

step.json.statement: Compare the diagram structures proposed in Herrmann's Pahlavi hypothesis against dated Arabic and Western comparators and the surviving Bundahišn horoscope. Source-masked readers agree that f69v has 28 alternating bars and that f67v2 has a fourfold pinwheel. Neither supplies the distinctive spatial and iconographic correspondences needed to favor a particular tradition.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Concentric bands with four separate cardinal ornaments. Central raised tiered object and two flanking humanlike figures. Possible short upward tongues at the top.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Concentric bands and four outer ornaments. A central upright stacked pedestal and inward-facing human figures flank it. Rising taper probable and exact tongue count uncertain.

visual_pairs.reader_1: About twenty-eight narrow radial sections with heterogeneous pictorial objects. No separate four or twelve grouping. The center has a rider on a long-eared animal.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Twenty-eight traced wedges with varied human and animal figures. No separate four or twelve grouping. A single mounted figure raises an arm in the center.

visual_pairs.reader_1: A five-column by six-row grid with two empty cells. Various dot or star patterns in the remaining cells.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A red five-by-six grid with twenty-eight populated cells. Star counts and arrangements vary. No central image or separate four- or twelve-part tier.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Fourteen long dark and fourteen shorter pale capped bars alternate. No clear independently marked four or twelve. A pale radial center lacks a raised base or flankers.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Exactly twenty-eight capped bars, fourteen elongated dark alternating with fourteen shorter pale. No independently marked four or twelve. Irregular light radial hub.

visual_pairs.reader_1: A curved pinwheel inside a four-sided frame with four green corners and axial marks. No raised base, flanking people or separate upward flames.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A pinwheel in a four-sided frame, green corners and four axes. No upright flames, separate base or flankers.

visual_pairs.reader_1: A central face surrounded by wavy rays and variable stars. No visible ruled radial cells or dominant four or twelve grouping.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A face with wavy rays throughout all directions. About thirty-nine visible stars, three green. No ruled sectors or separately marked four and twelve.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Twelve radial bands plus four diagonal spike groups. The central disk has a probable fourfold subdivision. The fours do not partition the twelve.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Twelve radial motifs with twelve intervening blue scalloped fields. A fourfold cross seems visible in the green center, without rule connections assigning three outer sectors per quarter.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Twelve bounded inner sections, a finer outer tier of about twenty-eight interrupted by seams, red and black distinction in the inner band and diverse outer dot groups.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A separate twelve-cell band with dark and striped alternating sections. The outer ring has about twenty-eight heterogeneous red dot cells, with precise count obscured at the seam.

visual_pairs.reader_1: A broad outer layer consistent with twelve fields, a dense mid-thirties set of finer cells and other finer rings. The middle is a ruled circular text panel.
visual_pairs.reader_2: Twelve broad outer sectors and an uneven finer dot tier with a mid-thirties count. Sparse and dense groups, no alternating bars. A circular ruled central text panel.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Nine main squares in three rows and columns. Four corner diagonals produce twelve peripheral compartments plus one central square.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A nine-cell square grid whose four corner diagonals yield twelve surrounding regions. The central square contains writing. No radiating bars or central figure.

visual_pairs.reader_1: Four axial marks and four separately drawn diagonal stems or heads. Neither delimits surrounding cells. A curved pinwheel sits in a green-cornered frame, without an upright scene.
visual_pairs.reader_2: A pinwheel framed by green corners and four slender axial lines with terminals. Four separate diagonal decorated stems are independent of the central square. No surrounding sectors.

visual_protocol.blinding: Randomize nine crops with seed 28067, then present two anonymous supplementary crops. Two auxiliary image-model readers receive anonymous images, a fixed structural rubric and no identifications or proposed readings. Published captions and article prose are outside the cropped diagrams. Script, media and recognizable stylistic details remain visible. Their absence of a name assignment means blinding is to supplied provenance and predictions.
visual_protocol.inference: A naked count or radial format shared with a well-identified comparator has low specificity. Identify a directional alignment only from differential markers with an independent anchor to the meaning of a direction. Identify an outside-to-inside sphere order only with evidence identifying two named layers. Zero explicit match on these structures leaves the proposed attribution unresolved. No composite similarity score or probability of origin is inferred.
visual_protocol.rubric: Record the dominant topology and visible repeating unit count, independently marked fours or twelves and their relation to the principal unit, alternation, differentiated star groups, central form and whether an upright support, rising flames, flanking people or a four-sided enclosure can be traced. Keep any uncertain count or ambiguous contour explicitly qualified. Code the supplementary f67v2 view for slender axes and separate diagonal decorated motifs.
visual_protocol.selection: Use the two named Voynich targets, an adjacent internal control, the earlier Or.133 comparator, two additional medieval mansion diagrams, one Latin non-mansion wind diagram and one definite historical altar. Use a supplementary attested Persian horoscope and a wider view of f67v2. Keep the differing purposes and media of these controls explicit.

historical_claims.note: Stolfi discusses f33v, including disk, rays and possible bracts, and objections from leaf division, apparent insertion, divided ray tips and rounded underground forms.
O’Neill 1944 says fol. 93, identified as Helianthus annuus and supported by six botanists, without listing diagnostic sunflower characters there.

Tucker and Talbert 2013 specify f93r for O’Neill’s sunflower, discuss compression of a tall plant, and propose Psacalium peltigerum separately for f33v. The latter identification is outside these coded comparisons.

Janick 2020 records that the surviving Hernández 1651 sunflower plates use substituted European images, one reversed from the 1633 Gerard edition. We do not count that illustration as an independent comparator.

method.coding: A ray is long at or above half the local disk radius, short below, absent if no distinct rays, and U if the relation is not clear. Margin or open basal notch is edge and attachment directly to a stem is sessile. Multiple means two or more visibly developed heads. All categories describe drawn structures. U means obscure, inapplicable, or not shown, with reasons below.
method.head_sampling: Top-left f33v head used as primary; upper-right scored separately as a crop sensitivity, sharing one page and artist. f93r is a distinct target. Dodoens single head and Besler largest central open head. Old World controls chosen for disk, compact head or ambiguous attachment; credits below. The right scabious crop and the water lily crop omit part of the ray perimeter. The Dodoens crop cuts some peripheral tip strokes. Retain uncertainty codes and inspect original when coverage matters.
prior_exposure: The organizer knew all sources and the original arguments before mask preparation and did not enter the independent ratings.

Four model reader instances scored separate panels, two per region. All report no previous viewing they could recall of the exact masked images or each other’s ratings. They received anonymous IDs and no identity key or literature.

The sunflower topic was inferable from the task or folder. Some readers recognized engraving, manuscript writing and sunflower-like silhouettes, and one head reader noticed the likely repeat. This was label masking with independent scoring, with incomplete provenance blinding.
The readers are model instances in one agent session, with shared model family and some general manuscript context. Four votes are not four independent botanical assessments.
method.scores: All matches use number of equal non-U categories followed by number of jointly visible categories, separately for each reader, no weighting. At least three comparisons are required for ranking; tables also retain the smaller denominators. Readers were given rubric and independent codes before seeing the source map. Sample is purposive; ranks are descriptive.
method.whole_sampling: Show full plant and the root region when present. Nymphaea shows only two separate leaf/flower shapes in the mask and cyclamen is a deliberately restricted root-only comparison. The latter cannot enter whole-plant rankings. The root systems of Dodoens and Besler, and one concealed f33v attachment, cannot be compared.

qualitative_checks.observation: Pale interior marks and inward-running veins are visible in several blades. Neither whole reader could trace a clear petiole-to-blade junction through the opaque fill. Nymphaea offers a visible marginal notch comparator; Petasites attachment was disputed between readers.

Both readers marked round enlargements attached to branches on f33v. Both coded the cropped cyclamen root U because the organ context was insufficient, and neither historical sunflower prints the root. The c. 1280–1350 Egerton MS 747 f18v (https://bl.digirati.io/images/ark:/81055/vdc_100058663074.0x00002c/canvas/c/44) also offers a round body with radiating fine strokes, but the two herbal cyclamen images may be descended from a related illustrated tradition. Root specificity remains unresolved.

Besler shows several heads with side branches and exposed pointed structures, so those characters can occur in historical sunflower illustrations. Whole readers split on whether its main stem dominates.

The pointed, continuous head has fine dots. Both head readers recorded absent outer rays and unknown ray-tip shape. Whole readers agree on one dominant upright and one head, direct-looking blade contacts, and fine root strands. They disagree on broad/narrow. There is no combined f33v/f93r score.

No taxon can be rejected reliably from this small purposive image sample. Historical images can inherit other images and visual features are correlated. Head masks and whole drawings answer different questions and cannot be combined as independent evidence. There is no held-out score and no text pairing.

qualitative_checks.description: Mattioli 1565 p.1122, named Umbilicus Veneris. The organizer observed clear interior blade dimples and underside views on the Old World navelwort plate. The two whole readers kept the corresponding f33v contact unknown. This is a supplementary unmasked illustration check without points.

detail.question: K-033-open-1; Stolfi 1998 open question about f33v. These are completed observations attached to the desk step.

features: short radiating marks around round form
root_crop_sensitivity.findings: Both readers agreed on every category. The two related cyclamen illustrations show a single outlined body with short peripheral marks and upright stems. The paired outer f33v bodies have similar peripheral marks and join laterally at a shared stem; contact at the partly clipped third body is less clear. A round outlined organ with radiating marks can occur in Old World depictions, while this sample distinguishes the number and positions of the bodies. Calendula was coded thick-axis from the whole view and fine strands from the restricted region, showing scope sensitivity at a thick stem neck.
root_crop_sensitivity.method: Two head readers independently rated a new six-panel grayscale root-only sheet after storing head results, with a separate code map. They saw no whole panels, though prior head exposure and recognizable illustration conventions could indicate the context. Dodoens and Besler cannot be rated because their plates omit the root region. Radius-like lines can be visible without proving anatomical type.

sensitivity.interpretation: Dropping disk boundary, outer ray length and silhouette retains two more specific head features. Both f33v views remain closer to the sampled Calendula than to either sunflower in this subset. Crosshatched textures can arise from different drawing conventions, so this is not a biological identification.

detail.source_coordinate_convention: Fractional boxes are xyxy fractions of source dimensions, rounded to nearest pixel before grayscale crop. Control pixel boxes are xyxy in the indicated original file frames. Controls used a first resize to fit 880×1070; the common final ceiling was 500×650, then small separate contact sheets for inspection. Rectangular fills cover external captions, numerals or portions of writing where separate from plant strokes.

besler.reference: Basilius Besler, Hortus Eystettensis, 1613, summer order V, plate 2, Flos Solis prolifer
besler.role: Independent named Helianthus annuus engraving with several developed heads and exposed bracts; image stops at the stems

butterbur.reference: Leonhart Fuchs, De historia stirpium, 1542, p. 644, PETASITES
butterbur.role: Pointed compact head, radially veined broad blades, thick lower axis

calendula.role: Rayed head and drawn root; catalogue and derivative differ on species, so comparison is at genus level

cyclamen.reference: British Library Sloane MS 4016, c. 1440, f31r, cyclamen root detail
cyclamen.role: Root-shape illustration only; organ relation and other characters scored unknown in the short mask

dodoens.reference: Rembert Dodoens, Florum, et coronariarum odoratarumque nonnullarum herbarum historia, 1568, p. 295, CHRYSANTH. PERVVIANVM.
dodoens.role: Named Helianthus annuus woodcut, one prominent head, no below-ground view

egerton_cyclamen.reference: British Library Egerton MS 747 f18v, c. 1280–1350, De ciclamine
egerton_cyclamen.role: Second rounded root detail, from a related illustrated tradition to Sloane MS 4016

nymphaea.reference: Auslasser, 1479, BSB Clm 5905 f264r, water lily
nymphaea.role: Broad blades with a deep marginal notch and a radiate flower; lower stalk tails omitted, no discernible root on source

oxeye.reference: Auslasser, 1479, BSB Clm 5905 f241r, white daisy form
oxeye.role: Three rayed heads with discrete disks and an illustrated root; no dependence on exact species identification

scabious.reference: Auslasser, 1479, BSB Clm 5905 f255r, identified as Scabiosa in the derivative
scabious.role: Clustered heads and lobed leaves; the exact modern species attribution is secondary

detail.statement: On the sampled drawings f33v shares a bounded oval disk and projecting rays with the named sunflower prints. Both head readers distinguish their simple ray tips from the divided f33v tips, and the 1479 Calendula head matches f33v on all five coded features. Whole-plant readers agree on deeply divided f33v blades and rounded lower bodies, while both named sunflower prints show simple blades and lack a below-ground region. They leave f33v leaf insertion unknown. The separate f93r head is tapered, punctate and lacks a discrete ray fringe in these views. Its head scores are higher against the 1542 Petasites illustration than against either sunflower, although f93r has a closer whole-plant score with Dodoens. These comparisons do not establish either plant identity or a word-to-picture anchor.

step.json.statement: On the sampled drawings f33v shares a bounded oval disk and projecting rays with the named sunflower prints. Both head readers distinguish their simple ray tips from the divided f33v tips, and the 1479 Calendula head matches f33v on all five coded features. Whole-plant readers agree on deeply divided f33v blades and rounded lower bodies, while both named sunflower prints show simple blades and lack a below-ground region. They leave f33v leaf insertion unknown. The separate f93r head is tapered, punctate and lacks a discrete ray fringe in these views. Its head scores are higher against the 1542 Petasites illustration than against either sunflower, although f93r has a closer whole-plant score with Dodoens. These comparisons do not establish either plant identity or a word-to-picture anchor.

source: Torsten Timm, How the Voynich Manuscript was created, first posted 2014, revised 2015 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.6639), section 5, graphs 2–4 and appendices VI–VII. This tests the layout-matched comparative claim for altered forms. F-015 tested exact same-word recurrence and was refuted. F-021 established bounded previous-line one-edit excess against a within-page null and reported a public reference comparison without registering it. Here the token selection, lags, minimum length, and edit distance are inherited without tuning, and the explicit above-all reference comparison is the sole test. The pinned DSL uses single character insertion, deletion, or replacement on stored transliteration strings. Eligible current tokens have four earlier consecutive selected numbered lines on the same page. References are in source order within calibration blocks and poured into the exact selected word slots, with short corpora excluded. The measure is an adaptation of Timm's 20-line analysis, which allowed cross-page comparisons and used a different script representation. The above_all comparator passes ties and uses zero margin. This test is sensitive to the strongest reference and its calibration excerpts, and does not determine a cause of recurrence. Exploratory public checks are recorded below. The two successful prior attacks R-022 and R-024 show that a positive local excess of altered forms is compatible with nonlinguistic copying procedures; the present comparison does not adjudicate those procedures.
statement: In certain paragraph text, the share of current words of at least four transliteration characters that have a spelling exactly one character edit away on the previous line, minus the corresponding share four lines back, is at least the largest value for any reference corpus measured on the same selected word slots.

experiment.json.summary: Register whether previous-line one-edit variants exceed the strongest layout-matched reference, using the fixed F-021 repetition statistic.

exploratory_paragraph_null.interpretation: The edit-near result weakens when exact selected line lengths are preserved. The small sample is compatible with subtle layout effects and lower power. Matching selected line length does not fix the number of eligible long tokens across positions. Voynich grammar and the production process cannot be identified by these tests.
exploratory_paragraph_null.method: Use P paragraphs from explicit opening and ending markers. Keep contiguous interior runs of at least five certain-token lines. Exclude first and last paragraph lines. For each current eligible token record binary exact hits (minimum length 2) and one-character-edit hits (minimum length 4), previous line minus four back. Shuffle whole intact lines inside each eligible run with 199 permutations, Python Random seed 408, once unrestricted and once restricted to equal certain-token counts. One-sided p with ties counted toward the null. This is a smaller public subset with a different question from the reference comparison.

detail.statement: A tall green-stemmed plant drawing with layered coiled blade-like parts, six separate blue painted lobes at the upper right, and a rounded, lightly outlined lower body at the foot of the stem.
visual_uncertainty: The bold blue lobe count is six. Fine, unpainted lines around the small rosette do not consistently close into additional separate lobes. A fine short stalk appears to run from its underside into the upper crown, with the lower join partly hidden.

Five visible blade-like shapes are distinguishable by drawn edges, innermost notches, or stalk connections. The green and olive curved areas behind them share concealed boundaries and are grouped into one painted region. This grouping does not establish that they are one leaf.

A pale two-line stalk ends in a small loop inside the lower part of the central blade. Thin branches in the fan overlap; isolated lines were not counted as separate stalks. Five short upper-leaning stubs can be traced at least partly to the main stem, with the two thinnest brown connections less certain.

The broad lowest form is called root by position only. Its outer line is partly faint in the lower right margin. Numerous interior hooks and shorter marginal scallops are visible; their number and anatomy are uncertain.
Faint reversed or offset marks in the left background and marginal number-like marks lack visible joins to the plant. They are not assigned to the drawing. No taxon is identified.

interpretation: Three matched editions share both reported written endings. Frequency varies by edition, and chi alone occurs in all four matched editions and in the Highland Puebla treebank.

Much of chi counting comes from a few frequent spellings. A terminal letter string can belong to unrelated stems or forms, so it does not by itself identify the proposed owl root. Counts across books preserve the same presence pattern.

Living regional varieties in the proposed areas are independently documented. The published label assays leave the manuscript’s variety unassigned and support no extinction conclusion for a specific historical speech community.

A sound correspondence supported in independently read examples at several word positions could establish affinity to groups retaining that reflex. The raw letter-sequence indicator gives a limited comparison among written editions.

parallel_corpus_method.comparability: Parallel text controls much of the subject matter. Each edition has its own orthography, contributors, vocabulary and morphosyntax. The printed strings are not phonetic measurements or language genealogies. Report the Highland treebank as an unmatched genre check. The 3,755 verse-number preliminary match permitting bridged markers gave the same qualitative result. Remove bridged verses in the principal result. Historical works are independent follow-up controls, with different genres and orthographic conventions.
parallel_corpus_method.data_scope: Local descriptive comparison using publicly readable editions. Only aggregate results and a few word examples are used here. The colonial Nahuatl, modern dictionaries and nonparallel Highland sample do not enter the four-edition counts.
parallel_corpus_method.selection: All chapters of Matthew, Mark, Luke and John in four eBible HTML packages. Include a verse ID only when the displayed number is a single number equal to that ID in every edition and text remains. Remove chapter headings, navigation, section headings, references, superscript verse numbers and footnotes. Count all remaining Unicode letter/mark tokens after NFC and casefold, retaining internal apostrophes and lexical saltillo. Run a second normalization without combining marks and report type as well as token counts. Count tl, tli, tle, chi and chih as literal ending sequences, including complete tokens that match the sequence.

published_label_assay.interpretation: With printed 2013 spellings, the cactus and agave already conflict under this symbol rule. Harmonizing the final i/y permits nine partial assignments, all eliminated by the original fish reading. With the later fish reading RF1b has one assignment at four examples and predicts the fifth published spelling exactly. Some choices of ZL alternatives give two or three solutions for all five, and other choices give zero. IT2a gives zero after adding its fish reading in all tested settings. These are published examples chosen before this audit but used by the underlying authors to develop the hypothesis. A correspondence calculation on them says little about predicting a new passage or locating a dialect.
published_label_assay.location_caveat: The p.75 fish panel has the two Pisces fish and is f70v2 in the current foliation. The legacy Stolfi interlinear label list attaches the corresponding word to the central star. An exclusive relation to the fish is unresolved. The cube is f102v2 at locus 6 across the compared pinned editions.
published_label_assay.method: Use the named labels from the authors’ published argument in order cactus, agave, fish-associated, cube, paddle-shaped root. Read the exact pinned ZL3b/IT2a/RF1b locus strings. At ZL alternatives, enumerate both stated values in brackets. Split EVA with ch as one symbol and every other visible symbol in these words as a single character. For each pair in order, exhaustively enumerate all nonempty output-string prefixes for newly encountered symbols, reusing the same output whenever a symbol reappears. Allow homophones, any nonempty output length and unaligned boundaries. Compare printed spellings, a terminal i/y harmonization sensitivity, and the reported later fish reading with accent marks removed. Test the alternate cube gloss atlan separately. Counts are partial mappings satisfying constraints on these examples.

detail.statement: Tucker and Talbert used final tl and chi and several names borrowed between languages to propose a central or northern Mexican dialect. Both written endings occur in all four Gospel books of the Tetelcingo Morelos, Northern Puebla and Southeastern Puebla editions examined in 3,738 matching verse numbers. The Isthmus-Mecayapan edition and Highland Puebla treebank also have chi, with zero literal final tl in these samples. Five published Voynich label examples admit a partial mapping under spelling harmonization and a revised fish reading in some transliterations. The exact 2013 readings fail the same consistency model. The available observations leave the historical variety and its speaker community undetermined.

statement: Use the project’s existing g_self_citation implementation at its default seed 2, with the public ZL practice training pages as its only input for word and glyph weights. Its initial stock is five draws from the 200 most frequent training forms, and each output copies uniformly from up to the last 40 items and makes zero, one, one or two attempts at a glyph change in EVA-basic. Replacement, insertion and deletion use the existing thresholds and learned marginal glyph frequencies. Run it on one dummy page of 1,000 rows of 12 placeholder slots, so it never resets its memory or reads an actual line number, paragraph position or page identity inside its loop. Concatenate the outputs and let the scorer put the continuous stream into the manuscript line layout. Freeze the sampler settings and use seed 2 unless rejected by screening of markers and all contiguous four-word sequences, including those spanning transport rows. Seed 2 passed the guard before any scoring of the sample. There is no edit targeting a line or its place on the page. Public controls independently permute the same stock within page, with and without fixed lengths at every slot.

detail.check: Recover plan.json byte-for-byte from reproduction.plan_json_bytes and both frozen scripts in one scratch directory. From the repository root on PYTHONPATH, run right_context.py calibrate, then right_context.py evaluate. Check the plan, script, calibration and evaluation digests and tables; run verify_right_context.py for the independent entropy/sampling audit. A next test should calibrate contextual and word-position conditioning on new contrasts before any manuscript use, particularly investigating the repeatable us/um reversal. All weights, cutoffs, contrasts and seed lists in this experiment remain frozen.
findings: On the primary calibration condition (exact-left matching, full matched-pool replacement), all 30 paired trials favor the genuine candidate under bilateral JS. The automatically chosen cutoff is 0.13251493881410006, with strict loss < cutoff-1e-12 acceptance. It accepts 15/30 genuine candidates and 1/30 calibration decoys. This empirical calibration count does not establish a population error rate.

With the same fixed rule on evaluation text beyond the control prefix used in P-L1-007, bilateral JS gives 24 genuine wins and 6 decoy wins across 30 repeats (six language/contrast strata, five seeds each). Its frozen cutoff accepts 14/30 genuine candidates and 0/30 decoys. Left-only JS and the inherited eight-rule prose loss each tie all 30 times and accept 5/30 candidates of each origin at their separately calibrated cutoffs.

Evaluation wins by contrast: English in/is 4/5, an/at 5/5; Latin re/ra 5/5, us/um 0/5; Italian la/le 5/5 and ra/ri 5/5. Seeds reuse the same text and are not independent language samples. The us/um reversal is stable under all five fixed seeds.

At half matched-pool replacement with exact-left matching, bilateral JS gives 26 genuine wins and 4 decoy wins; the cutoff accepts 11/30 genuine candidates and 1/30 decoys. These are secondary sensitivity results with the full-coverage calibration cutoff retained.

Matching only word-boundary positions, without equal incoming contexts, reduces full-coverage evaluation performance to 16 genuine and 14 decoy wins. The frozen bilateral cutoff accepts 8/30 genuine candidates and 0/30 decoys. This limits transfer beyond the primary matched-left design.

Matching both incoming and outgoing glyph counts forces equal left and right probability distributions for X and Z, so both JS scores tie. All 30 full-coverage evaluation trials and all 25 supported half-coverage evaluation trials behave this way. Five half-coverage trials fail the preregistered minimum support; exclusions are retained in the tables.

Under the same frozen cutoff, bilateral JS accepts no candidates among 118 scored letter/component combinations on three untouched natural streams and no candidates among 2368 combinations on sixty new first-order direct-emission streams. All sixty chains emit one glyph at a time without a fusion operation. The corresponding left-only JS cutoff accepts 45 generated-text combinations across 31 of the 60 streams; inherited eight-rule raw-loss cutoff accepts none. These finite and dependent controls do not prove a zero general false-positive rate.

A separate entropy-form implementation verifies 1440 paired JS values and 4972 negative-control JS values, with maximum absolute discrepancy 9.43689570931383e-16 and identical cutoff decisions. Independent cumulative-table sampling regenerates all sixty chain hashes; hashes of the three natural streams also match.
limitations: The evaluated objects are planted substitutions in normalized public natural text, not manuscript signs. No manuscript result or decipherment claim is made.

Six selected contrasts in three languages are the evidence units; five seeds per contrast are robustness repetitions. Training, calibration and evaluation use different blocks/windows from the same pinned books, not independent authors or genres.

The empirical negative cutoff pools thirty related calibration trials. Zero observed decoy/negative acceptances in evaluation does not bound the population false-positive rate without additional assumptions.

The new statistic uses normalized raw adjacency distributions including spaces, while the inherited score uses trimmed incidence entries. The baseline here is a separately calibrated raw loss, not the paper's original five-percent rank criterion.

Partial planting and grammar can change the residual component contexts. The stable us/um reversal and weaker word-position-only result show that adding right context does not eliminate this confounding.
All matching, support, seed, cutoff and sample-window rules were frozen publicly before their corresponding evaluation. No outcome-driven retuning was performed.

plan.manuscript_gate: Do not evaluate manuscript candidate triplets in this experiment. A positive result on these selected controls would still need new language/text and scan validation.

scripts.reproduce.py:
"""Extract the submitted protocol and reproduce byte-identical Windows outputs.

Run from the repository root: python reproduce.py STEP_JSON SCRATCH_DIRECTORY
"""
import hashlib
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys

submission = json.loads(Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
scratch = Path(sys.argv[2]).resolve()
scratch.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
(scratch/'plan.json').write_bytes(submission['reproduction']['plan_json_bytes'].encode('utf-8'))
for name, script in submission['reproduction']['scripts'].items():
    (scratch/name).write_bytes(script.encode('utf-8'))
env = dict(os.environ)
env['PYTHONPATH'] = str(Path.cwd()) + os.pathsep + env.get('PYTHONPATH', '')
def digest(name):
    actual = hashlib.sha256((scratch/name).read_bytes()).hexdigest()
    assert actual == submission['output_digests'][name], (name, actual)
for name in ('plan.json', 'right_context.py', 'original_triplet.py'):
    digest(name)
for command, output in [(['right_context.py', 'calibrate'], 'calibration.json'),
                         (['right_context.py', 'evaluate'], 'evaluation.json'),
                         (['verify_right_context.py'], 'verification.json')]:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-X', 'utf8', str(scratch/command[0]), *command[1:]],
                   env=env, check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    # Original outputs used native Windows CRLF. Preserve their published raw hashes
    # across operating systems; the frozen measurement code is left untouched.
    path = scratch/output
    path.write_bytes(path.read_bytes().replace(b'\r\n', b'\n').replace(b'\n', b'\r\n'))
    digest(output)
    print(output, 'exact digest matched', flush=True)

"""Extract the submitted protocol and reproduce byte-identical Windows outputs.

Run from the repository root: python reproduce.py STEP_JSON SCRATCH_DIRECTORY
"""
import hashlib
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys

submission = json.loads(Path(sys.argv[1]).read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
scratch = Path(sys.argv[2]).resolve()
scratch.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
(scratch/'plan.json').write_bytes(submission['reproduction']['plan_json_bytes'].encode('utf-8'))
for name, script in submission['reproduction']['scripts'].items():
    (scratch/name).write_bytes(script.encode('utf-8'))
env = dict(os.environ)
env['PYTHONPATH'] = str(Path.cwd()) + os.pathsep + env.get('PYTHONPATH', '')
def digest(name):
    actual = hashlib.sha256((scratch/name).read_bytes()).hexdigest()
    assert actual == submission['output_digests'][name], (name, actual)
for name in ('plan.json', 'right_context.py', 'original_triplet.py'):
    digest(name)
for command, output in [(['right_context.py', 'calibrate'], 'calibration.json'),
                         (['right_context.py', 'evaluate'], 'evaluation.json'),
                         (['verify_right_context.py'], 'verification.json')]:
    subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-X', 'utf8', str(scratch/command[0]), *command[1:]],
                   env=env, check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL)
    # Original outputs used native Windows CRLF. Preserve their published raw hashes
    # across operating systems; the frozen measurement code is left untouched.
    path = scratch/output
    path.write_bytes(path.read_bytes().replace(b'\r\n', b'\n').replace(b'\n', b'\r\n'))
    digest(output)
    print(output, 'exact digest matched', flush=True)

The score averages Jensen-Shannon divergences between candidate/first-component left contexts and candidate/second-component right contexts. With exact left-context matching, genuine candidates beat decoys in 24/30 evaluation repeats across six contrasts; the left-only and inherited eight-rule losses tie in every repeat. The frozen bilateral cutoff accepts 14 genuine candidates and zero decoys. However, us/um fails in all five repeats, word-position-only matching gives just 16/30 genuine wins, and exact matching of both sides forces ties. statement: One procedure, fitted on the public practice pages only. A scribe writes a book page by page. At each word: (1) with small probability he copies the word just written or a word from the line above, varying its ending by one glyph; 6 times in 10 the variant is a shape his tables do not hold at all. When copying from the line above he prefers a source word that does not also sit four lines back. (2) Otherwise he reaches for tables of how words sit: a successor table keyed on the last glyph of the previous word, a line-opening table, and a line-ending table keyed on the last glyph of the previous line's last word; paragraph-opening first lines follow their own tables. Words he already wrote on this page are 2.5 times likelier to be written again, words from the last 15 pages somewhat likelier. (3) When no table covers the place, 9 times in 100 he writes a word of his own devising, drawn from a fitted glyph chain; otherwise the chain itself is the fallback. Tables are counts from the public pages only; no rule names a target pattern.

visual_test.exposure: The organizer knew the source mapping from the catalogue. The readers saw anonymous IDs and a recognizable manuscript visual style, and had earlier general exposure to other manuscript tasks. They reported no use of the identity map or each other’s scores. They are two instances of one model family; these comparisons are a reproducible descriptive assessment, with a separate human review needed for stronger visual claims.

features.B1: Dominant elongated lateral root axis markedly asymmetric in the illustrated orientation
features.B2: At least two recurved root tips turning back upward toward the crown
features.B3: Repeated separate branchlets descending from a shared broad horizontal root span
features.C1: Broad compact crown with several blunt rounded edge lobes
features.C2: At least one traceable exposed blade with at least two pronounced rounded sinuses
features.C3: Three or more fine stalks converging on a common crown junction
features.C4: Multiple overlapping blades whose separate boundaries can be traced

visual_test.method: Two model reader instances scored the same anonymous fragments independently using Y/N/U with U for a missing, obscured or unresolved feature. Reference remained visible to both. Per region and per reader report number of equal codes and number of jointly known codes. A descriptive crown ranking needs at least two comparable features. The eight local lower figures include damaged or faint shapes. Do not combine crown and root into a single anatomical claim.
outcomes: Fragment 35 shares both the broad blunt-lobed crown and the fan of fine converging stalks. Reader A also matches individual and overlapping blade traits; reader B could not reliably trace those reference traits through overlapping paint.

The spreading base on fragment 35 is pale and roughly balanced across its junction. The f35v main base is more strongly lateral and asymmetric, with groups of returning tips and a repeated array of downward branchlets. The completeness of some edges on fragment 35 remains unclear.

Fragment 33 has more visible deep recesses on individual blades than many neighboring pieces. Its overall outline and descending base give a different combination. Several lowermost controls appear faint or overlap traces, which limits how much a low match count tells us.
visual_test.sampling: All 16 plant fragments indexed on f89r2 (33–38 and 40–49), in same-page controls. Reference is f35v crown and base in two cropped tiers. The readers saw anonymous IDs and a recognizable manuscript visual style, and had earlier general exposure to other manuscript tasks. They reported no use of the identity map or each other’s scores. They are two instances of one model family; these comparisons are a reproducible descriptive assessment, with a separate human review needed for stronger visual claims.

features.B1: Dominant elongated lateral root axis markedly asymmetric in the illustrated orientation
features.B2: At least two recurved root tips turning back upward toward the crown
features.B3: Repeated separate branchlets descending from a shared broad horizontal root span
features.C1: Broad compact crown with several blunt rounded edge lobes
features.C2: At least one traceable exposed blade with at least two pronounced rounded sinuses
features.C3: Three or more fine stalks converging on a common crown junction
features.C4: Multiple overlapping blades whose separate boundaries can be traced

visual_test.method: Two model reader instances scored the same anonymous fragments independently using Y/N/U with U for a missing, obscured or unresolved feature. Reference remained visible to both. outcomes: Fragment 35 shares both the broad blunt-lobed crown and the fan of fine converging stalks. Reader A also matches individual and overlapping blade traits; reader B could not reliably trace those reference traits through overlapping paint.

The spreading base on fragment 35 is pale and roughly balanced across its junction. The f35v main base is more strongly lateral and asymmetric, with groups of returning tips and a repeated array of downward branchlets. The completeness of some edges on fragment 35 remains unclear.

Fragment 33 has more visible deep recesses on individual blades than many neighboring pieces. Its overall outline and descending base give a different combination. Several lowermost controls appear faint or overlap traces, which limits how much a low match count tells us.
visual_test.sampling: All 16 plant fragments indexed on f89r2 (33–38 and 40–49), in same-page controls. Reference is f35v crown and base in two cropped tiers. Grayscale images omit surrounding text and mask recognisable label bands where separable. Partial neighboring traces persist in tight zones, especially fragments 37/38 and 46/47. statement: One general procedure — a scribe's shop — fitted on the PUBLIC CURRIER B PAGES ONLY; no rule of it mentions m or line endings. What it fits from those pages: (1) positional word tables — the successor word given the last glyph of the word before it, the words that open a line, and the words that end a line given the last glyph of the previous line's last word (paragraph-opening lines keep their own tables); (2) a glyph chain over the line (2-4 glyph history, restarted at each line start) used where no table covers the place and as the fallback; (3) the line-length distribution; (4) memory — words already written on the page are 2.5 times likelier to be written again, words from the last 15 written pages somewhat likelier; (5) copying — with small probability the scribe copies the word just written or a word from the line above (preferring a source absent four lines back), varying its ending by one glyph, 6 times in 10 landing on a shape the tables do not hold. The scribe knows where each line begins and ends; every line is written whole. All counts come from the public Currier B training pages; the hidden pages are never touched. Statistics fitted: word successor and line-position word frequencies by last glyph, glyph-transition counts, line lengths, page and recent-page word reuse. Practice split: the line-final to mid-line ratio reaches 22.1 against the line of 10, and beats the within-line shuffle null (p <= 0.01, 199 perms).

justi_printing_audit.locus: German translation p. 4, digital PDF p. 489, Chapter II opening
justi_printing_audit.scope: Exploratory exact-repeat requirement for the literal comma-separated German printing. Allow unresolved EVA glyphs to match in place. The check does not supply Herrmann’s omitted choices or resolve how to segment the more variable Pahlavi source names.

protocol.alignments: Primary maximum over 28 rotations and both directions. Secondary scan-cue sensitivity uses clockwise starts f69v.8, f69v.9 and f69v.10 fixed by P-L4-025. It is exploratory because a ring gap need not establish the beginning of the radial roster.
protocol.extra_sensitivity: Before scoring, add a secondary full-rotation sensitivity that exchanges names only within joint classes of length and initial symbol. It preserves the earlier initial-equality result exactly. Report the number of distinct possible label assignments in each direction, including degenerate classes.
protocol.historical_normalization: Use the spelling in each named source, join multiword labels without spaces, casefold, remove accent marks, and retain alphabetic characters including written ʾ and ʿ. For the scholarly Arabic romanization, collapse th, dh, kh, sh and gh to single units. Keep prefixes, connectors and first-name editorial restorations as printed. No stripping or substitution optimized from EVA readings.
protocol.justi_audit: Check separately whether Justi’s 1868 source cited by Herrmann gives an unambiguous complete ordered 28-vector in the print. No reconstruction or inserted missing label goes into the primary three-list comparison.
protocol.nulls: Use 3,999 uniform whole-label permutations separately in the named list and the Voynich list. Exchange only labels of equal normalized length and keep undefined labels at their observed slots. Retain the same set of alignments for observed and shuffled scores. Primary combined p is the larger of the two permutation p-values. Apply Holm correction across the three sources and two paired transcriptions. Show both single-null probabilities and report three-start sensitivity separately.
protocol.prior_exposure: The prior public reports and some comparator names were already known. This plan fixes the new score before calculating any prefix alignment. Names and radial loci come from already documented editions.
sources: Ragep et al. al-Muiniyya II.3[11] Arabic names in scholarly transcription
Sela et al. Henry Bate Pal.lat.1407 §5.2 table, first name per numbered row
protocol.synthetic_check: Circularly rotate/reverse a bijective relabeling of every historical list. Re-run the score at 0 percent and 2 percent independent symbol replacement with eight seeds per list and 999 null permutations per side. This checks sensitivity in an idealized prefix-preserving symbolic encoding.
protocol.targeted_check: Separately test an intact shared-head diagnostic with the three fixed clockwise starts: al-Muiniyya positions 22–25 (Saʿd), Henry Bate table positions 22–23 (Sade), and Anklesaria positions 25 and 28 (Kaht). Record the initial two EVA units of each required locus. This direct necessity only applies to a consistent prefix-preserving encoding of those particular names.
protocol.threshold: Primary score is the Pearson association across the 378 unordered pairs of sector positions between their initial runs of shared symbols in each list. Score prefix depth beyond the first unit as max(0, min(4, prefix_length) - 1), so a first-unit match alone contributes zero. Skip any pair with an uncertain Voynich label. An alignment with zero variance is uninformative.
protocol.voynich: The 28 radial loci f69v.4–31, in Zandbergen–Landini clockwise locus order. Use ZL and Takahashi as paired primary transcriptions. Keep each locus as one label, segment each written word separately with eva-basic, then concatenate its units. Exclude an uncertain label from the prefix score without moving its slot.

detail.statement: Across 56 circular alignments, shared prefixes longer than one EVA unit do not match the ordered Anklesaria, al-Tusi, or Henry Bate lists beyond the same-length permutation controls. The lowest combined primary p-value is 0.70675 before adjustment, and all six Holm-adjusted p-values are 1.0. The three clockwise scan-cued starts and the sensitivity that also fixes initial classes yield no positive score against both nulls. The chosen test detects 24/24 clean and 24/24 noisy synthetic prefix-preserving encodings of the same lists at p ≤ 0.01. The four consecutive Arabic entries sharing the three written letters سعد require a four-locus common three-unit prefix under direct grapheme substitution. Each of the 56 alignments conflicts with at least two clear units in both primary transliterations. The literal Justi Chapter II German print branches from the Greater Bundahishn list and contains consecutive Parviz entries. An exact repeated-label rule has no compatible adjacent pair in ZL or Takahashi, with one ambiguous pair in RF. The published 20 proposed Herrmann pairs are omitted in the source, leaving that proposal without a recoverable full mapping for this page.

protocol.alignments: Primary maximum over 28 rotations and both directions. Secondary scan-cue sensitivity uses clockwise starts f69v.8, f69v.9 and f69v.10 fixed by P-L4-025. It is exploratory because a ring gap need not establish the beginning of the radial roster.
protocol.extra_sensitivity: Before scoring, add a secondary full-rotation sensitivity that exchanges names only within joint classes of length and initial symbol. It preserves the earlier initial-equality result exactly. Report the number of distinct possible label assignments in each direction, including degenerate classes.
protocol.historical_normalization: Use the spelling in each named source, join multiword labels without spaces, casefold, remove accent marks, and retain alphabetic characters including written ʾ and ʿ. For the scholarly Arabic romanization, collapse th, dh, kh, sh and gh to single units. Keep prefixes, connectors and first-name editorial restorations as printed. No stripping or substitution optimized from EVA readings.
protocol.justi_audit: Check separately whether Justi’s 1868 source cited by Herrmann gives an unambiguous complete ordered 28-vector in the print. No reconstruction or inserted missing label goes into the primary three-list comparison.
protocol.nulls: Use 3,999 uniform whole-label permutations separately in the named list and the Voynich list. Exchange only labels of equal normalized length and keep undefined labels at their observed slots. Retain the same set of alignments for observed and shuffled scores. Primary combined p is the larger of the two permutation p-values. Apply Holm correction across the three sources and two paired transcriptions. Show both single-null probabilities and report three-start sensitivity separately.
protocol.prior_exposure: The prior public reports and some comparator names were already known. This plan fixes the new score before calculating any prefix alignment. Names and radial loci come from already documented editions.

protocol.synthetic_check: Circularly rotate/reverse a bijective relabeling of every historical list. protocol.targeted_check: Separately test an intact shared-head diagnostic with the three fixed clockwise starts: al-Muiniyya positions 22–25 (Saʿd), Henry Bate table positions 22–23 (Sade), and Anklesaria positions 25 and 28 (Kaht). protocol.threshold: Primary score is the Pearson association across the 378 unordered pairs of sector positions between their initial runs of shared symbols in each list. statement: Hannig's 2020 Voynich-to-Hebrew table re-transcribed from scratch out of the PDF's embedded Voynich-1.01 font (the Voynich column is PUA text, U+F0xx = the v101 letter, so no eyeballing was needed) and scored as a frozen substitution key on the gc transliteration: practice FAIL on all five criteria, savings -0.240, and the two rows that C.13 prints for <k> and <h> are pixel-identical duplicates carrying two different Hebrew values each, so the table is internally inconsistent before any scoring. The consonant map agrees letter-for-letter with fleet-corpora's reading of the same table (their held-out savings -0.260, my practice savings -0.237 for that same map), which is a clean replication of a negative result; the only difference here is that his own two-way tables read the vowel markers as matres lectionis (<i> = י, <c> = ו), which changes little (savings -0.240, coverage 0.26-0.43 against 0.36-0.48 for the null-vowel map). All five criteria fail for every vowel reading tried, and the kill tests show why: word-order-shuffled, within-word-shuffled and random-glyph decoys decode no worse than the real pages, so the key is too free to be evidence. Note for the desk: criterion (c) needs 3 confirmed anchors and the record has 1 (4 of the 5 are disputed), so no key submission can reach a full PASS until the swarm confirms anchors.

key.json.notes: Frozen table, no search. Two glyph rows in C.13 are pixel-identical duplicates of another row and give one glyph two Hebrew values: <k> is listed for both ט and ת, <h> for both ק and כ (rendered cells compared at 600 dpi: IoU 1.000). The book's own two-way tables resolve this the other way round - ט is assigned to <K> and <k>, ק to <H> and <h>, while ת is assigned only to <k> and כ only to <h> - so the exclusive value is kept: k=ת, h=כ, and ט and ק end up with no glyph of their own. Final forms are written as base letters because the pinned Hebrew corpora are normalized with finals folded (refcorpus.HEB_FINALS) and pointing removed. The vowel markers are read the way his Hebrew-to-Voynich table reads them: <i> = י (vocalic yod, also the j of the imperfect) and <c> = ו (vocalic vav, u in the middle of a word); <o>, his 'Hauptvokal, Platzhalter für Vokal', is given no Hebrew equivalent anywhere in the book and is left unmapped (a null). Also left unmapped: <*> (End-k, 'noch nicht identifiziert'), regular צ ('noch nicht identifiziert'), the ligatures <ý> and <.>, and <\>. The same table with <i> and <c> as nulls instead was also scored on the practice split; the numbers are in the experiment summary.
key.json.source: Rainer Hannig (2020), Voynich-Hebräisch: Der Weg zur Entzifferung, self-published PDF (rainer-hannig.com): the correspondence table in section C.13 and its continuations C.14-C.22, cross-checked against the two-way alphabet tables at the end of the book. The Voynich column was read out of the PDF's embedded Voynich-1.01 font (PUA U+F0xx = the ASCII code of the v101 letter), so the codes below are v101 codes and the key runs on the 'gc' transliteration.

limits: One analyst examined selected examples after reading the existing notes and catalogue descriptions. These are unblinded exploratory readings, not independent blinded ratings or statistical classification accuracy.

Dating is established through the holding institutions' records or image metadata, independently of visual resemblance to Voynich. Nearby date statements alone do not establish a line of transmission or a common workshop.

The next discriminating check is the visible construction of its projection and grip, not whether an oval can be placed near a body.

Green's authored discussion of this manuscript at https://remedianetwork.wordpress.com/2015/10/13/crafting-a-written-science-of-surgery-the-first-european-surgical-texts/ and the plate list for her book, Making Women's Medicine Masculine, figures 3.2-3.3, https://toc.library.ethz.ch/objects/pdf/z01_978-0-19-921149-4_01.pdf.
laud96v.observation: Round/pear-shaped cups recur at limbs, shoulder/neck and the torso of seated recipients, with another person manipulating an implement. The bottom panel shows repeated ovals on a front-facing torso. The series supplies multiple examples of the illustrator's cup convention, but these panels belong to one manuscript and are not independent historical samples.
laud96v.reference: Same manuscript, f96v, three illustrated panels in the left column

morgan_bladder_staff.date: Bologna, c.1270, as catalogued by the holding library; substantially earlier than the proposed Voynich milieu
morgan_bladder_staff.identification_support: The library calls the terminal a bladder on a stick and the figure a fool. This is a control for shape specificity, not a proposed identity for the f80r person.
morgan_bladder_staff.observation: A seated figure grips a long narrow rod with a round orange terminal while the other hand raises a broad bowl to the mouth. The rod extends much farther than the terminal's diameter and the grip is remote from the bulb. It is therefore a poor constructional match for f80r, despite supplying a nonmedical round-object-and-stem silhouette.
morgan_bladder_staff.reference: Morgan Library & Museum, MS G.38.II, f47r, historiated initial D

morgan_cup.date: France, perhaps Rouen, c.1440-1450, as catalogued by the holding library
morgan_cup.identification_support: The holding library explicitly identifies the occupational scene as cupping.
morgan_cup.observation: A clothed attendant stands behind a seated, partly undressed recipient. One hand steadies the shoulder and the other applies a small rounded implement to the upper back. Its applied edge is substantially occluded by hands and body. There is no separately traceable long nozzle. This is a distinct manuscript example, though selected for its known cupping scene rather than sampled at random.
morgan_cup.reference: Morgan Library & Museum, MS M.165, f24r

morgan_pitcher.date: Paris, c.1418, as catalogued by the holding library
morgan_pitcher.identification_support: The library cautiously identifies the action as pouring water (?) from a pitcher, and marks the bathing scene with a question mark. Those qualifications are retained. This is the reused P-L4-038 bathing control.
morgan_pitcher.observation: The marginal bather holds a rounded vessel above the shoulder. A curved line descends toward the head separately from the vessel's body. Its elevated grip and stream differ from the lowered f80r item. This is an ordinary bathing comparison; it has no medical operation identified in the catalogue.
morgan_pitcher.reference: Morgan Library & Museum, MS M.919, f117r, right margin

target.observation: The bent arm reaches behind the waist. Fingers overlap the upper/right side of an oval outline. A small pointed extension emerges at its lower left, with parchment between its end and the figure's body. The other hand is raised with open fingers. I cannot trace an unambiguous open mouth, bore or separate transverse stop. An enlarged JPEG interpolates the original small drawing and supplies no additional optical resolution.
target.reference: Yale, Beinecke MS 408, f80r, upper row, second figure from the left

wellcome_clyster.date: The manuscript is catalogued Early 15th Century; the coloured miniature is a pasted inset whose attachment date is not separately established here
wellcome_clyster.identification_support: The holding library identifies the scene as administration of a clyster. This source was already in P-L4-038 and is used here as a reused positive control.
wellcome_clyster.observation: A separate attendant holds an apparatus behind a bent/kneeling recipient. The thin connecting part reaches the recipient's rear. The round body, narrowed connection and separate operator make a useful comparison for a reservoir-and-tube construction. They do not duplicate the isolated f80r object and same-person grip.

step.json.statement: Two cupping manuscripts, Bodleian Laud Misc. 724 ff96r-v (c.1400) and Morgan M.165 f24r (c.1440-1450), add a medical comparison in which rounded objects act on the outside of the body. The Laud lower-left scene on f96r includes a cup at the lower back or hip. This is a useful control for the proximity argument, but its visible contact, separate attendant and repeated cups differ from f80r. The f80r oval has a short pointed extension and a visible gap to its holder's body; neither a broad cup mouth nor a narrow open cannula is resolved. A pitcher and a bladder-on-stick provide nonmedical controls for rounded held objects. None of these selected scenes identifies the f80r item. The next discriminating check is the visible construction of its projection and grip, not whether an oval can be placed near a body.

sources: Beinecke MS 408, f100r, canvas 1006248. The drawing and its label: https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006248/880,600,340,560/full/0/default.jpg (drawing plus label); the label alone at https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006248/950,1010,200,140/full/0/default.jpg.

ZL 3b locus f100r.8 (pinned data/raw/ZL3b-n.txt) gives soity for this label; the eleven short labels of the upper two registers of f100r are f100r.1..11 and their left-to-right order on the scan was checked directly (f100r.1 chosaroshol, f100r.2 sochorcfhy, f100r.3 otear are the three labels of the top row, left to right).

Arthur O. Tucker and Rexford H. Talbert, 2013, A Preliminary Analysis of the Botany, Zoology, and Mineralogy of the Voynich Manuscript, HerbalGram 100:74-89, https://web.archive.org/web/20150226041323/http://cms.herbalgram.org/herbalgram/issue100/HG100-voynich-online.pdf. p. 76: 'plant No. 8 of the 16 plants on folio 100r; this is obviously a cactus pad or fruit, i.e., Opuntia spp., quite possibly Opuntia ficus-indica (L.) Mill. (Cactaceae)... Thus, [glyph] is quite easily transliterated as nashtli, a variant of nochtli, the Nahuatl (Aztec) name for the fruit of the prickly pear cactus or the cactus itself'. The appendix entry repeats it under Cactaceae (p. 79).

The same article's plant No. 4 on folio 100r is read as maguoey (maguey, Agave atrovirens); its inline glyph image matches the label ZL gives as f100r.4 chofary in shape sequence and in position on the page, which is what fixes their plant numbering to the ZL locus numbers (checked on the same scan: https://collections.library.yale.edu/iiif/2/1006248/1330,90,420,200/full/0/default.jpg).
detail.statement: UNCERTAIN; here is what I checked. On the scan, the label ZL transcribes as soity (f100r.8) stands at the lower right of a single drawing: a flattened oval green body, widest above and tapering below into a narrow neck and a reddish-brown taproot, with short stiff projections spaced along both margins and a few wavy hair-like lines on the left edge, and two small dots on the surface. Of the sixteen drawings on the folio this is the one that most reads as a prickly-pear pad, so Tucker and Talbert's 'plant No. 8' and this drawing appear to be the same object. Their numbering is not defined in the article, so I pinned it two ways: their inline glyph image for the No. 4 name maguoey matches the shape and position of the label ZL gives as f100r.4 chofary, and their inline glyph image for nashtli matches the shape sequence of this label (a 2-like s, a loop o, a tall middle glyph, and a final descender), so No. N = f100r.N. What is against it: the projections along the margin are drawn the way this scribe draws leaf teeth elsewhere on the same page, and a flattened pad that narrows into a neck and a taproot is not how Opuntia pads are drawn in the 16th-century Mexican sources Tucker and Talbert compare with; the pale dome ringed by radiating leaflets two drawings to the left (f100r.7) is at least as good a candidate for a bristled fruit. There is one published identification here, not two, and the Nahuatl reading of the label is the authors' own proposal rather than an independent identification of the drawing. Exposure: I read Tucker and Talbert's claims for f100r before looking at the scan, so this is not a blind round; it is a check of whether their claim survives looking, which for the pad it narrowly does.
detail.title: UNCERTAIN: f100r plant 8, a spiny flattened pad with the label soity, which Tucker and Talbert read as nashtli (nochtli, prickly pear)

step.json.statement: At main commit 50274c2ac760189465c12ca87606f7c396a18d8c, python -X utf8 -m vs facts exits successfully with no output although the registry contains 22 facts. All 22 use detail.spec; facts.battery selects only detail.metric and therefore returns an empty list. In an isolated mixed fixture the same path evaluates the legacy fact and silently omits both a passing and a failing DSL fact. A scratch dispatcher that retains both schemas and gives spec precedence restores coverage using the existing evaluators. The omission is in the local advisory command: static call-site inspection and a synthetic red-team control do not support a claim that authoritative scoring or language-family power is affected.

synthetic_control_results.notes: The diagnostic reimplements published #348 settings where specified. It fits a separate rank-five NMF on each synthetic reconstruction of the eligible training layout. Unplanted backgrounds use the pinned generator and do not use hand labels. Terms are generated using the real training-only vocabulary; test words are used only to specify the public certain-token layout. No manuscripts were scored. A correct synthetic assignment is a margin above 1e-12.
